title: 1  Line Search Methods
text:
1.1 Sufficient Decrease Condition
The line search methods choose a direction \(\mathbf{p}_k\) and search along this direction for next point hoping the function value decree, and continue this process until converge. In general, we hope to find the step length s.t. \[
\min_{\alpha>0}f(\mathbf{x}_k+\alpha\mathbf{p}_k)
\]
For line search methods, the algorithm generally has two major steps:
We first discuss generally a descent direction, then in details about step length selection.
Once the descent direction has been selected, we still need to pick up a appropriate step length \(\alpha\).
In the inexact line search methods, we need certain condition that stop the iteration of finidng \(\alpha\). The simplest choice would be just require a decrease in function value, i.e. \(f(\mathbf{x}_k + \alpha_k\mathbf{p_k})< f(\mathbf{x_k})\). However, this condition is not sufficient to ensure the convergence to a local minimizer.
The Example 1.1 shows that the too small function value drop should be avoid otherwise the algotihem would not be efficient.
To avoid this issue, a sufficient decrease condition can be imposed. As the name suggested, the condition imposed the the drop of function value for a specific chosed step length should be suffificently large.
One popular measure of sufficient decrease is the Armijo condition, which state as follow
Figure 1.1 shows the acceptable region of the Armijo line search.
Figure 1.1: Sufficient-decrease (Armijo) condition: \(\phi(\alpha)=f(\mathbf{x}_k+\alpha\mathbf{p}_k)\) (blue), the tangent at \(\alpha=0\) with slope \(\phi^\prime(0)=\nabla^{\mathsf T}f_k\,\mathbf{p}_k\) (dotted), and the sufficient-decrease line \(l(\alpha)=f(\mathbf{x}_k)+c_1\alpha\,\nabla^{\mathsf T}f_k\,\mathbf{p}_k\) (dashed). Armijo accepts the step lengths where \(\phi(\alpha)\le l(\alpha)\) (shaded).
In practice, the Armijo condition can be satisified using Backtracing line search algorithm

title: 1  Line Search Methods
text:
Definition 1.2 (Armijo Condition) For \(\mathbf{x}_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and descent direction \(\mathbf{p}_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), step length \(\alpha_k\) satisfied Armijo condition if \[
f(\mathbf{x}_k+\alpha_k\mathbf{p}_k)\leq f(\mathbf{x}_k) + c_1\alpha_k\nabla^Tf(\mathbf{x}_k)\mathbf{p}_k,\quad \text{for some } c_1\in (0, 1)
\]







Idea behind



We can denote the LHS of the inequality in Definition 1.2 as a function of \(\alpha\) as \(\phi(\alpha)\), and the RHS as a linear function \(l(\alpha)\) with a negative slop \(c_1\nabla^Tf(\mathbf{x}_k)\mathbf{p}_k\). Note that this slop is between the horizontal line and the tangent line at \(\phi(0)\). The Armijo condition is thus requiring the selected step length drop the function value larger than a predifined linear function, which derease slower than the steepest local function drop.






Backtracking Algorithm
The idea of the backtracking line search is to start with a relatively large step length and shrink \(\alpha\) every iteration till the Armijo condition is satisfied.
import numpy as np
from numpy.typing import NDArray
from typing import Callable

def backtracking_search(
    f: Callable,
    gradf_xk: NDArray,
    xk: NDArray,
    pk: NDArray,
    alpha0: float,
    c1: float = 1e-4,
    tau: float = 0.5,
) -> float:
    """Step length search using Armijo backtracking methods

    Args:
        f (Callable): objective function
        gradf (Callable): gradient of objective function
        xk (NDArray): current position
        pk (NDArray): descent direction
        alpha0 (float): initial step length. Default to 1. 
        c1 (float): control variable for Armijo condition. Default to 1e-5
        tau (float): contraction coefficient for step length. Default to 0,5. 

    Returns:
        float: final step length
    """
    alpha = alpha0
    f_xk = f(xk)
    while f(xk + alpha * pk) > f_xk + c1 * alpha * np.dot(gradf_xk, pk):
        alpha = tau * alpha
    return alpha






Note




The initial guess of step length typically is 1, but might vary depens on \(\mathbf{p}_k\)
Require only function evaluation during the search
Will terminated in finite steps
The backtracking approach avoid too small step length as it star with large step and will usually stop before the step length becomes too small.



Though the Armijo condition ensure the sufficient decrease of the function value. However, the selected step length could be too small and leading to inefficient progress. The following curvature condition make sure the the step length would not be too short.

title: 1  Line Search Methods
text:
1.2 Curvature Condition

Definition 1.3 (Curvature Condition) For \(\mathbf{x}_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and descent direction \(\mathbf{p}_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\), step length \(\alpha_k\) satisfied curvature condition if \[
\nabla^Tf(\mathbf{x}_k+\alpha_k\mathbf{p}_k)\mathbf{p_k}\geq c_2\nabla f(\mathbb{x}_k),\quad c_2\in(c_1, 1)
\] \(c_1\) is the constant from Definition 1.2







Idea behind



Again if we consider \(\phi(\alpha) = f(\mathbf{x} + \alpha\mathbf{p})\) as a function if \(\alpha\). Then the LHS of the inequality in Definition 1.3 is \(\phi^\prime(\alpha_k)\), which is the slope of the tangent line at the accepted step length. Since the RHS is negative, the curvature condition requires the curvature of \(\phi\) at the accepted step length should be “flat” comparing to that at the starting point, which is measured by the coefficient \(c_2\). Thus, the accepted step length can not be too close to the staring point


Figure 1.2 shows the acceptable region satisfying the curvature condition.








Figure 1.2: Curvature condition: the accepted step lengths (shaded) are those where the slope \(\phi^\prime(\alpha)\ge c_2\,\phi^\prime(0)\) is flat enough, i.e. not too steeply negative. Short segments show the slope of \(\phi\) at the two ends of the accepted interval.





Combine the two condition together, we get the Wolf conditions

title: 1  Line Search Methods
text:
1.3 Wolf Condition

Definition 1.4 (Wolf Condition) For \(\mathbf{x}_k\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and descent direction \(\mathbf{p}_k\in\mathbb{R}\), step length \(\alpha_k\) satisfied Wolf condition if \[
\begin{aligned}
f(\mathbf{x}_k+\alpha_k\mathbf{p}_k)&\leq f(\mathbf{x}_k) + c_1\alpha_k\nabla^Tf(\mathbf{x}_k)\mathbf{p}_k\\
\nabla^Tf(\mathbf{x}_k+\alpha_k\mathbf{p}_k)\mathbf{p_k}&\geq c_2\nabla f(\mathbb{x}_k)
\end{aligned}
\] for some \(0<c_1<c_2<1\)







Note




If \(c_1\geq c_2\), the exsistance of Wolf condition might not be satisfied
The Wolf condition requires evaluations of both function and gradient values at each iteration



Figure 1.3 shows the acceptable region satisfying the Wolf condition, which is the intersection of the sufficient decrease and curvature conditions.








Figure 1.3: Wolf condition: the accepted region (green) is the intersection of the Armijo/sufficient-decrease region (\(\phi(\alpha)\le l(\alpha)\)) and the curvature region (\(\phi^\prime(\alpha)\ge c_2\phi^\prime(0)\)).





The Wolf condition can be strengthened to the strong Wolf condition.

Definition 1.5 (Strong Wolf Condition) Change the curvature condition in Definition 1.4 to \[
|\nabla^{\mathsf T}f(\mathbf{x}_k+\alpha_k\mathbf{p}_k)\mathbf{p}_k| \leq c_2\,|\nabla^{\mathsf T}f(\mathbf{x}_k)\mathbf{p}_k|
\]

This restrict too large positive slope, which is also away from minimum.

Line Search Algorithm Satisfying Wolf Condition
def wolf_search(
        f: Callable[[NDArray], float],
        gradf: Callable[[NDArray], NDArray],
        xk: NDArray,
        pk: NDArray,
        c1: float=1e-4,
        c2: float=0.9,
        max_iter: int=1000
) -> float:
    """wolf line search methods

    Args:
        f (Callable[[NDArray], float]): objective function
        gradf (Callable[[NDArray], float]): gradient of objective function
        xk (NDArray): current position for starting the line search
        pk (NDArray): current search direction
        c1 (float, optional): parameter for Amijor contion. Defaults to 1e-4.
        c2 (float, optional): parameter for curvature condition. Defaults to 0.9.
        max_iter(float, optional): maximum iteration of line search. Defaults to 1000.
    Returns:
        float: return the step length
    """    
    
    alpha = 1
    alpha_l = 0
    alpha_u = np.inf

    f_xk = f(xk)
    gradf_xk = gradf(xk)
    phi_prime_0 = np.dot(gradf_xk, pk)

    # check c1 < c2:
    if c1 > c2:
        raise ValueError("c1 must smaller than c2")
    
    # if the input search direction is not descent direction, just return
    if phi_prime_0 >= 0:
        return 1

    counter = 0
    while True:
        # break the line search if the iteration take to much
        if counter > max_iter:
            return alpha
        # if armijo condition not satisfied, shrink the upper bond of allowed step length
        if f(xk + alpha * pk) > f_xk + c1 * alpha * phi_prime_0:
            alpha_u = alpha

        else:

            # if armojo satsified but curvature condition is not, increase the lower bond of allowed step length
            if np.dot(gradf(xk + alpha * pk), pk) < c2 * phi_prime_0:
                alpha_l = alpha
            else:
                return alpha
        
        # if the Armijo condition has not been violated once, increase the lower bound
        if alpha_u < np.inf:
            alpha = (alpha_l + alpha_u) / 2
        else:
            alpha = 2 * alpha
        counter += 1

section: 1.4 Existence and Convergence of Line Search
text:
1.4 Existence and Convergence of Line Search
We now discuss when the step-length conditions can actually be satisfied.


Theorem 1.1 (Existence of Armijo Condition) If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is \(C^1\) and bounded below, then for a descent direction \(\mathbf{p}_k\) at \(\mathbf{x}_k\), there exists \(\alpha^\prime>0\) s.t. the Armijo condition is satisfied for \(\forall\alpha\in[0, \alpha_{\max}]\).
In addition, if \(\nabla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz continuous, then \[
\alpha^\prime = \frac{2(c_1-1)\,\nabla^{\mathsf T}f(\mathbf{x}_k)\mathbf{p}_k}{L\|\mathbf{p}_k\|^2}
\]


Remark 1.3. 

Notice that \(\phi(0)+c_1\alpha\phi^\prime(0)\) is a line go to unbounded below, thus \(l(\alpha)\) must intersect with \(\phi(\alpha)\), thus there exists \(\alpha_{\max}\) which is the smallest intersection, s.t. \(\alpha^\prime<\alpha_{\max}\) is the one we need.
To show the second part, can use inequality \[
f(\mathbf{y}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla^{\mathsf T}f(\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}) + \frac{L}{2}\|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\|^2
\]



Theorem 1.2 (Existence of Wolf Condition) If \(f\) is \(C^1\) and is bounded below, for a descent direction at \(\mathbf{x}_k\), then there exists an interval for \(\alpha_k\) s.t. the Wolf condition is satisfied.


Remark 1.4. 

The existence for Armijo condition show the exist interval bounded above by line \(l(\alpha)\), use Taylor’s theorem can show tangent line.
Continuity of \(f\) can show the existence of interval satisfying Wolf condition.

title: 2  Quasi Newton Methods
text:
2.1 Generic Approach of Quasi-Newton Methods
Newton Method: Require calculation of Hessian matrix \(H_{ij}=\frac{\partial^2f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\)
Steepest Descent: Find the descent direction using local quadratic approximation with identity matrix as Hessian. \[
\min_{\mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(\mathbf{x}_k)+\nabla f^T(\mathbf{x}_k)\mathbf{p}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{p}^TI\mathbf{p}
\]

title: 2  Quasi Newton Methods
text:
Quadratic Objective Function
The descent direction \(\mathbf{p}_k\) at each iteration is found by finding the minimizer of the following qudratic approximation of the objective function. \[
\min_{\mathbf{p}}f_k+\nabla f_k^T\mathbf{p} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{p}^TB_k\mathbf{p}
\]






Approximate Hessian \(B_k\)




symmetric (a Hessian matrix would be symmetric)
Positive definite (to make sure existence of minimizer)




Remark 2.1. The minimizer can be found as \(\mathbf{p}_k=-B^{-1}_k\nabla f_k\), which would be a descent direction if \(B_k\) is PD.







Note



Remark 2.1 can be verified using Remark 1.2.




Secant Condition
The idea of secant condition in quasi Newton method is to approximate the Hessian matrix with gradient difference. In 1D case, this is simply
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2f}{\mathrm{d}^2x}\approx\frac{\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}x}\right|_{x_{k+1}} - \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}x}\right|_{x_k}}{x_{k+1}-x_k}
\]
Generalized to multi-variable case, using Taylor expansion of \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1})\) \[
\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) \approx \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k) + \nabla ^2 f(\mathbf{x}_k)(\mathbf{x}_{k+1} - \mathbf{x}_k)
\] therefor, we can approximate the Hessian with matrix \(B_{k+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) satisfy the secant condition \[
\underbrace{\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) - \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)}_{\mathbf{y}_k} = B_{k+1}\underbrace{(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}-\mathbf{x}_k)}_{\mathbf{s}_k}
\]
The same secant condition can also be derived by matching the next-step model \(m_{k+1}(\mathbf{p}) = f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) + \nabla f_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{p} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{p}^{\mathsf T}B_{k+1}\mathbf{p}\) to the true gradient at the last two iterates: \[
\nabla m_{k+1}(0) = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}), \qquad \nabla m_{k+1}(-\alpha_k\mathbf{p}_k) = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)
\] \[
\Rightarrow \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}) + B_{k+1}(-\alpha_k\mathbf{p}_k) = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k) \Rightarrow B_{k+1}(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}-\mathbf{x}_k) = \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1})-\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)
\] From the Taylor expansion perspective, \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_{k+1})-\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k) = \nabla^2 f|_{\mathbf{x}^\ast}(\mathbf{x}_{k+1}-\mathbf{x}_k)\), so \(B_{k+1}\) is the multi-direction slope of the linear approximation of the gradient.


Positive Definite Condition
As we mentioned before, \(B_{k+1}\) has to be positive definite so that the quadratic objective function has minimizer and \(\mathbf{p}_k\) found is a descent direction. If the quasi Newton methods shown later (DFP and BFGS), it can be shown that if previous step \(B_{k}\) is PD, then \(B_{k+1}\) is PD if \[
\mathbf{s}_k^T\mathbf{y}_k>0
\]
This follows from the secant condition by left-multiplying \(B_{k+1}\mathbf{s}_k=\mathbf{y}_k\) with \(\mathbf{s}_k^{\mathsf T}\): \[
B_{k+1}\mathbf{s}_k=\mathbf{y}_k \Rightarrow \mathbf{s}_k^{\mathsf T}B_{k+1}\mathbf{s}_k = \mathbf{s}_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{y}_k>0
\]

if \(f\) is strongly convex, then \(\mathbf{s}_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{y}_k>0\) holds for \(\forall\,\mathbf{s}_k,\mathbf{y}_k\)
\(\mathbf{s}_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{y}_k>0\) not always true for general \(f\)
in use Wolf or strong Wolf line search, \(\mathbf{s}_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{y}_k>0\) holds



Additional Condition
It is obvouse that \(B_k\) should be symmeteric, i.e. \(B^T_k = B_k\). However, the \(B_k\) satisfied the secant condition and symmetric is not unique. Counting the degrees of freedom:

\(B_k\) is symmetric \(\rightarrow n(n+1)/2\) unique element
secant condition \(\rightarrow n\) equations

so \(B_k\) is not uniquely determined.
To uniquely detemines \(B_k\), additional condition should be imposed and one resonable would be requring the \(B_{k+1}\), the Hessian for next interation be a symmetric matrix satisfying secant condition and also closest to previouse Hessian in some sence, i.e. require \(B_{k+1}\) be the one that closest to \(B_k\): \[
B_{k+1} = \arg\min_{B}\left(\lVert B - B_k \rVert \;\middle|\; B = B^{\mathsf T},\ B\mathbf{s}_k = \mathbf{y}_k\right),
\] where \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\) be some matrix norm.


Summary
The quasi Newton methods search the descent direction for next step by approximate the function locally with quadratic function \[
m_k(\mathbf{p}) = f(\mathbf{x}_k) + \nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{p} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{p}^{\mathsf T}B_k\mathbf{p} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mathbf{p}_k = \arg\min_{\mathbf{p}} m_k(\mathbf{p}) = -B_k^{-1}\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_k)
\] The approximate Hessian \(B_k\) is required to satisfy the secant condition, be symmetric and positive definite (\(\mathbf{s}_k^{\mathsf T}\mathbf{y}_k>0\)), and a further additional closeness condition (in some matrix norm) to be uniquely determined: \[
B_{k+1} = \arg\min_B\left(\lVert B - B_k\rVert \;\middle|\; B = B^{\mathsf T},\ B\mathbf{s}_k = \mathbf{y}_k\right)
\]
Figure 2.1 collects the requirements imposed on \(B_k\).








Figure 2.1: The requirements imposed on the approximate Hessian \(B_k\) in a quasi-Newton method.

title: 2  Quasi Newton Methods
text:
2.2 DFP Update
The DFP update measures the closeness of \(B\) to \(B_k\) (the additional condition above) with a weighted Frobenius norm: \[
\lVert\cdot\rVert_W := \lVert W^{1/2}AW^{1/2}\rVert_F, \qquad \lVert\cdot\rVert_F^2 := \sum_{ij} a_{ij}^2
\] where \(W\) should satisfy \(W\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{s}_k\). One example is \(W = \bar{G}_k^{-1}\), where \[
\bar{G}_k = \int_0^1 \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{x}_k + \tau\alpha_k\mathbf{p}_k)\,\mathrm{d}\tau
\] is the average Hessian.

title: 3  Conjugate Gradient Methods
text:
3.1 Linear Conjugate-Gradient Methods
Linear CG solve the linear system of equation \[
Ax = b \qquad (\text{goal}), \qquad A \text{ symmetric and PD}.
\] which is equivalent to the following quadratic minimization \[
\min \phi(x) \overset{\text{def}}{=} \frac{1}{2}x^{\mathsf T}Ax - b^{\mathsf T}x.
\]

title: 3  Conjugate Gradient Methods
text:
Note



\[
Ax - b = 0 \iff \lVert Ax - b\rVert_2^2 = 0 \iff \min \lVert Ax - b\rVert_2^2
\]

title: 3  Conjugate Gradient Methods
text:
3.2 Iteration idea
If \(A\) is diagonal, do minimization along each basis (diagonal quadratic): \[
\alpha_j = \arg\min_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}} \phi(x_j + \alpha\hat{e}_{j+1}) \;\to\; \text{update} \quad x_{j+1} = x_j + \alpha_j\hat{e}_{j+1}
\]

\(\hat{e}_j\) is the along the basis with \(\lVert e_j\rVert_2 = 1\).

issue: not work if \(A\) is not diagonal — the minimum along the principal axis no longer match the orthogonal directions.








Figure 3.1: Coordinate-wise minimization of the quadratic \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12 x^{\mathsf T}Ax-b^{\mathsf T}x\). Left: when \(A\) is diagonal the contours are axis-aligned, so minimizing along each coordinate basis reaches the minimum (\(+\)). Right: when \(A\) is not diagonal the contours are tilted, so the coordinate directions no longer match the principal axes and the same procedure zig-zags.





Solution: “rotate” \(\to\) transform \(A\) s.t. it is diagonal in the new axis.

title: 3  Conjugate Gradient Methods
text:
3.3 Conjugacy

Definition 3.1 (Conjugacy) A set of \(\{p_0, p_1, \dots p_l\}\) with \(\forall\, p_i \neq 0\) is the conjugate with respect to the positive definite symmetric matrix \(A\) if \[
p_i^{\mathsf T}A p_j = 0, \qquad \forall\, i \neq j.
\]







Relation with the eigenvalue problem



Since \(A\) is real-symmetric, it is possible to find an orthogonal matrix \(p\) \[
p = (v_1\ v_2\ \cdots\ v_n)
\] composed of eigenvectors, \(Av_i = \lambda_i v_i\), s.t. \[
v_j^{\mathsf T}A v_i = \lambda_i v_j^{\mathsf T}v_i = \lambda_i\delta_{ij} \;\Rightarrow\; v_i, v_j \text{ form conjugate.}
\]

Conjugate can be viewed as orthonormal eigenvectors.

title: 3  Conjugate Gradient Methods
text:
3.4 Transforming to diagonal coordinates
thus \(p^{-1} = (p_0\ p_1\ \cdots\ p_{n-1})\) transform \(x\) as \(\hat{x} = p^{-1}x\).

and \[
\hat{\phi}(\hat{x}) = \phi(p\hat{x}) = \frac{1}{2}\hat{x}^{\mathsf T}\underbrace{(p^{\mathsf T}A p)}_{\text{diagonal}}\hat{x} - (p^{\mathsf T}b)^{\mathsf T}\hat{x}
\] and can use the search method before.

title: 4  Theory of Constrained Optimization
4  Theory of Constrained Optimization
text:
4.2 Some terminology
Feasibility set — \(x\) that satisfies the constraints. \[
\Omega := \{\, x \mid G_i(x)=0,\ i\in\mathcal{E},\ \ G_i(x)\geq 0,\ i\in\mathcal{I} \,\}
\]

Non-smooth \(\Omega\) can be represented by smooth constraints.


Definition 4.1 (Global minimizer) \(x^\ast\in\Omega\) is called a global minimizer on \(\Omega\) if \(f(x^\ast)\leq f(x)\), \(\forall x\in\Omega\).


Definition 4.2 (Local minimizer) \(x^\ast\in\Omega\) is called a local minimizer on \(\Omega\) if there exists a neighbourhood \(N\) of \(x^\ast\) s.t. \(f(x^\ast)\leq f(x)\), \(\forall x\in N\cap\Omega\); or \[
\exists\,\varepsilon>0,\ \text{s.t.}\ f(x^\ast)\leq f(x),\ \forall x\in\Omega\cap B_\varepsilon(x^\ast) := \{x\in\mathbb{R}^n \mid \lVert x-x^\ast\rVert<\varepsilon\}.
\]


Definition 4.3 (Strict / strong local minimizer) Strict inequality: \[
\exists\,\varepsilon>0,\ \text{s.t.}\ f(x^\ast) < f(x),\ \forall x\neq x^\ast \text{ and } x\in\Omega\cap B_\varepsilon(x^\ast).
\]


Definition 4.4 (Isolated local minimizer) \[
\exists\,\varepsilon>0,\ \text{s.t.}\ x^\ast \text{ is the only local minimizer in } \Omega\cap B_\varepsilon(x^\ast).
\]

isolated local minimizer \(\Rightarrow\) local minimizer.



Definition 4.5 (Convex set) A set \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is called a convex set if \(\forall x,y\in\Omega\) and \(\forall\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[
\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y \in \Omega.
\]









Figure 4.1: A convex set \(\Omega\): for any two points \(x,y\in\Omega\) the whole segment between them stays inside \(\Omega\).





Remark: if \(f(x)\) is a convex function and \(\Omega\) is a convex set, then any local minimal is a global minimal.

title: 4  Theory of Constrained Optimization
text:
4.3 Optimality condition
Similarly to the unconstrained case, conditions for judging a local minimum for \(C^1\) & \(C^2\) \(f, G_i\) can be given.

Terminology / Def

Definition 4.6 (Active set) The equality constraint & the boundary of an inequality: \[
A(x) := \{\, i\in\mathcal{E}\cup\mathcal{I} : G_i(x)=0 \,\}
\] is called the active set at any feasible point.

Remark: Noticed that this is useful as the constraint that is not strictly at the boundary at \(x\) can be disregarded, as a small neighbourhood of \(x\) can always be found s.t. the constraint is disregarded.

Definition 4.7 (Cone) \(C\) is called a cone if \(\forall x\in C\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\), \(\alpha x\in C\).

A cone might not be a convex set.




First-order consideration
Consider a move \(x\to x+\alpha p\): \[
\begin{cases}
f(x+\alpha p) \approx f(x) + \alpha\nabla f^{\mathsf T}p \\
G_i(x+\alpha p) \approx G_i(x) + \alpha\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p
\end{cases}
\qquad (\text{linearize the boundaries})
\]
If we wish \(x+\alpha p\) is still a feasible point, we wish \[
\begin{cases}
G_i(x) + \alpha\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p = 0, & i\in\mathcal{E} \\
G_i(x) + \alpha\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p \geq 0, & i\in\mathcal{I}
\end{cases}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\begin{cases}
\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p = 0, & i\in\mathcal{E} \\
G_i(x) + \alpha\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p \geq 0, & \text{if } G_i(x)>0 \\
\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p \geq 0, & \text{if } G_i(x)=0
\end{cases}
\]


\(i\in\mathcal{I}\), and \(G_i(x)>0\) \(\to\) \(x\) is strictly inside the feasible region. We can always find \(\alpha\) s.t. \(G_i(x)+\alpha\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p\geq 0\).
\(i\in\mathcal{I}\), and \(G_i(x)=0\) \(\to\) \(x\) is at the boundary of the inequality constraint, and we need \(\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p\geq 0\), \(i\in A(x)\cap\mathcal{I}\) (the intersecting region between hyperplanes).

In another word, if \(x^\ast\) is a local minimal, then any feasible direction would cause \(f\) to increase.
\(\nabla^{\mathsf T}f\) has to be the linear combination of the normal vector of the hyperplanes: \[
\nabla f = \sum_i \lambda_i \nabla G_i(x), \quad i\in\mathcal{E}\cup(A(x)\cap\mathcal{I}), \qquad \text{Lagrangian multiplier } \lambda_i\geq 0
\]








Figure 4.2: At a solution, \(\nabla f\) lies in the cone (shaded) of the active constraint gradients \(\nabla G_i\) — i.e. it is a non-negative linear combination of them, with Lagrangian multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge0\).





We can combine this with the non-active constraint and require \[
\nabla f^{\mathsf T}p = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}\cup\mathcal{I}} \lambda_i \nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}p, \qquad \& \quad \lambda_i G_i(x)=0,\ i\in\mathcal{E}\cup\mathcal{I}
\]
This condition implies that if \(G_i(x)>0\) (not active), \(\lambda_i=0\) for sure. This is the familiar Lagrangian multiplier: \[
\mathcal{L} := f - \sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}\cup\mathcal{I}} \lambda_i G_i(x).
\]


First-order optimality condition (KKT)

Theorem 4.1 (First-order optimality condition (KKT)) Suppose \(x^\ast\) is a local solution, and \(f\) and \(G_i\) are all \(C^1\), and LICQ holds at \(x^\ast\). Then there is a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda^\ast\), s.t. the following holds: \[
\nabla_x\mathcal{L}(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \nabla f(x^\ast) = \sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}\cup\mathcal{I}} \lambda_i^\ast\,\nabla G_i(x^\ast)
\] \[
\left.
\begin{aligned}
G_i(x^\ast) &= 0, && \forall i\in\mathcal{E} \\
G_i(x^\ast) &\geq 0, && \forall i\in\mathcal{I}
\end{aligned}
\right\} \text{feasible condition}
\] \[
\lambda_i^\ast\,G_i(x^\ast) = 0,\ i\in\mathcal{E}\cup\mathcal{I} \quad\to\ \text{complementary condition}
\] \[
\lambda_i^\ast \geq 0,\ \forall i\in\mathcal{I}
\]

\(\lambda_i^\ast\) can only be non-zero for an active constraint.

title: 4  Theory of Constrained Optimization
text:
4.4 Constraint Qualification
Previous discussion are based on the fact that at the region of constrained, we can use linear approximation (bunch of hyperplanes). However, linear approx might not be a “good” approx to the feasible set \(\Omega\) in some case (\(\Omega\) is a point, for example). The condition that the linearized problem is “similar” to the geometry of \(\Omega\) is needed.

Terminology / Def

Definition 4.8 (Linearized feasible set) The set of linearized feasible directions \(F(x)\) at a point \(x\in\Omega\) (choose the linear approx geometry): \[
F(x) := \Big\{\, d\in\mathbb{R}^n : \nabla G_i(x)^{\mathsf T}d=0,\ i\in\mathcal{E};\ \ \nabla G_i(x)^{\mathsf T}d\geq 0,\ i\in\mathcal{I}\cap A(x) \,\Big\}
\]

\(F(x)\) is a cone.



Definition 4.9 (Feasible sequence) A feasible sequence \(\{z_k\}\) approaching a feasible point \(x\in\Omega\) is a sequence \(\lim_{k\to\infty} z_k = x\), and \(z_k\in\Omega\) for \(\forall k\geq N\), \(\exists N\in\mathbb{N}^{+}\).

a local minimum then is \(x\in\Omega\) s.t. \(\forall\{z_k\}\) feasible sequence satisfy \(f(z_k)\geq f(x)\), for \(k\) sufficiently large.




Definition 4.10 (Tangent) A vector \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is called a tangent to \(\Omega\) at \(x\in\Omega\), if there exists a feasible sequence \(\{z_k\}\) at \(x\), and positive scalars \(\{t_k\}\to 0\) s.t. \[
\lim_{k\to\infty} \frac{z_k-x}{t_k} = d, \qquad \text{or equiv}\quad \Big\{\, d=0 \Big\}\cup\Big\{\, \frac{d}{\lVert d\rVert} = \lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{z_k-x}{\lVert z_k-x\rVert} \,\Big\}.
\]


Definition 4.11 (Tangent cone) The geometric representation of feasible directions: \[
T_\Omega(x^\ast) := \{\, \text{all tangent } d \text{ to } \Omega \text{ at } x^\ast \,\}
\]

\(T_\Omega(x^\ast)\) is a cone.
\(T_\Omega(x^\ast)\) is only rely on the local geometry, not its algebraic specification.
\(F(x)\subseteq T_\Omega(x)\).



Remark: from our previous discussion, we see that if \(x^\ast\) is optimal, then any feasible direction should cause \(f(x)\) increase. Using \(T_\Omega(x)\) this can be stated as: if \(x^\ast\) is a local minimum, \[
\nabla f(x^\ast)^{\mathsf T}d\geq 0,\ \forall d\in T_\Omega(x^\ast) \qquad \text{if } f \text{ is } C^1.
\]
A condition on \(G_i\) should be imposed so that \(F(x)\) is “similar” to \(T_\Omega(x)\). For example \[
G_1(x) = 1 - x_1^2 - (x_2-1)^2 \geq 0, \quad G_2(x) = x_2 \geq 0 \;\to\; \Omega=\{(0,0)\},\ T_\Omega=\{(a,0)\}.
\]








Figure 4.3: A case where the linear approximation is not similar to \(\Omega\): with \(G_1=1-x_1^2-(x_2-1)^2\ge0\) (disk) and \(G_2=x_2\ge0\) (upper half-plane), the feasible set \(\Omega\) is the single point \((0,0)\) where the disk touches the axis.





Many constraint qualifications can be applied to impose similarity; the following is often used.

Definition 4.12 (Linear Independence Constraint Qualification (LICQ)) For \(x\in\Omega\) and \(A(x)\), LICQ holds if \(\{\nabla G_i(x),\ i\in A(x)\}\) is linearly independent.


Remarks:

if LICQ holds at \(x\), then \(T_\Omega(x) = F(x)\).
if all \(G_i\), \(i\in\mathcal{E}\cup\mathcal{I}\), are linear, then \(T_\Omega(x) = F(x)\).

title: 4  Theory of Constrained Optimization
text:
4.5 Second-order consideration
The first-order condition gives the necessary condition that the first-order derivative should satisfied. However, it is not sufficient, just like the case in the unconstrained settings.
Noticed that when the KKT condition is satisfied, any feasible direction \(w\in F(x)\) will not decrease \(f\) to the first order, \(w^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x^\ast)\geq 0\). However, the ambiguous direction where \(w^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x^\ast)=0\), the first-order approx show no insight on whether \(f\) increase or decrease. The second-order condition impose further condition on such ambiguous direction.

Critical cone
The critical cone picks out the ambiguous directions. \((x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\) satisfies the KKT condition; the critical cone \(C(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\) is defined as \[
w\in C(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast) \iff
\begin{cases}
w\in F(x^\ast), \\
\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}(x^\ast)w = 0, & \forall i\in\mathcal{E} \\
\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}(x^\ast)w = 0, & \forall i\in A(x^\ast)\cap\mathcal{I} \text{ with } \lambda_i^\ast>0 \\
\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}(x^\ast)w \geq 0, & \forall i\in A(x^\ast)\cap\mathcal{I} \text{ with } \lambda_i^\ast=0
\end{cases}
\]
Remark: if \(w\in C(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\Rightarrow w^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x^\ast)=0\). \(C(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\) contains directions from \(F(x^\ast)\) s.t. it is ambiguous direction in first-order.
Special case for strict complementary. \((x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\) satisfy KKT, and exactly one of \(\lambda_i^\ast\) and \(G_i(x)=0\) for each \(i\in\mathcal{I}\) \(\iff \lambda_i^\ast>0\) for \(\forall i\in A(x^\ast)\cap\mathcal{I}\). In this case \[
C(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast) = \{\, \nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}(x^\ast)w=0,\ \forall i\in A(x^\ast) \,\}.
\]


Second-order necessary condition

Theorem 4.2 (Second-order necessary condition) Suppose \(x^\ast\) is a local minimum with LICQ satisfied, and \(\lambda^\ast\) be the Lagrange multiplier that satisfies KKT. Then \[
w^{\mathsf T}\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal{L}(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\,w \geq 0, \qquad \forall w\in C(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast).
\]



Second-order sufficient condition

Theorem 4.3 (Second-order sufficient condition) Suppose for some \(x^\ast\in\Omega\), \(\exists\lambda^\ast\) s.t. \((x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\) satisfies KKT, and \[
w^{\mathsf T}\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal{L}\,w > 0, \qquad \forall w\in C(x^\ast,\lambda^\ast),\ w\neq 0.
\] Then \(x^\ast\) is a strict local minimum.

constraint qualification not required.

title: 5  Quadratic Programming
text:
5.1 Equality Constrained Quadratic Programming (EQP)
The Quadratic Programming solves a constrained optimization problem with quadratic objective and linear constraints: \[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} \tfrac{1}{2}x^{\mathsf T}Gx + x^{\mathsf T}c, \quad \text{s.t.}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}x = b_i,\ i\in\mathcal{E};\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}x \geq b_i,\ i\in\mathcal{I}.
\]
Remark: if \(G\) is not PD (semi), then the objective is not convex and is more challenging. We will be discussing PD (semi) \(G\), s.t. the problem is convex, in the general case.
The first-order KKT condition of the equality constrained problem is \[
\begin{bmatrix} G & A^{\mathsf T} \\ A & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} x^\ast \\ -\lambda^\ast \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} -c \\ b \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\lambda^\ast = \begin{pmatrix} \lambda_{i_1}^\ast \\ \vdots \\ \lambda_{i_n}^\ast \end{pmatrix} \text{ is the Lagrangian multiplier.}
\]
Q: Will the KKT condition has solution?
Solve the KKT equation for the optimal solution.

title: 5  Quadratic Programming
text:
Theorem 5.1 (Existence of EQP solution) If \(A\) has full row rank (independent) and \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) is a null space basis of \(A\) (\(AZ=0\)), if \(Z^{\mathsf T}GZ\) is PD, then the KKT matrix is non-singular and there is a unique solution.



Null space method
Let \(Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\), \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) together form a basis in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(Z\) form the null basis of \(A\).

chose a base \(Z\) from \(AZ=0\), and find \(Y\).
\(x^\ast = YP_Y + ZP_Z\) (base of \(\mathbb{R}^n\)): \[
P_Y \to (AY)P_Y = b, \qquad P_Z \to (Z^{\mathsf T}GZ)P_Z = -Z^{\mathsf T}c - Z^{\mathsf T}GYP_Y
\]
find \(\lambda^\ast\) using \((AY)^{\mathsf T}\lambda^\ast = Y^{\mathsf T}c + Y^{\mathsf T}Gx^\ast\).

Remarks:

\(Z\) can be chosen, and could lead to ill-conditioned \(Z^{\mathsf T}GZ\).
useful for small \(n-m\), and don’t require PD condition on \(G\).



Schur-complement method (dual method)
If \(G\) is PD.

Apply \(AG^{-1}\): \(\quad [AG^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}]\lambda^\ast = b + AG^{-1}c\)
Get \(x^\ast\) \(\leftarrow\) \(Gx^\ast = A^{\mathsf T}\lambda^\ast - c\)

Remarks:

\(G\) needs to be PD.
It is recommended if \(G\) is PD, and easy to find inverse.



Direct factorization

title: 5  Quadratic Programming
text:
5.2 General Case (with \(\mathcal{I}\))
The KKT condition is \[
Gx^\ast + c - \sum_{i\in A(x^\ast)} \lambda_i^\ast\, a_i = 0
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
a_i^{\mathsf T}x &= b_i, && \forall i\in\mathcal{E} \\
a_i^{\mathsf T}x &\geq b_i, && \forall i\in\mathcal{I}\setminus A(x^\ast) \\
\lambda_i^\ast &\geq 0, && \forall i\in\mathcal{I}\cap A(x^\ast).
\end{aligned}
\]

Consider the case \(G\) is PD (semi).

title: 5  Quadratic Programming
text:
5.3 Active set methods
idea: if we know the final optimal active set \(A(x^\ast)\), then we can reduce the problem to \[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} \tfrac{1}{2}x^{\mathsf T}Gx + x^{\mathsf T}c, \quad \text{s.t.}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}x = b_i,\ i\in A(x^\ast)
\] and use EQP \(\to\) Want to iteratively guess the optimal active set.

Approach
1. Start with a feasible point \(x_k\), and a guess of active set \(W_k\), check if \(x_k\) is optimal of the \(W_k\): \[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} \tfrac{1}{2}x^{\mathsf T}Gx + x^{\mathsf T}c, \quad \text{s.t.}\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}x = b_i,\ i\in W_k.
\] if not, we look for a new point \(p_k+x_k\) s.t. it is the optimum: \[
\min \tfrac{1}{2}(x_k+p_k)^{\mathsf T}G(x_k+p_k) + (x_k+p_k)^{\mathsf T}c \;\iff\; \min_{p\in\mathbb{R}^n} \tfrac{1}{2}p^{\mathsf T}Gp + p^{\mathsf T}(Gx_k+c)
\] \[
\text{s.t. } a_i^{\mathsf T}(x_k+p_k),\ i\in W_k \qquad\qquad \text{s.t. } a_i^{\mathsf T}p = 0,\ i\in W_k \quad (\text{sub problem})
\]
2. Solve the sub problem, and get \(p_k^\ast\), meaning the vector required to shift \(x_k \to x_k+p_k^\ast\), s.t. the new point now is the optimum of \(W_k\).
i) if \(p_k^\ast = 0\), then means \(x_k\) is the optimal set. The KKT of the sub problem: \[
Gx_k + c - \sum_{i\in W_k}\lambda_i^\ast a_i = 0, \qquad a_i^{\mathsf T}x = b,\ \forall i\in W_k, \qquad a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k \geq b_i,\ \forall i\in\mathcal{I}\setminus W_k
\] for \(x_k, \lambda_i^\ast\) to satisfies the KKT of the original problem, need verify the sign of \(\lambda_i^\ast\), for \(i\in W_k\cap\mathcal{I}\).

if \(\lambda_i^\ast<0\), then this means \(i\) should not be active, as \(\nabla f = \sum_i \lambda_i^\ast \nabla G_i\) could be negative leading to a descent direction. Thus, remove its from \(W_k\), i.e. \(W_k \leftarrow W_k\setminus\{i\}\).

if multiple \(\lambda_i^\ast<0\), we drop the most negative one \(i = \arg\min_i \lambda_i^\ast\).

if \(\lambda_i^\ast\geq 0\) for all \(i\in W_k\cap\mathcal{I}\), then we have found the optimal with \(\lambda^\ast = \begin{cases}\lambda_i^\ast, & i\in W_k \\ 0, & i\notin W_k\end{cases}\)

Remark: It can be shown that by removing \(j\in W_k\) and \(\lambda_j<0\), the optimal \(p^\ast\) in the next iteration is feasible for \(j\), and \(p\) is also a descent direction.
ii) if \(p_k\neq 0\), this means \(x_k\) is not optimal for the subproblem, and \(x_k+p_k\) is. However, \(x_k+p_k\) may not be feasible for the original problem. The idea will be shrink \(p_k\) s.t. \(x_k+\alpha p_k\) is feasible.

\(i\in W_k\): \(\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}(x_k+\alpha p_k) = a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k + \alpha\, a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k = 0\)
\(i\notin W_k\): \(\quad a_i^{\mathsf T}(x_k+\alpha p_k) = \underbrace{a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k}_{\geq b_i} + \alpha\,\underbrace{a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k}_{\text{unknown}}\)

if \(a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k\geq 0\), \(x_k+p_k\) stays feasible;
if \(a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k< 0\), not necessary feasible.


if \(a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\), we chose \(\alpha\) s.t. \(x_k+\alpha p_k\in\Omega\): \[
a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k + \alpha\, a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k \geq b_i \;\Rightarrow\; \alpha \leq \frac{b_i - a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k}{a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k}, \text{ for specific } i \;\Rightarrow\; \alpha = \min_{a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k<0}\frac{b_i - a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k}{a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k}.
\]
In summary, choose \[
\alpha = \min\left(1,\ \min_{i\notin W_k,\ a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k<0}\frac{b_i - a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k}{a_i^{\mathsf T}p_k}\right).
\]
Note: \(\alpha_k=0\) is possible, as there could be a case that \(i\) is not in the current \(W_k\), but \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x_k = b_i\) (\(i\) is active).
In the end we need to add \(\{i\}\), the index that attains the minimum, as \(\alpha\) is chosen s.t. \(x_k\) is on the boundary.
The overall iteration is summarized below.






flowchart TD
    A["Start: feasible x_k, guess active set W_k"] --> B["Solve QP subproblem for p_k"]
    B --> C{"p_k = 0 ?"}
    C -->|no| H["alpha = min(1, min ratio over blocking i)"]
    H --> I["x_k+1 = x_k + alpha p_k"]
    I --> J{"a blocking constraint was hit ?"}
    J -->|yes| K["add that index to W_k"]
    J -->|no| G["k = k + 1"]
    K --> G
    C -->|yes| D{"lambda_i >= 0 for all i in W_k and I ?"}
    D -->|yes| E["Stop: optimal"]
    D -->|no| F["remove the most-negative index from W_k"]
    F --> G
    G --> B




Figure 5.1: Active-set iteration for inequality-constrained QP.





Remark: the worst-case complexity is \(O(2^n)\), but the average is good.

title: 6  Sequential Quadratic Programming
text:
6.1 Equality Constrained Case
Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) is extended method of quadratic programming to solve general constrained optimization problem using Newton’s method and QP at each iterations. It solves a nonlinear constrained optimization with Newton’s method.
\[
\min f(x), \quad f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}, \qquad \text{s.t.}\quad C(x)=0, \quad C:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m.
\]
The KKT condition is \[
\nabla f(x^\ast) - \sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}\lambda_i^\ast\,\nabla C_i(x^\ast) = 0, \qquad C(x^\ast)=0
\] \[
\iff F(x,\lambda) = \begin{bmatrix} \nabla f(x) - A^{\mathsf T}(x)\lambda \\ C(x) \end{bmatrix} = 0, \qquad A = \big[\,\nabla C_1,\ \nabla C_2,\ \cdots\big].
\]
Then use Newton to find an approx solution.

title: 6  Sequential Quadratic Programming
text:
Newton’s method
\[
\begin{bmatrix} x_{k+1} \\ \lambda_{k+1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} x_k \\ \lambda_k \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} P_x \\ P_\lambda \end{bmatrix} \quad (\text{Newton step}), \qquad \nabla_z F(z_k)\,\delta z_k = -F(z_k),\ \ z=(x,\lambda).
\]
\[
\Rightarrow
\begin{bmatrix} \nabla^2\mathcal{L}(x_k,\lambda_k) & -A(x_k)^{\mathsf T} \\ A(x_k) & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} P_x \\ P_\lambda \end{bmatrix}
= -\begin{bmatrix} \nabla f(x_k) - A(x_k)^{\mathsf T}\lambda_k \\ C(x_k) \end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\iff
\begin{bmatrix} \nabla^2\mathcal{L} & A^{\mathsf T} \\ A & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} P_x \\ -(P_\lambda+\lambda_k) \end{bmatrix}
= -\begin{bmatrix} \nabla f(x_k) \\ C(x_k) \end{bmatrix}
\]
Remarks: The step is well defined if \[
\begin{cases}
A \text{ has full row rank} \\
d^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2\mathcal{L}\,d > 0,\ \forall d\neq 0 \text{ s.t. } Ad=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Note: The Newton step equation is equivalent to the QP \[
\min_{p\in\mathbb{R}^n} \nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}p + \tfrac{1}{2}p^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2\mathcal{L}(x_k,\lambda_k)p, \qquad \text{s.t.}\quad C(x_k) + A(x_k)p = 0.
\] \[
\Rightarrow P_x = P^\ast, \qquad \lambda^\ast = \lambda_k + P_\lambda \to \text{next } \lambda.
\]
Thus SQP solve QP in sequence, where at each step solve

Quadratic approx of objective
Linear approx of constraints.

title: 6  Sequential Quadratic Programming
6  Sequential Quadratic Programming
text:
6.3 Remarks on Convergence
It can be shown that if \((x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\) is a KKT point and \(x^\ast\) is a local solution of the NLP, and LICQ and strict complementary holds. Then there exists \((x_k^\ast,\lambda_k^\ast)\), a local solution of \(\mathrm{QP}_k\) s.t. \(A_k = A(x^\ast)\), when \((x_k^\ast,\lambda_k^\ast)\) is sufficiently close to \((x^\ast,\lambda^\ast)\). Then, the IQP reduced to an EQP on the optimal \(A(x^\ast)\) (and not change \(A_k\) in subsequence). SQP can be applied, and will converge quadratically.

title: 6  Sequential Quadratic Programming
text:
6.4 Quasi-Newton Approximation
Similarly like the unconstrained case, we can use a PD matrix \(B_k\) to approximate \(\nabla^2\mathcal{L}\), and update like BFGS.

title: 7  Penalty Methods
text:
7.1 Quadratic Penalty Function
Constrained optimization problem: \[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x), \quad \text{s.t.}\quad
\begin{cases} G_i(x)=0, & i\in\mathcal{E} \\ G_i(x)\geq 0, & i\in\mathcal{I} \end{cases}
\]
We need to minimize the problem as well as achieving feasibility.
Motivation: construct an auxiliary objective function s.t. the deviation from feasibility is penalized.

title: 7  Penalty Methods
text:
Equality constrained case
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x), \quad \text{s.t.}\quad G_i(x)=0,\ i\in\mathcal{E}.
\]
penalty function \[
Q(x,\mu) := f(x) + \frac{\mu}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}} G_i^2(x), \qquad \mu>0 \text{ is the penalty parameter.}
\]
larger \(\mu\) \(\to\) more penalty on \(G_i(x)\) \(\to\) close to the exact constraint.
Sequential consideration. consider a sequence \(\{\mu_k\}\to\infty\), and the quadratic problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} Q(x,\mu_k)\) for each \(k\), with optimizer \(x_k\).
Comparing the original problem with the penalty problem: \[
\underbrace{\min f(x),\ G_i(x)=0}_{\displaystyle \nabla f(x) - \sum_i \lambda_i\nabla G_i(x)=0}
\qquad\qquad
\underbrace{\min f(x) + \tfrac{\mu}{2}\textstyle\sum_i G_i^2(x)}_{\displaystyle \nabla f(x) + \mu\sum_i G_i(x)\nabla G_i(x)=0}
\] For the penalty problem, \(\mu\to\infty\), \(G_i(x)\to 0\) to keep a finite value. We would hope that when \(\mu_k\to\infty\), \(x_k=\arg\min Q(x,\mu_k)\to x^\ast\).

Theorem 7.1 (Convergence condition) suppose the original problem has a global minimizer. Let \(x_k\) be the global minimizer of \(Q(x,\mu_k)\), and \(\mu_k\to\infty\). Then every limit point \(x^\ast\) of \(x_k\) is a global solution of the original problem.



Convergence property
Let \(x_k\) be generated by the quadratic penalty method with \(\tau_k\to 0\) and \(\mu_k\to\infty\). Let \(x^\ast\) be a limit point of the sequence \(\{x_k\}\).

if \(x^\ast\notin\Omega\), then it is a stationary point of \(\lVert C(x)\rVert^2\).
if \(x^\ast\in\Omega\), and LICQ hold at \(x^\ast\), then \(x^\ast\) is a KKT point with \(\lambda^\ast\), and satisfy \[
\lim_{k\in K} -\mu_k G_i(x_k) = \lambda_i^\ast,\ \forall i\in\mathcal{E} \quad\text{and infinite subsequence } \lim_{k\to K} x_k = x^\ast.
\]

Remarks:

The quadratic penalty may not converge to a feasible point.
If converge to a feasible point, \(\lim_{k\to\infty} -\mu_k G_i(x_k) = \lambda_i^\ast\) reduce to the KKT condition (\(\mu_k\to\infty\), \(G_i(x_k)\to 0\)).



Issues: ill-conditioned Hessian
\[
\nabla^2 Q = \nabla^2 f + \sum_i \mu_k G_i(x)\nabla^2 G_i(x) + \mu_k\sum_i \nabla G_i\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}
\] if converge to feasible: \[
\nabla^2 Q = \underbrace{\nabla^2 f - \sum_i \lambda_i^\ast\nabla^2 G_i(x)}_{\nabla^2\mathcal{L}} + \underbrace{\mu_k\sum_i \nabla G_i\nabla G_i^{\mathsf T}}_{\text{ill condition when }\mu\to\infty}
\] Newton’s method might struggle.


Inequality constrained case
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x), \quad \text{s.t.}\quad G_i(x)=0,\ i\in\mathcal{E};\quad G_i(x)\geq 0,\ i\in\mathcal{I}.
\] \[
\Rightarrow Q(x,\mu) = f(x) + \frac{\mu}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}} G_i^2(x) + \frac{\mu}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}} \big(\max\{0,\,-G_i(x)\}\big)^2
\] which is \(C^1\) only.

title: 7  Penalty Methods
text:
7.2 Augmented Lagrangian Method
In the quadratic penalty method, we wish \(-\mu_k G_i(x)\to\lambda_i^\ast \iff G_i(x) = -\dfrac{\lambda_i^\ast}{\mu_k}\), so \(\mu_k\to\infty\) to make sure \(G_i(x)=0\). However, \(\mu_k\) won’t need to go unbounded if we can make the numerator \(\to 0\).

Equality constrained case
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x), \quad \text{s.t.}\quad G_i(x)=0,\ i\in\mathcal{E}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mathcal{L}_A(x,\lambda;\mu) = f(x) - \sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}}\lambda_i G_i(x) + \frac{\mu}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{E}} G_i^2(x)
\]
The KKT of the original problem is \(\nabla f - \sum_i \lambda_i\nabla G_i = 0\), \(G_i(x)=0\).
consider a sequence \(\lambda_k, \mu_k\): \[
\nabla\mathcal{L}_A = \nabla f - \sum_i \lambda_i^k\nabla G_i(x) + \mu_k\sum_i G_i\nabla G_i = \nabla f - \sum_i \big(\lambda_i^k - \mu_k G_i(x)\big)\nabla G_i(x_k).
\] wish \(\lambda_i^k - \mu_k G_i(x)\to\lambda_i^\ast\) and \(x_k\to x^\ast\).
now \[
G_i(x) = \frac{\lambda_i^k - \lambda_i^\ast}{\mu_k} \to 0 \quad\text{if } \lambda_i^k\to\lambda_i^\ast.
\]


Convergence properties

title: 8  Recap on Probability
text:
8.1 Concentration Inequalities
The guiding theme: a sample average concentrates around its expectation, i.e.
\[
\Big|\,\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i} X_i - \mathbb{E}\big[\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\big]\,\Big|
\quad \text{is small, guaranteed with high probability.}
\]

title: 8  Recap on Probability
text:
8.2 Markov’s Inequality

Theorem 8.1 (Markov’s inequality) Let \(X\) be a non-negative random variable. Then for all \(a > 0\), \[
P(X \ge a) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[X]}{a}.
\]


Remark. The probability of \(X\) being “too large”, \(P(X \ge a)\), is bounded. 


Proof. If \(X\) is a continuous R.V. with pdf \(f_X(x)\), then \[
\mathbb{E}(X) = \int_0^{+\infty} x\, f_X(x)\,dx
= \int_0^{a} x\, f_X(x)\,dx + \int_a^{\infty} x\, f_X(x)\,dx
\ge \int_a^{\infty} x\, f_X(x)\,dx
\ge a \int_a^{\infty} f_X(x)\,dx
= a\, P(X \ge a).
\]


Remark. 

\(+\) : almost always works (\(X\) non-negative).
\(-\) : the bound is weak (not precise).

Power trick \(\to\) sharper bound: \[
P(X^r \ge a^r) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}(X^r)}{a^r}
\qquad (\text{assuming the } r\text{-th moment } \mathbb{E}(X^r) \text{ exists}).
\]
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 8  Recap on Probability
text:
8.3 Chebyshev’s Inequality

Theorem 8.2 (Chebyshev’s inequality) Let \(X\) be a random variable. Then for all \(c > 0\), \[
P\big(|X - \mathbb{E}(X)| \ge c\big) \le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{c^2}.
\]


Proof. Apply the power trick of Markov’s inequality: \[
P\big(|X - \mathbb{E}(X)| \ge c\big)
= P\big(|X - \mathbb{E}(X)|^2 \ge c^2\big)
\le \frac{\mathbb{E}\big[(X - \mathbb{E}(X))^2\big]}{c^2}
= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{c^2}.
\]
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 8  Recap on Probability
text:
8.4 Master Tail Bound

Theorem 8.3 (Master tail bound) Let \(X = X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n\), where \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are i.i.d. and

\(\mathbb{E}(X_i) = 0\),
\(\mathbb{E}(X_i^2) \le \sigma^2\),
\(\big|\mathbb{E}(X_i^s)\big| \le \sigma^2\, s!\) for \(s = 3, 4, \dots, \big\lfloor \tfrac{a^2}{4n\sigma^2}\big\rfloor\).

Then, for \(0 \le a \le \sqrt{2}\, n\sigma^2\), \[
P(|X| \ge a) \le 3\, e^{-\frac{a^2}{12 n \sigma^2}}.
\]



Proof. (Sketch — the full proof is deferred to an appendix.)
(1) Choose \(r\) an even integer such that \(0 < r \le s\). Then \[
P(|X| \ge a) = P(X^r \ge a^r) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}(X^r)}{a^r}.
\]
(2) By the multinomial theorem and independence, \[
\mathbb{E}(X^r) = \mathbb{E}\Big[(X_1 + \cdots + X_n)^r\Big]
= \sum_{\substack{r_1 + \cdots + r_n = r \\ r_i \ge 0}} \frac{r!}{r_1!\, r_2! \cdots r_n!}\, \mathbb{E}\big(X_1^{r_1} \cdots X_n^{r_n}\big)
= \sum_{\substack{r_1 + \cdots + r_n = r \\ r_i \ge 0}} \frac{r!}{r_1! \cdots r_n!}\, \prod_i \mathbb{E}\big(X_i^{r_i}\big).
\]
(3) Since \(\mathbb{E}(X_i) = 0\), \(\mathbb{E}(X_i^2) \le \sigma^2 \le 2\sigma^2\), and \(\mathbb{E}(X_i^{r_i}) \le r_i!\, \sigma^2\), any term with some \(r_i = 1\) vanishes, so the sum is restricted to indices with \(r_i = 0\) or \(r_i \ge 2\). Let \(t = \#\{i : r_i \neq 0\}\); then \[
1 \le t \le \tfrac{r}{2} \qquad (\text{each non-zero } r_i \text{ is at least } 2).
\]
(4) Enumerate the multi-indices by \(t\): for a fixed \(t\) there are \(\binom{n}{t}\) ways to choose which \(r_i\) are non-zero, and (after that choice) \(\binom{r-t-1}{t-1}\) ways to distribute the remaining mass. 
(5) Hence, with \(\sigma^{2t}\) from the moment bounds, \[
\mathbb{E}(X^r) \le r! \sum_{t=1}^{r/2} \binom{n}{t}\binom{r-t-1}{t-1} \sigma^{2t},
\qquad \text{using } \binom{n}{t} \le \frac{n^t}{t!}, \quad \binom{r-t-1}{t-1} \le 2^{\,r-t-1}.
\]
(6) This leads to \[
\mathbb{E}(X^r) \le \Big(\frac{2\, r\, n\, \sigma^2}{a^2}\Big)^{r/2} =: g(r),
\]  and \(g(r)\) decreases while \(r - 1 \le \tfrac{a^2}{4n\sigma^2}\). Choosing \(r\) to be the largest even integer with \(r \le \tfrac{a^2}{6 n \sigma^2}\) gives \[
P(|X| \ge a) \le \big(\tfrac{1}{3}\big)^{r/2} \le e^{-r/2} \le e \cdot e^{-\frac{a^2}{12 n \sigma^2}} \le 3\, e^{-\frac{a^2}{12 n \sigma^2}}.
\]


Remark. The master tail bound is a general probability tail bound for a sum of i.i.d. random variables that gives tighter concentration than the CLT. Tail bounds for various distributions can be derived from it.

title: 8  Recap on Probability
text:
8.5 Chernoff Bound

Example 8.1 (Chernoff bound (i.i.d. Bernoulli)) Let \(Y_1, \dots, Y_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\), i.e. \(Y_i = \begin{cases} 1, & p \\ 0, & 1-p \end{cases}\), and let \(Y = Y_1 + \cdots + Y_n\). Then for all \(c \in [0,1]\), \[
P\Big[\,\big|\tfrac{Y}{n} - p\big| \ge \sqrt{2}\, c\, p(1-p)\,\Big] \le 3\, e^{-\frac{n\, c^2\, p(1-p)}{6}}.
\]


Proof. Apply the master tail bound to \(X_i = Y_i - p\), so \(\mathbb{E}(X_i) = 0\) and \[
\mathbb{E}(X_i^2) = \mathbb{E}\big((Y_i - p)^2\big) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i^2) + p^2 - 2p\,\mathbb{E}(Y_i) = \mathbb{E}(Y_i^2) - \mathbb{E}(Y_i)^2 = \operatorname{Var}(Y_i),
\] \[
\big|\mathbb{E}(X_i^s)\big| = \big|\, p(1-p)^s + (1-p)(-p)^s \,\big| \le p(1-p) = \operatorname{Var}(Y_i).
\]  The Chernoff bound is then obtained directly from the master tail bound with \(a = n\sqrt{2}\, c\, p(1-p)\).

title: 8  Recap on Probability
section: 8.6 Concentration via the Moment Generating Function
text:
8.6 Concentration via the Moment Generating Function
Instead of applying Markov’s inequality to \(|X|^r\), apply it to \(e^{\lambda X}\): \[
P(X \ge t) = P\big(e^{\lambda X} \ge e^{\lambda t}\big) \le \frac{\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda X}]}{e^{\lambda t}}, \qquad \forall\, \lambda > 0
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
P(X \ge t) \le \inf_{\lambda > 0} e^{-\lambda t}\, \mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda X}],
\] noting that \(\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda X}]\) is the moment generating function (MGF).

Theorem 8.4 (Tail bound for a Gaussian) For \(X \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathbb{E}(e^{\lambda X}) = e^{\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \lambda^2}\), hence \[
P(X \ge t) \le \inf_{\lambda > 0} e^{-\lambda t}\, e^{\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 \lambda^2} = e^{-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}}.
\]
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 8  Recap on Probability
text:
8.7 Hoeffding’s Inequality

Theorem 8.5 (Hoeffding’s theorem) Let \(X_i\) be independent random variables with \(X_i \in [a_i, b_i]\) almost surely, and let \(Y = \sum_i X_i\). Then for all \(t \ge 0\), \[
P\big(|Y - \mathbb{E}(Y)| \ge t\big) \le 2\, e^{-\frac{2 t^2}{\sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2}}.
\]


Lemma 8.1 (Hoeffding’s lemma) If \(X\) is a bounded random variable with \(X \in [a, b]\) almost surely, then \[
\mathbb{E}\big(e^{\lambda(X - \mathbb{E}(X))}\big) \le e^{\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{b-a}{2}\right)^2 \lambda^2} = e^{\frac{\lambda^2 (b-a)^2}{8}}.
\]


Proof. Hoeffding’s theorem. Use the Markov tail bound for the exponential: \[
P\Big(\sum_i X_i - \mathbb{E}(X_i) \ge t\Big) \le e^{-\lambda t}\, \mathbb{E}\Big(e^{\lambda\left(\sum_i X_i - \mathbb{E}(X_i)\right)}\Big)
= e^{-\lambda t} \prod_i \mathbb{E}\big(e^{\lambda(X_i - \mathbb{E}(X_i))}\big).
\] By Hoeffding’s lemma (Lemma 8.1), \(\mathbb{E}\big(e^{\lambda(X_i - \mathbb{E}(X_i))}\big) \le e^{\frac{1}{2}\frac{(b_i - a_i)^2}{4}\lambda^2}\), and minimizing the resulting exponent over \(\lambda\) gives \[
P\Big(\sum_i X_i - \mathbb{E}(X_i) \ge t\Big) \le e^{-\frac{2 t^2}{\sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2}}.
\] The same argument applied to \(-X_i\) shows \(P\big(\sum_i X_i - \mathbb{E}(X_i) \le -t\big)\) obeys the same bound, so \[
P\Big(\big|\textstyle\sum_i X_i - \mathbb{E}(X_i)\big| \ge t\Big) \le 2\, e^{-\frac{2 t^2}{\sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2}}.
\]
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 8  Recap on Probability
text:
8.8 \(\chi^2\) Tail Bound

Theorem 8.6 (\(\chi^2\) tail bound) Let \(Z_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)\) and \(X = \sum_i Z_i^2 \sim \chi^2(n)\), so \(\mathbb{E}(X) = n\). Then for all \(t \ge 0\), \[
P\big(|X - \mathbb{E}(X)| \ge t\big) \le 2\exp\!\Big[-c \min\big(t, \tfrac{t^2}{n}\big)\Big].
\]


Proof. Upper tail: with \(\lambda \in (0, \tfrac12)\), \[
P\big(X - \mathbb{E}(X) \ge t\big) \le e^{-\lambda t}\, e^{-n\lambda}\, \mathbb{E}\big(e^{\lambda \sum_i Z_i^2}\big)
= e^{-\lambda t}\, e^{-n\lambda} \prod_i \mathbb{E}\big(e^{\lambda Z_i^2}\big),
\] where \(\mathbb{E}(e^{\lambda Z_i^2})\) is the MGF of \(\chi^2(1)\), equal to \((1 - 2\lambda)^{-1/2}\). Thus \[
P\big(X - \mathbb{E}(X) \ge t\big) \le e^{-\lambda t}\big(1 - 2\lambda\big)^{-n/2} e^{-n\lambda}
= e^{-\lambda t}\Big(\underbrace{e^{-\lambda}(1 - 2\lambda)^{-1/2}}\Big)^{n}
\le e^{-\lambda t + 2 n \lambda^2}, \qquad \forall\, \lambda \in (0, \tfrac14),
\]  so that \[
\min_{\lambda \in (0, 1/4)} e^{-\lambda t + 2 n \lambda^2} = \exp\!\Big(-c \min\big(t, \tfrac{t^2}{n}\big)\Big)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
P\big(X - \mathbb{E}(X) \ge t\big) \le \exp\!\Big(-c \min\big(t, \tfrac{t^2}{n}\big)\Big).
\] Lower tail: similarly, \[
P\big(X - n \le -t\big) = P\big(-(X - n) \ge t\big) \le e^{-\lambda t}\, e^{n\lambda}\, \mathbb{E}\big(e^{-\lambda X}\big)
= e^{-\lambda t}\, e^{n\lambda}(1 + 2\lambda)^{-n/2}
\le e^{-\lambda t}\, e^{n \lambda^2}, \quad \forall\, \lambda > 0,
\] which gives \(P(X - n \le -t) \le e^{-\frac{t^2}{4n}}\).  Combining the two tails, \[
P\big(|X - \mathbb{E}(X)| \ge t\big) \le 2\exp\!\Big(-c \min\big(t, \tfrac{t^2}{n}\big)\Big).
\]

title: 9  Properties of High Dimensional Data
text:
9.2 Random Sampling in unit ball
We star with a useful problem, how to draw a random sample uniformlly from a unit ball in \(n\) dimension.






Close Ball in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)



\[
\mathbb{B^n}\coloneqq\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n: x_1^2+x_2^2+\cdots+x_n^2\leq 1\}
\]



Example 9.1 Consider a 2D case, we can draw \(X_1, X_2\~ \mathrm{Unif}(-1, 1)\), and return \(\mathbf{X}=(X_1, X_2)^T\) if \(X_1^2+X_2^2\leq 1\).










If we generalized the approch in Example 9.1 to \(n\) dimension case, that means draw each coordinate \(X_i\sim \mathrm{Unif}(-1, 1)\) and keep the sample if \(\lVert\mathbf{X}\rVert_2^2\leq 1\). However, this will not work as the volume of the unit ball approaches to zero.






Volume of \(\mathbb{B}^n\)



\[
V(n)=\frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{n\Gamma(n)}\xrightarrow{n\rightarrow\infty}0
\]


This means the acceptance probability of the sample is \(V(n)/\mathrm{Vol}[-1, 1]^d=V(n)/2^n\) approaches zero when the dimensality is high.






Note



This low probability means that we only accept very few point from a large draw of Monte-Carlo samples from uniform \([-1, 1]^n\)

title: 10  Randomized Projection
text:
10.1 Projection map \(\phi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^r\)
Idea: Compress high dimension data to lower dimension to reduce computation / storage.
Approach: map the original data \(X \in \mathbb{R}^d\) into \(\mathbb{R}^r\), with \(r < d\), while maintaining their pairwise distance unchanged (or at least approximately).
Let the original data lie in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and \(S_r\) an \(r\)-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with orthonormal basis \((v_1, v_2, \dots, v_r)\) spanning \(S_r\).
A random projection map \(\phi\) is when \(S_r\) is a random \(r\)-dimensional subspace.
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 10  Randomized Projection
text:
Definition 10.1 (Linear projection map) A linear projection map \(\phi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^r\) is defined as
\[
Y = \phi(x) = \big(\langle x, v_1\rangle,\ \langle x, v_2\rangle,\ \dots,\ \langle x, v_r\rangle\big)^{\mathsf{T}}
= \begin{pmatrix} -\,v_1^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \\ -\,v_2^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \\ \vdots \\ -\,v_r^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \end{pmatrix} x
= \Phi\, x,
\quad \Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d},\ x \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ y \in \mathbb{R}^r .
\]
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 10  Randomized Projection
text:
10.2 Approx. distance preservation
\(y_i = \Phi x_i\), we wish for small \(\varepsilon > 0\)
\[
(1-\varepsilon)\,\|x_i - x_j\|_2^2 \ \le\ \|y_i - y_j\|_2^2 \ \le\ (1+\varepsilon)\,\|x_i - x_j\|_2^2,
\qquad \forall\, i, j \in \{1, \dots, n\}.
\]
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 10  Randomized Projection
text:
10.3 Gaussian Projectors
Consider random projection \(\phi = \begin{pmatrix} -\,u_1^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \\ -\,u_2^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \\ \vdots \\ -\,u_r^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \end{pmatrix}\) where \(u_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(u_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0, I_d)\) spherical Gaussian vectors.

Theorem 10.1 (Gaussian projection) For \(\forall v \in \mathbb{R}^d\), \(\exists\, c > 0\) s.t. \(\forall \varepsilon \in (0,1)\)
\[
P\Big(\big|\,\|\phi v\|_2 - \sqrt{r}\,\|v\|_2\,\big| \ge \varepsilon \sqrt{r}\,\|v\|_2 \Big) \le 3 e^{-c r \varepsilon^2}.
\]


Remark. The projected vector \(\phi v\) will be close to \(\sqrt{r}\,\|v\|\) length, with high probability.


Proof. \[
\phi_{ij} \sim N(0,1) \;\Rightarrow\; \phi_{ij} v_j \sim N(0, v_j^2)
\;\Rightarrow\; \sum_j \phi_{ij} v_j \sim N(0, \|v\|^2)
\]
thus
\[
\frac{1}{\|v\|}\sum_j \phi_{ij} v_j \sim N(0,1)
\;\Rightarrow\; \frac{1}{\|v\|}(\phi v)_i \sim N(0,1)
\;\Rightarrow\; \frac{1}{\|v\|}\phi v \sim N(0, I_r)
\]
using the Gaussian Annulus Theorem.
\[
\begin{align}
P\Big(\big|\,\|\frac{1}{\|v\|_2}\phi v\|_2 - \sqrt{r}\,\,\big| \ge \varepsilon\sqrt{r}\, \Big) &\le 3 e^{-c r \varepsilon^2} \\
\Rightarrow P\Big(\big|\,\|\phi v\|_2 - \sqrt{r}\,\|v\|_2\,\big| \ge \varepsilon\sqrt{r}\,\|v\|_2 \Big) &\le 3 e^{-c r \varepsilon^2}.
\end{align}
\]
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 10  Randomized Projection
text:
10.4 Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma

Lemma 10.1 (Johnson–Lindenstrauss) Let \(x_1, \dots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}^d\), and Gaussian random projection \(\phi = \begin{pmatrix} -\,u_1^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \\ -\,u_2^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \\ -\,u_r^{\mathsf{T}}\,- \end{pmatrix}\). then \(\exists\, c > 0\) s.t. \(\forall \varepsilon \in (0,1)\) and \(\delta > 0\), if
\[
r \ge \frac{c}{\varepsilon^2}\,\log\!\left(\frac{3 n^2}{\delta}\right),
\]
then
\[
P\Big(\big|\,\|\phi (x_j -  x_k)\| - \sqrt{r}\,\|x_j - x_k\|\,\big| \le \varepsilon \sqrt{r}\,\|x_j - x_k\| \Big) \ge 1 - \delta,
\qquad \forall\, j, k .
\]


Remark. The JL lemma states that the distance between projected points
\[
(1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{r}\,\|x_i - x_j\| \ \le\ \|\phi(x_i - x_j)\| \ \le\ (1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{r}\,\|x_i - x_j\|
\]
with high probability.


Proof. Let \(v_{ij} = x_i - x_j\), from the Gaussian projection theorem (Theorem 10.1), we know \(\exists\, c_{ij},\ \varepsilon_{ij} \in (0,1)\) s.t.
\[
P\Big(\big|\,\|\phi v_{ij}\| - \sqrt{r}\,\|v_{ij}\|\,\big| \ge \varepsilon_{ij}\sqrt{r}\,\|v_{ij}\| \Big) \le 5 e^{-c_{ij} r \varepsilon_{ij}^2}.
\]
to show JL lemma, we need a union bound of event
\[
E_{ij}:\quad \big|\,\|\phi v_{ij}\| - \sqrt{r}\,\|v_{ij}\|\,\big| \ge \varepsilon_{ij}\sqrt{r}\,\|v_{ij}\|
\]
so that above is true for \(\forall i, j\).
\[
P\Big(\bigcup_{ij} E_{ij}\Big) \le \sum_{ij} P(E_{ij}) \le \sum_{ij} 3 e^{-c_{ij} r \varepsilon_{ij}^2} \le \binom{n}{2} e^{-c r \varepsilon^2} 3
\]
where \(c = \min\{c_{ij}\}\), \(\varepsilon = \min\{\varepsilon_{ij}\}\), \(\sum_{ij}\) has \(\binom{n}{2}\) terms. Therefore
\[
P\Big(\bigcup_{ij} E_{ij}\Big) \le 3\binom{n}{2} e^{-c r \varepsilon^2} \le 3\tfrac{1}{2} n^2 e^{-c r \varepsilon^2} \le \delta
\]
\[
\Rightarrow\ \delta \ge 3 n^2 e^{-c r \varepsilon^2}
\ \Rightarrow\ r \ge \frac{1}{c \varepsilon^2}\,\log\!\left(\frac{3n^2}{\delta}\right).
\]

title: 10  Randomized Projection
text:
10.5 Computing Random Projection
Direct computing requires \(O(nrd)\) time, \(n\) is sample size.
Idea: if \(X = (x_1, \dots, x_d)\) has iid entry, we can randomly select \(r\) entry and approximate \(\|x\|^2_2 \approx \tfrac{d}{r}\sum_{k}^rv_{ik}\), where \(i_k\) is randomly selected in \(\{1,2,\cdots,d\}\). Thus \(\phi = \sqrt{\tfrac{d}{r}}\, P\), where \(P\) is a random selection matrix should approximatly satisfy \(\|\phi x\|_2 \approx \|x\|_2\).
Issue: \(X\) is usually not iid entry, but tends to be sparse.
Fix: consider if \(x\) is sparse (\(\delta\)-function peaks), its Fourier transform would be smooth (sin function). We can find a similar transform matrix s.t. the transformed \(X\) is flat.
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 10  Randomized Projection
text:
10.6 Hadamard transform

Definition 10.2 (Hadamard transform) Hadamard transform matrix \(H_m \in 2^m \times 2^m\) is defined recursively as
\[
\begin{align}
H_1 &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
H_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} H_1 & H_1 \\ H_1 & -H_1 \end{pmatrix},
\quad \dots \quad\\
H_m &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix} H_{m-1} & H_{m-1} \\ H_{m-1} & -H_{m-1} \end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
\]
each entry \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2^m}}\).


Remark. 

\(H_m\) is orthogonal, \(H_m H_m^{\mathsf{T}} = H_m^{\mathsf{T}} H_m = I\).
\(H_m x\) can be computed using a similar algorithm as FFT, with \(O(2^m \log(2^m))\) time.
\(H_m\) maps a sparse vector to a flat vector.
flatness can be further improved by randomization.


\[
D_{ij} = \begin{cases} \delta_{ij}, & p = \tfrac{1}{2} \\[4pt] \delta_{ij} & p = \tfrac{1}{2} \end{cases}
\]
\(H_m D\) is the randomized Hadamard transform (independent random sign flip).

Lemma 10.2 (Flatness of \(H_m D x\)) \[
\forall x \in \mathbb{R}^d, \qquad P\big(\|H D x\|_\infty \ge t\big) \le 2d\, e^{-\frac{d\, t^2}{2\|x\|^2}}.
\]


Proof. \(u_i := (H D x)_i=\sum_{j=1}^da_jx_j\), with
\[
a_{ij} = \begin{cases} \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, & p = \tfrac{1}{2} \\ -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{d}}, & p = \tfrac{1}{2} \end{cases}
\]
for each entry \(i\):
\[
P(|u_i| \ge t) \le 2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2 \cdot \frac{1}{d}\|x\|^2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{?}}\right)
\quad \text{(Hoeffding)}
= 2 \exp\!\left(-\frac{d\, t^2}{2\|x\|^2}\right)
\]

\[
P(\|u\|_\infty \ge t) \le d\, P(|u_i| \ge t) \le 2d \exp\!\left(-\frac{d\, t^2}{2\|x\|^2}\right).
\]


Remark. \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\|H D x\|_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\|x\|_2\); if \(t = k \frac{\|x\|}{\sqrt{d}}\) then the probability of \(\|H D x\|_2\) not flat (one component is very large comparing to other \(\leftrightarrow \|x\|/\sqrt{d}\) with large \(k\)) would be small.

title: 11  Singular Value Decomposition
text:
Definition 11.1 (First right singular vector) The first right singular vector \(v_1\) of \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) is defined as: \(v_1 \in \mathbb{R}^d\), and \(v_1 = \text{argmax}_{\|v\|_2=1} \|Xv\|_2\) and the first singular value is \(\sigma_1 = \|Xv_1\|_2\)


Proposition 11.1 Definition 11.1 is equivalent as \[
v_1 = \underset{\|v\|_2=1}{\mathrm{argmin}} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \|x_j - P_{v_1}(x_j)\|_2^2,
\] where \(P_{v_1}(x_j)\) is the projected vector of \(x_j\) in the subspace spanned by \(v_1\). Here, we have \[
X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d} =
\begin{pmatrix} -x_1^T- \\ -x_2^T- \\ \vdots \\ -x_n^T- \end{pmatrix}
\]


Proof. \[
\begin{align}
\sum_{j} \|x_j - P_{v}(x_j)\|_2^2 &= \sum_{ij}\left(x_{i,j}-\langle\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{x}_j\rangle v_i\right)^2 \\
&=\sum_{ij}x^2_{i, j} + \langle\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{x}_j\rangle v_i^2 - 2x_{i,j}v_i\langle\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{x}_j \rangle\\
&=\sum_{ij}x^2_{i,j} + \sum_j\left(\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{x}_j\rangle ^2 -2\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{x}_j\rangle^2\right)\\
&=C - \sum_j\langle\mathbf{v},\mathbf{x}_j\rangle^2=C-\|X\mathbf{v}\|^2_2
\end{align}
\] where \(C\) is a constant. Thus we have the \[
\underset{\|v\|_2=1}{\mathrm{argmin}} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \|x_j - P_{v_1}(x_j)\|_2^2 = \underset{\|v\|_2=1}{\mathrm{argmax}} \|Xv\|_2^2
\]







Note



Proposition 11.1 shows that the first singular vector can be understood as a line that minimizes least square error of projected data, i.e., a best fitting line.




Definition 11.2 (Second Singular Vector) The second right singular vector \(v_2 \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is defined as \[
v_2 = \underset{{v \perp v_1, \|v\|_2=1}}{\mathrm{argmin}} \|Xv\|_2,
\] and second singular value defined correspondingly as \[
\sigma_2 = \|Xv_2\|_2
\]



Proposition 11.2 (Best-Fitting 2D Subspace) Let \(v_1, v_2\) be the first and second right singular vectors of \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\). Let \(V = \text{span}(v_1, v_2) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be the two-dimensional subspace they span.
Then \(V\) is the solution to the following minimization: \[
V = \underset{W:\,\dim(W)=2}{\mathrm{argmin}} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \|x_j - P_W(x_j)\|_2^2
\] where \(P_W:\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^2\) is the orthogonal projection onto the subspace \(W\).


Proof. Let \(w_1, w_2\) be two orthonormal bases for any 2-dimensional subspace \(W\). We can always select \(w_2\) s.t. \(\langle w_2,v_1 \rangle = 0\) (such \(w_2\) can be found by the intersection between \(W\) and subspace that perpendicular to \(v_1\)).
A figure perhaps showing the constructiong of w1 and w2 \[
\begin{align}
&\sum_j \|x_j - \langle P_W(x_j)\rangle\|_2^2 = \sum_j \langle x_j-P_W(x_j), x_j-P_W(x_j) \rangle\\
={}&\sum_j\langle x_j - P_w(x_j), x_j\rangle + \sum_j\langle x_j - P_W(x_j), -P_W(x_j)\rangle\\
={}&\sum_j\|x_j\|^2_2 - 2\sum_j\langle P_W(x_j), x_j\rangle + \|P_W(x_j)\|^2_2\\
\end{align}.
\] Noticed that \[
\begin{align}
\langle P_W(x_j), x_j \rangle &= \langle w_1\langle w_1, x_j\rangle + w_2\langle w_2, x_j\rangle, x_j\rangle\\
& = \langle w_1, x_j\rangle^2 + \langle w_2, x_j\rangle^2=\|P_W(x_j)\|^2_2,
\end{align}
\] thus \[
\sum_j\|x_j - P_W(x_j)\|^2_2 = C - (\sum_j \langle w_1, x_j \rangle^2 + \langle w_2, x_j \rangle^2),
\] where \[
C = \sum_{j=1}^n \| x_j \|_2^2
\] is a constant.
Since \(v_1\) maximizes \(\|Xv\|_2^2\) among all \(\|v\|_2=1\) , and \(v_2\) maximizes \(\|Xv\|_2^2\) among \(v \perp v_1\) and \(\|v\|_2=1, thus\)$ _jw_1,x_jsum_jv_1, x_j, _jw_2, x_jv_2, x_j $$ and thus \(V\) minimize \(\|x_j-P_W(x_j)\|^2_2\) among all 2-dim subspace.







Note



Proposition 11.2 meaning that the \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) we constructed form the best fitting subspace (2-dimensional) that minimizes projected least square error.




Definition 11.3 (r-right Singular Vector) The leading \(r\) right singular vectors \(v_1, \dots, v_r \in \mathbb{R}^d\) are defined as:
\[
v_k := \underset{
  \substack{
  \|v\|_2=1,\, \\ v \perp \text{span}\{v_1, \dots, v_{k-1}\}
  }
  }{\mathrm{argmax}}{} \|Xv\|_2
\]
with the corresponding singular values as \(\sigma_k = \|Xv_k\|_2\).


Proposition 11.3 (Greedy construction for best-fit subspace) Let \(v_1, \dots, v_r\) be the leading right singular vectors constructed by Definition 11.3, and \(V = \mathrm{span}(v_1, \dots, v_r) \subset \mathbb{R}^d\) be the subspace spanned by them. Then \[
V \in \underset{
  \substack{W\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \\ \mathrm{dim}(W) = r \\ \text{linear subspace}}
}{\mathrm{argmin}}\sum_j \|x_j - P_W(x_j)\|_2^2
\] i.e., \(V\) is the best-fit linear subspace in terms of least square error.


Remark 11.1. 

Proposition 11.3 can be proved similarly as in the 2 dimensional case (Proposition 11.2).
Proposition 11.3 shows that the greedy construction of r-right singularvectors formed a best-fit subspace in terms of least square error.

title: 11  Singular Value Decomposition
text:
11.2 Singular Value Decomposition

Theorem 11.1 (Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)) For any matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\), there exist orthogonal matrices \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) and \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) and a non-negative diagonal matrix \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) such that
\[
X_{n \times d} = U_{n \times n}\, \Sigma_{n \times d}\, V_{d \times d}^T
\]


Remark 11.2. 

The diagonals of \(\Sigma\), arranged in non-increasing order, are the singular values defined in Proposition 11.3.
Columns of \(U\) are the left singular vectors of \(X\).
The left singular vectors \(u_i := \frac{1}{\sigma_i} X v_i\), where \(\sigma_i\) is the \(i\)-th diagonal element of \(\Sigma\).
Columns of \(V\) are the right singular vectors of \(X\) defined in Proposition 11.3.
SVD can be viewed as ‘generalized diagonolization’ of an arbitrary matrix.


The existence of SVD can be shown as follow

Proof 11.1. Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) and \(C = X^T X \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\), then \(C\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite. Let the orthogonal decomposition of \(C\) be: \[
C = V \Lambda V^T,
\] where \(V^T V = I\) and \(\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots, \lambda_d), \lambda_i \geq 0 ,\forall i\in\{1, 2, \cdots, d\}\).
Consider \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) such that \(\Sigma^T \Sigma = \Lambda\). If \(\mathrm{rank}(X) = r \leq d\), we can arrange the diagonal element of \(\Lambda\) s.t. \(\lambda_1\geq\lambda_2\cdots\lambda_r\geq0,\lambda_{r+1} = \cdots=\lambda_d=0\). Then \[
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}
\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\cdots,\sqrt{\lambda_r}) & 0\\
0 & 0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
We define the left singular vector \(u_i\) as: \[
u_i := \frac{1}{\sigma_i} X v_i,\quad i = 1, \dots, r.
\] Then \(u_i\) are orthonormal: \[
u_i^T u_j = \frac{1}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} v_i^T X^T X v_j = \frac{1}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} v_i^T C v_j = \frac{1}{\sigma_i \sigma_j} \lambda_j \delta_{ij} = \delta_{ij}.
\] We can then extend \(u_{r+1}, \dots, u_n\) such that \(U = [u_1\,|\,u_2\,|\,\dots\,|\,u_n] \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is orthogonal.
Thus, we have \(\sigma_i u_i = X v_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots, r\) and \(X v_i = 0\) for \(i > r\), which gives \(X = U \Sigma V^T\).


Remark 11.3. This proof can be extended to \(X \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times d}\) with unitary matrices \(U\) and \(V\).

title: 11  Singular Value Decomposition
text:
11.3 Greedy Construction and SVD

Proposition 11.4 The SVD of \(X = U \Sigma V^T\) is the same as the greedy construction; i.e., \(V\) and \(\Sigma\) are right singular vectors and singular values constructed by the greedy definitions.


Proof 11.2. Let \(v_1' := \mathrm{argmax}_{\|v\|_2=1} \|Xv\|_2\) be the first right singular vector.
Write \(X = U \Sigma V^T\) where \(V = [v_1, \dots, v_d] \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) and \(v_i^T v_j = \delta_{ij}\).
Then: \[
\|Xv\|_2 = \|U \Sigma V^T v\|_2 = \|\Sigma V^T v\|_2
\] Let \(z = V^T v\), then \(\|z\|_2 = 1\) since \(V\) is orthogonal and \(\|v\|_2 = 1\).
So \[
\|Xv\|_2 = \|\Sigma z\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{i} (\sigma_i z_i)^2}
\] Suppose \(\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \dots \geq \sigma_r\). Notice \[
\sum \sigma_i^2 z_i^2 \leq \sigma_1^2 \left(\sum z_i^2\right) = \sigma_1^2
\] Equality is attained when \(z_1 = 1\) \(\Rightarrow v = v_1 \Rightarrow v_1' = v_1\).
Next, \(v_2' := \mathrm{argmax}_{\|v\|_2=1,\, v \perp v_1} \|Xv\|_2\). We proceed similarly, but now \(z_1 = 0\) (since \(v \perp v_1\)).
Then \[
\|Xv\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{i=2} (\sigma_i z_i)^2} \leq \sigma_2
\] Equality when \(z_2 = 1 \Rightarrow v_2' = v_2\).
Similarly, we find all \(v_i\) by the greedy construction.

title: 11  Singular Value Decomposition

11.4 Skinny SVD and Full SVD
Full SVD:
\[
X_{n \times d} = U_{n \times n} \Sigma_{n \times d} V_{d \times d}^T
\] where \(\mathrm{rank}(X) = r \leq \min(n, d)\).
Notice \((\sigma_{r+1}, \dots, \sigma_{\min(d,n)}) = 0\).
Truncated SVD (Skinny SVD):
Let - \(U_r := [u_1, \dots, u_r] \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}\) - \(V_r := [v_1, \dots, v_r] \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}\) - \(\Sigma_r = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_r)\)
then \[
X_{n \times d} = U_r \Sigma_r V_r^T = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T
\]

title: 11  Singular Value Decomposition
text:
11.5 Computing SVD

Power Method
Idea: Let \(C = X^T X \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) and \(X = U \Sigma V^T = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T\). Then
\[
C = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^2 v_i v_i^T
\quad\xrightarrow{\text{iterate}}\quad
C^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^4 v_i v_i^T
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
C^k = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^{2k} v_i v_i^T .
\]
If \(\sigma_1 > \sigma_2\), then for \(k\) large enough \(\sigma_1^{2k} \gg \sigma_2^{2k}\), so
\[
C^k \approx \sigma_1^{2k}\, v_1 v_1^T
\;\Rightarrow\;
C^k \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
= C^k e_1 \approx \sigma_1^{2k}\, v_1(1)\, v_1
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{C^k e_1}{\|C^k e_1\|_2} = \pm\, v_1 .
\]
Linear rate of convergence. To check the convergence rate, we look at
\[
\min\Big\{\, \|v^{(k)} - v_1\|_2^2,\ \|v^{(k)} + v_1\|_2^2 \,\Big\} = 2 - 2\,\big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_1\rangle\big|,
\qquad v^{(k)} := \frac{C^k e_1}{\|C^k e_1\|_2}.
\]
Since the \(v_i\) are orthonormal,
\[
1 = \|v^{(k)}\|_2^2 = \sum_{i} \big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_i\rangle\big|^2 = \big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_1\rangle\big|^2 + \sum_{i=2}^{r} \big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_i\rangle\big|^2 .
\]

For convergence we wish \(|\langle v^{(k)}, v_1\rangle| \approx 1\), i.e. the projection onto the other subspace is small:
\[
\frac{\sum_{i=2}^{r} \big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_i\rangle\big|^2}{\big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_1\rangle\big|^2}
= \frac{\sum_{i=2}^{r} \sigma_i^{4k}\, v_i^2(1)}{\sigma_1^{4k}\, v_1^2(1)}
\le \frac{\sum_{i=2}^{r} \sigma_i^{4k}}{\sigma_1^{4k}\, v_1^2(1)}
\le \frac{(r-1)\, \sigma_2^{4k}}{\sigma_1^{4k}\, \delta^2},
\qquad \text{if } |v_1(1)| \ge \delta > 0 ,
\]
hence
\[
\frac{1 - \big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_1\rangle\big|^2}{\big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_1\rangle\big|^2}
\le (r-1)\, \frac{\sigma_2^{4k}}{\sigma_1^{4k}\, \delta^2}
\;\longrightarrow\; \text{linear convergence, as } \sigma_2 < \sigma_1 .
\]

Remark. Computing \(C^k\) is costly \(\to\) compute \(C^k q\) instead; each step only needs a matrix–vector product (efficient when one dimension of \(X\) is small, or \(X\) is sparse).


The same analysis holds for an arbitrary starting vector \(q\) (not just \(e_1\)):

Proposition 11.5 (Convergence to the near-top singular subspace) Let \(q \in \mathbb{R}^d\) with \(|\langle q, v_1\rangle| \ge \delta > 0\), and let \(U\) be the linear subspace spanned by the \(v_i\) such that \(\sigma_i \ge (1-\varepsilon)\sigma_1\). Let \(v^{(k)} = \dfrac{C^k q}{\|C^k q\|_2}\) be the \(k\)-th power iteration. Then it can be shown that
\[
\big\|\operatorname{Proj}_{U^{\perp}}\big(v^{(k)}\big)\big\|_2 \le \varepsilon,
\qquad \forall\, \varepsilon > 0, \quad \text{when } k \ge \frac{\log(1/\varepsilon\delta)}{2\varepsilon}.
\]


Proof. Expand \(q = \sum_{i} c_i v_i\) in the orthonormal basis \(\{v_1, v_2, \dots, v_d\}\) of \(\mathbb{R}^d\). Then
\[
C^k q = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^{2k} v_i v_i^T \sum_{j} c_j v_j = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^{2k}\, c_i\, v_i,
\qquad
\|C^k q\|_2^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^{4k}\, c_i^2 .
\]
For the first (single-vector) case, with \(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \cdots\),
\[
\frac{\sum_{i=2}^{r} \big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_i\rangle\big|^2}{\big|\langle v^{(k)}, v_1\rangle\big|^2}
= \frac{\sum_{i=2}^{r} \sigma_i^{4k}\, c_i^2}{c_1^2\, \sigma_1^{4k}}
\le \frac{\sum_{i=2}^{r} \sigma_i^{4k}}{c_1^2\, \sigma_1^{4k}}
\le \Big(\tfrac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}\Big)^{4k}\, (r-1)\, \frac{1}{\delta^2},
\]
where we assume \(\|q\|_2 = 1\) and \(|c_1| = |\langle v_1, q\rangle| \ge \delta > 0\).
For the subspace statement, suppose \(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_m\) satisfy \(\sigma_i \ge (1-\varepsilon)\sigma_1\), so that the component of \(v^{(k)}\) orthogonal to \(U\) is composed of indices \(i = m+1, \dots, r\). Then
\[
\big\|\operatorname{Proj}_{U^{\perp}}\big(v^{(k)}\big)\big\|_2^2
= \frac{\sum_{i=m+1}^{r} \sigma_i^{4k}\, c_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{r} c_i^2\, \sigma_i^{4k}}
\le \frac{(1-\varepsilon)^{4k}\, \sigma_1^{4k}}{c_1^2\, \sigma_1^{4k}}
\le \frac{(1-\varepsilon)^{4k}\, \sigma_1^{4k}}{\delta^2\, \sigma_1^{4k}},
\]

hence
\[
\big\|\operatorname{Proj}_{U^{\perp}}\big(v^{(k)}\big)\big\|_2
\le \frac{(1-\varepsilon)^{2k}}{\delta}
\le \frac{e^{-2k\varepsilon}}{\delta}
\le \varepsilon
\qquad \text{when } k \ge \frac{\ln(1/\varepsilon\delta)}{2\varepsilon}.
\]


Remark. Note the above convergence analysis assumes \(\sigma_1 > \sigma_2\) strictly.  In fact, the power method converges to some vector in the span of the singular vectors with “nearly highest” singular value.
\(q\) can be chosen at random, e.g. \(q \sim N(0, I_d)\). When chosen randomly, \(|\langle q, v_1\rangle| \ge \delta > 0\) can be shown to hold with high probability.



Subspace (Orthogonal Iteration) Power Method
Finding the right singular vectors is the same as finding the eigenvectors of \(X^T X\). One can use the orthogonal iteration algorithm for that.
Let \(M \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\) be positive semidefinite with eigendecomposition \(M = V \Lambda V^T = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \lambda_i v_i v_i^T\).






Orthogonal iteration
Initialize \(Q_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times \ell}\), a random \(\ell\)-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
Repeat until convergence:

\(t + 1 \leftarrow t\)
\(Z_{t+1} = M \cdot Q_t\)
\(Q_{t+1} = \mathrm{QR}[Z_{t+1}]\), where \(\mathrm{QR}[Z] := Q\) when \(Z = QR\) is the QR decomposition.

\(Q\) then represents the first \(\ell\) right singular vectors.
