title: 11  Singular Value Decomposition
text:
11.6 Best rank-\(k\) Approximation

Recap on matrix norms
Frobenius norm \(\|\cdot\|_F\): \[
\|X\|_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i,j} x_{ij}^2} = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^2}
\quad (\sigma_i \text{ singular values}).
\]
Schatten \(p\)-norm \(\|\cdot\|_{S_p}\): operates on the singular values. For \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) with \(r \le \min(n,d)\) equal to \(\mathrm{rank}(X)\), \[
\|X\|_{S_p} := \Big(\sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^p(X)\Big)^{1/p}, \qquad 1 \le p < \infty .
\]

The spectral norm \(\|\cdot\|_2 = \|\cdot\|_{S_\infty} = \sigma_1\), and \(\|\cdot\|_F = \|\cdot\|_{S_2}\).
\(\displaystyle \|X - X_k\|_{S_p} = \min_{B:\ \mathrm{rank}(B) \le k} \|X - B\|_{S_p} = \Big(\sum_{i=k+1}^{r} \sigma_i^p\Big)^{1/p}\).



Best rank-\(k\) approximation

Definition 11.4 (\(k\)-truncated SVD) Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) with \(\mathrm{rank}(X) = r \le \min\{n, d\}\). The \(k\)-truncated SVD of \(X\) is \[
X_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T, \qquad k \in \{1, 2, \dots, r\},
\] where \(X = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T\) is the full SVD.


Theorem 11.2 (Best rank-\(k\) approximation (Eckart–Young–Mirsky)) \(X_k\) is the “best” rank-\(k\) approximation of \(X\) in terms of any orthogonally invariant norm \(\|\cdot\|\): \[
X_k = \underset{B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d},\ \mathrm{rank}(B) \le k}{\arg\min} \|X - B\| ,
\] i.e. \(X_k\) is the closest rank-\(k\) matrix to \(X\).


Remark. A norm \(\|\cdot\|\) is orthogonally invariant if \(\|O_1 X O_2\| = \|X\|\) for all \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) and all orthogonal \(O_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\), \(O_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\). Examples: the Frobenius norm \(\|\cdot\|_F\) and the spectral norm \(\|\cdot\|_2\).


Proof. Spectral norm. (In the manuscript \(A\) is used for \(X\) in this proof.) Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}\) with \(\mathrm{rank}(X) = r \le \min\{n,d\}\), \(X = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T\) and \(X_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T\). Then \[
\|X - X_k\|_2 = \Big\|\sum_{i=k+1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T\Big\|_2 = \sigma_{k+1},
\] so we hope to show \(\|X - B\|_2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}\) for any \(B\) with \(\mathrm{rank}(B) \le k\).
Consider \(w \in \mathbb{R}^d\) with unit norm \(\|w\|_2 = 1\). We can choose \(w \in \mathrm{Null}(B)\), i.e. \(Bw = 0\); on the other hand, we can also choose \(w \in \mathrm{span}\{v_1, \dots, v_{k+1}\}\). In this case \[
\|X w\|_2 = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 \cdots \sigma_{k+1}^2} \ge \sigma_{k+1} .
\]  Thus if \(w \in \mathrm{Null}(B) \cap \mathrm{span}\{v_1, \dots, v_{k+1}\}\), then \[
\|X - B\|_2 = \max_{v \in \mathbb{R}^d,\, \|v\|=1} \|(X-B)v\|_2 \ge \|(X-B)w\|_2 = \|X w\|_2 \ge \sigma_{k+1} .
\]


Proof. Frobenius norm. Consider \(\|X - B\|_F\), where \(\mathrm{rank}(B) = p \le k \le \mathrm{rank}(X) = r\). Denote \[
B = \begin{pmatrix} -\,b_1^T\,- \\ -\,b_2^T\,- \\ \vdots \\ -\,b_n^T\,- \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
X = \begin{pmatrix} -\,x_1^T\,- \\ -\,x_2^T\,- \\ \vdots \\ -\,x_n^T\,- \end{pmatrix}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\|X - B\|_F^2 = \|x_1 - b_1\|_2^2 + \cdots + \|x_n - b_n\|_2^2 .
\]
Let \(\{v_1, \dots, v_p\}\) be an orthonormal basis of the row subspace of \(B\), and extend to an orthonormal basis \(\{v_1, \dots, v_p, \dots, v_r\}\) for (the row space of) \(X\). Then expand \[
b_i = \beta_1^i v_1 + \beta_2^i v_2 + \cdots + \beta_p^i v_p, \qquad
x_i = \chi_1^i v_1 + \chi_2^i v_2 + \cdots + \chi_r^i v_r ,
\] so \[
\|b_i - x_i\|_2^2 = (\beta_1^i - \chi_1^i)^2 + \cdots + (\beta_p^i - \chi_p^i)^2 + \sum_{l=p+1}^{r} (\chi_l^i)^2 ,
\] which is minimized when \(b_i\) is the projection of \(x_i\) onto the subspace, i.e. \(\beta_1^i = \chi_1^i,\ \beta_2^i = \chi_2^i,\ \dots,\ \beta_p^i = \chi_p^i\). (This can be visualized in the 3D case, where the distance between two vectors is minimized when \(b_i\) is the projection of \(x_i\) onto the plane.)
Since we are looking over all subspaces \(V\) of dimension at most \(k\), there could be a specific subspace that is better. As claimed previously, the greedy construction of singular vectors minimizes the distance between the vectors and the orthogonal subspace, so \(\{v_1, \dots, v_k\}\) should be the first \(k\) singular vectors. The projection of \(X\) onto this subspace is \[
\hat{x}_j = (x_j^T v_1)v_1 + (x_j^T v_2)v_2 + \cdots + (x_j^T v_k)v_k , \qquad j = 1, \dots, n,
\] which gives \[
\hat{X} = \begin{pmatrix} -\,\hat{x}_1^T\,- \\ \vdots \\ -\,\hat{x}_n^T\,- \end{pmatrix}
= X \sum_{i=1}^{k} v_i v_i^T
= \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^T = X_k .
\]  Therefore \[
\|X - B\|_F \ge \|X - P_W^{p}(X)\|_F \ge \|X - P_W^{k}(X)\|_F \ge \|X - X_k\|_F .
\]

title: 12  Clustering
text:
12.1 The Easy Case
Given \(X = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\), find a disjoint partition \(X = \bigcup_i X_i\), with \(X_i \cap X_j = \emptyset\) for \(i \ne j\), such that points within \(X_i\) are “similar” to each other and “dissimilar” to points in \(X_j\) (\(i \ne j\)).
In an “easy” clustering case we have the following observation.
Observation. There exists a partition \(X = \bigcup_i X_i\) such that \[
\max_{\substack{x_i, x_j \in \text{ same } X_k}} \|x_i - x_j\|_2
\;\le\;
\min_{\substack{x_i, x_j \in \text{ different } X_k}} \|x_i - x_j\|_2 .
\]
In this case, define the distance matrix \(D_{ij} = \|x_i - x_j\|_2\), and let \(\text{LHS} < R < \text{RHS}\) of the inequality above. Then there exists a permutation \(\Pi : \{1, 2, \dots, n\} \to \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\) and a corresponding permutation matrix \[
P_\Pi = \begin{pmatrix} e_{\Pi(1)}^{\mathsf T} \\ e_{\Pi(2)}^{\mathsf T} \\ \vdots \\ e_{\Pi(n)}^{\mathsf T} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
e_i = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ \vdots \\ 1 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \leftarrow i,
\] such that \[
D_\Pi = P_\Pi\, D\, P_\Pi^{\mathsf T}
\] is “close” to a block-diagonal matrix: within a diagonal block \(D_{ij} < R\), and outside the diagonal blocks \(D_{ij} > R\).

title: 12  Clustering
text:
12.2 \(k\)-means Clustering
For \(X = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) with \(k\) partitions \(X = X_1 \cup X_2 \cup \dots \cup X_k\), and centers \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_k \in \mathbb{R}^d\), find the optimal \(\{X_i\}\) and \(\{\mu_i\}\) such that \[
\min_{\{X_j\}} \left( \min_{\{\mu_j\}} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x_j \in X_i} \|x_j - \mu_i\|_2^2 \right).
\]

Lemma 12.1 (Optimal centers for a fixed partition) For fixed \(\{X_j\}\), the minimizing centers are the cluster means: \[
\mu_j^* = \frac{1}{|X_j|} \sum_{x_i \in X_j} x_i,
\qquad
\{\mu_j^*\} = \underset{\{\mu_j\}}{\arg\min} \sum_{j} \sum_{x_i \in X_j} \|x_i - \mu_j\|_2^2 .
\]


Proof. Let \[
L = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{x_i \in X_j} \|x_i - \mu_j\|_2^2 = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{x_i \in X_j} \sum_{p} (x_{i,p} - \mu_{j,p})^2,
\] where \(x_{i,p}, \mu_{j,p}\) are the \(p\)-th components of \(x_i, \mu_j \in \mathbb{R}^d\). Then \[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mu_{\ell, q}}
= \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{x_i \in X_j} \sum_{p} 2(x_{i,p} - \mu_{j,p})\, \delta_{\ell j}\, \delta_{pq}
= \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{x_i \in X_j} 2(x_{i,q} - \mu_{j,q})\, \delta_{\ell j}
= \sum_{x_i \in X_\ell} 2(x_{i,q} - \mu_{\ell,q}^*) = 0,
\] hence \[
\sum_{x_i \in X_\ell} x_{i,q} - |X_\ell|\, \mu_{\ell,q}^* = 0
\;\Rightarrow\;
\mu_{\ell,q}^* = \frac{1}{|X_\ell|} \sum_{x_i \in X_\ell} x_{i,q},
\qquad \text{i.e.} \quad
\mu_\ell^* = \frac{1}{|X_\ell|} \sum_{x_i \in X_\ell} x_i .
\]


Lemma 12.2 (Optimal partition for fixed centers) For fixed \(\{\mu_j\}\), the minimizing partition assigns each point to its nearest center: \[
X_i^* = \Big\{ x_j \in X : \|x_j - \mu_i\|_2 \le \|x_j - \mu_{i'}\|_2,\ \forall\, i' \ne i \Big\},
\] with ties broken arbitrarily.


Proof. For fixed \(\{\mu_i\}\), the objective \[
\min_{\{X_j\}} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x_j \in X_i} \|x_j - \mu_i\|_2^2
= \min_{\{X_j\}} \Bigg[
\underbrace{\|x_1^1 - \mu_1\|_2^2 + \cdots + \|x_{|X_1|}^1 - \mu_1\|_2^2}_{x_i^1 \in X_1}
+ \underbrace{\|x_1^2 - \mu_2\|_2^2 + \cdots + \|x_{|X_2|}^2 - \mu_2\|_2^2}_{x_i^2 \in X_2}
+ \cdots
+ \underbrace{\|x_1^k - \mu_k\|_2^2 + \cdots + \|x_{|X_k|}^k - \mu_k\|_2^2}_{x_i^k \in X_k}
\Bigg].
\] Consider a point \(x_j \in X_i\) for which there exists \(\mu_k\) with \(\|x_j - \mu_k\|_2^2 \le \|x_j - \mu_i\|_2^2\). Then a new partition with \(X_i \leftarrow X_i - \{x_j\}\) and \(X_k \leftarrow X_k + \{x_j\}\) drops the objective value. Repeating this until no such case can be found, the objective is minimized when \[
X_i^* = \Big\{ x_j \in X : \|x_j - \mu_i\|_2 \le \|x_j - \mu_{i'}\|_2,\ \forall\, i' \ne i \Big\}.
\]

title: 12  Clustering
text:
12.3 Lloyd’s Algorithm
These two lemmas suggest an algorithm using alternating optimization.






Lloyd’s algorithm
Input: \(X = \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\), and \(k\).
Initialize: Choose \(k\) random initial guesses for the centers \(\mu_1^{(0)}, \dots, \mu_k^{(0)}\), and the correspondingly induced initial cluster assignment \(\hat{C}_1(0), \dots, \hat{C}_k(0)\) by associating each \(x_j\) to the closest center.
For \(t = 1, 2, \dots\) until convergence:

Use the current clusters \(\hat{C}_1(t-1), \dots, \hat{C}_k(t-1)\) to update the means: \[
\mu_j(t) = \frac{1}{|\hat{C}_j(t-1)|} \sum_{x_i \in \hat{C}_j(t-1)} x_i .
\]
Use the updated means to update the cluster assignments (assign \(x_i\) to its nearest cluster mean).





Convergence
Let \(X = X_1 \cup \dots \cup X_k\) and define the cost for a partition with optimal centers \[
L(X_1, \dots, X_k) := \sum_{i=1}^{k} \sum_{x_j \in X_i} \Big\| x_j - \tfrac{1}{|X_i|} \sum_{x_k \in X_i} x_k \Big\|^2 .
\]

Proposition 12.1 (Monotone decrease) In Lloyd’s algorithm, \[
L\big(X_1(t), \dots, X_k(t)\big) \ge L\big(X_1(t+1), \dots, X_k(t+1)\big).
\]


Proof. The updated (optimal) center is \(\hat{\mu}_j(t+1) = \frac{1}{|X_j(t)|} \sum_{x_i \in X_j(t)} x_i\), and the updated partition assigns each \(x_i\) to the nearest updated \(\mu_j\), so \(\forall x_i \in X_j\), \(\|x_i - \hat{\mu}_j\| \le \|x_i - \hat{\mu}_{j'}\|\) for \(j' \ne j\). By Lemma 12.1 and Lemma 12.2, \(\{X_j\}\) in Lloyd’s algorithm is the minimizer of \(L\), hence \[
L\big(X_1(t), \dots, X_k(t)\big) \ge L\big(X_1(t+1), \dots, X_k(t+1)\big).
\]


Corollary 12.1 (Finite termination) Let \(L(X_1(t), \dots, X_k(t))\) be the cost of Lloyd’s algorithm. Then \(\lim_{t \to \infty} L\) exists and is attained in finite time. Moreover, assuming all partitions have distinct cost (or the tie-breaking rule is chosen properly), the partition itself converges in finite time, i.e. \(\exists\, T > 0\) such that \[
\big(X_1(T), \dots, X_k(T)\big) = \big(X_1(T'), \dots, X_k(T')\big), \qquad T' \ge T.
\]


Proof. The existence of the limit follows because the loss drops monotonically (Proposition 12.1) and is bounded below by \(0\). Finite termination follows because the search space of partitions is always finite.



Complexity
At each iteration, Lloyd’s algorithm requires:

\(O(knd)\) time to assign \(n\) data points in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) to \(k\) centers (via \(\|\mu_i - x_j\|_2^2\));
\(O(nd)\) time to update the mean centers.


Remark. 

Lloyd’s algorithm is guaranteed to converge; however, it may only reach a local minimizer.
Random projection can be used to reduce time.
Lloyd’s is sensitive to initialization and may converge to various bad local minima.

title: 12  Clustering
text:
12.4 Initialization: \(k\)-means++
Since Lloyd’s algorithm is initialization-sensitive, one improvement is to initialize the mean centers as far apart as possible.






Farthest-point initialization
Pick \(\mu_1 \in \{x_1, \dots, x_N\}\) uniformly at random; set \(T = \{\mu_1\}\).
While \(|T| \le k\):

choose \(\mu_i \in X \setminus T\) that maximizes \(\min_{t \in T} \|x - t\|_2\);
\(T.\text{append}(\mu_i)\).




However, this initialization can be sensitive to outliers (an outlier very far from the rest would always be picked). The improvement is to add randomness, choosing farther points with higher probability.






\(k\)-means++
Pick \(\mu_1 \in X\) uniformly at random; set \(T = \{\mu_1\}\).
While \(|T| < k\):

pick \(\mu_{|T|+1} \in X \setminus T\) with probability \(\propto \min_{t \in T} \|x - t\|_2\);
\(T \leftarrow T \cup \{\mu_{|T|+1}\}\).





Remark. 

The initialization steps take \(O(knd)\), since we need \(\|x_j - t\|\) for \(x_j \in X\) (\(n\) of them) and \(t \in T\) (\(k\) of them) — same as one iteration of Lloyd’s.
This initialization does not guarantee anything by itself; however, it can be shown that the initial cost is “close” to the optimal cost by a factor of \(\log(k)\) on average.



Proposition 12.2 (\(k\)-means++ approximation guarantee) Let \(T \subseteq X\) be the initial means from \(k\)-means++, and \(T^* \subseteq X\) the optimal \(k\) centers. With the induced partition \(X_1 \cup X_2 \cup \dots \cup X_k = X\) chosen accordingly, define \[
L(T) := \min_{X_1 \cup \dots \cup X_k} \sum_{\mu_i \in T} \sum_{x_j \in X_i} \|x_j - \mu_i\|_2^2 .
\] Then \[
\mathbb{E}\big(L(T)\big) \le c \cdot O(\log k)\, L(T^*), \qquad c \text{ some constant.}
\]

title: 12  Clustering
text:
12.5 Geometric Interpretation
In Lloyd’s algorithm the partition for fixed means is updated via \[
X_i = \big\{ x \in X : \|x - \mu_i\| \le \|x - \mu_j\|,\ j \ne i \big\}.
\] Noting that \(\|x - \mu_i\|_2^2 \le \|x - \mu_j\|_2^2\) for \(i \ne j\), \[
\|x\|^2 + \|\mu_i\|^2 - 2\langle x, \mu_i\rangle \le \|x\|^2 + \|\mu_j\|^2 - 2\langle x, \mu_j\rangle
\;\Rightarrow\;
2\langle x, \mu_j - \mu_i\rangle \le \|\mu_j\|^2 + \|\mu_i\|^2 ,
\]  which defines a half-space separated by a hyperplane. Lloyd’s algorithm thus clusters into the intersection of \(k-1\) half-planes.


Remark. 

It can be shown that the partitions in Lloyd’s algorithm form a Voronoi diagram, and each cell is convex.
This means Lloyd’s algorithm essentially works with linearly separable, convex clusters.

title: 12  Clustering
text:
12.6 Kernel Trick and Kernel \(k\)-means
One way to deal with non-convex, non-linear clusters is to use dimension increasing: map the original data so that it becomes more linearly separable and convex in a higher dimension.

Example 12.1 (Lifting concentric data) Consider data in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (e.g. two concentric rings). Create the map \(\phi : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3\), \[
\phi(x_1, x_2) = \begin{pmatrix} x_1^2 \\ \sqrt{2}\, x_1 x_2 \\ x_2^2 \end{pmatrix},
\] after which the two rings become linearly separable in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).


However, boosting the dimension increases computational complexity. The kernel trick bypasses this by allowing implicit computation of the inner product of high-dimensional vectors via a low-dimensional function.
Example: let \(x, y \in \mathbb{R}^2\) and \(\phi(x) = (x_1^2, \sqrt{2}\, x_1 x_2, x_2^2)\), \(\phi(y) = (y_1^2, \sqrt{2}\, y_1 y_2, y_2^2)\). Then \[
\langle \phi(x), \phi(y)\rangle = x_1^2 y_1^2 + 2 x_1 x_2 y_1 y_2 + x_2^2 y_2^2 = (x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2)^2 = \langle x, y\rangle^2 =: K(x, y).
\]

Definition 12.1 (Kernel function) A symmetric map \(K : \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) is a kernel induced by \(\phi\) if there exists \(\phi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^n\) such that \[
K(x, y) = \langle \phi(x), \phi(y)\rangle .
\]


Remark. Examples:

\(K(x, y) = \langle x, y\rangle^r\);
\(K(x, y) = (\langle x, y\rangle + c)^r\);
\(K(x, y) = \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\|x - y\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\) — the Gaussian kernel.

For the Gaussian kernel, the inducing map is \(\phi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathcal{H}\), where \(\mathcal{H}\) is a Hilbert space.


Theorem 12.1 (Mercer’s theorem) Let \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d\) be a compact set and \(K : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}\) a continuous kernel. Define the linear integral operator associated with \(K\) on \(L^2\), \(T_K : L^2(X) \to L^2(X)\), as \[
T_K(f) := \int_X K(x, x')\, f(x')\, dx',
\] and suppose \(T_K\) is positive semidefinite, i.e. \[
\langle f, T_K f\rangle = \int_{X \times X} f(x)\, K(x, x')\, f(x')\, dx\, dx' \ge 0, \qquad \forall\, f \in L^2(X).
\] Then \(T_K\) has eigenfunctions \(\{\psi_i\}_{i=1,2,\dots} \in L^2\) with corresponding eigenvalues \(\lambda_i \in \mathbb{R}^+\) such that \[
K(x, x') = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \lambda_i\, \psi_i(x)\, \psi_i(x').
\]


Remark. This means we can view \(K(x, x')\) as induced by the feature map \(\varphi(x) := \big(\sqrt{\lambda_i}\, \psi_i(x)\big)_{i=1}^{\infty}\).


Kernel \(k\)-means
In Lloyd’s algorithm, the partition is updated based on the distance to the \(i\)-th center, \(\big\| x_j - \tfrac{1}{|X_i|} \sum_{x_i \in X_i} x_i \big\|_2^2\). We first show this distance can be expressed via inner products: \[
\Big\| x - \tfrac{1}{|X_i|} \sum_{x_j \in X_i} x_j \Big\|_2^2
= \langle x, x\rangle + \frac{1}{|X_i|^2} \sum_{x_j, x_k \in X_i} \langle x_j, x_k\rangle - \frac{2}{|X_i|} \sum_{x_j \in X_i} \langle x_j, x\rangle .
\] If we use a feature map \(\phi(x)\) to boost the dimension, then the distance in the transformed space can be expressed through the kernel: \[
\Big\| \phi(x) - \tfrac{1}{|X_i|} \sum_{x_j \in X_i} \phi(x_j) \Big\|_2^2
= K(x, x) + \frac{1}{|X_i|^2} \sum_{x_j, x_k \in X_i} K(x_j, x_k) - \frac{2}{|X_i|} \sum_{x_j \in X_i} K(x_j, x) .
\]
We modify Lloyd’s algorithm as follows to include the kernel.






Kernel \(k\)-means
Initialize: \(X_1^{(0)} \cup X_2^{(0)} \cup \dots \cup X_k^{(0)} = X\).
For \(t = 1, 2, \dots\) until convergence:
\[
X_i^{(t+1)} = \Big\{ x_j \in X : \big\| \phi(x_j) - \tfrac{1}{|X_i|} \textstyle\sum \phi(x_k) \big\|_2 \le \big\| \phi(x_j) - \tfrac{1}{|X_{i'}|} \textstyle\sum \phi(x_m) \big\|_2,\ \forall\, i' \ne i \Big\},
\]
where each distance is computed via the kernel expression above.




Remark. 

The distance is calculated using the expression with the kernel.
The centers are now not explicitly computed in feature space, but implicitly via kernels.
In practice, the kernels are precomputed each iteration.
Each iteration of kernel Lloyd’s takes \(O(N^2)\).

title: 13  Classification
text:
13.1 Support Vector Machine for Binary Classification
Given labelled training data, the goal of a classification problem is to predict a discrete label for each new (test) data point. This chapter develops the support vector machine (SVM) for binary classification, the Lagrangian duality theory behind its kernelized (dual) form, the soft-margin extension for non-separable data, and finally the reduction of multi-class classification to a collection of binary problems.
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 13  Classification
text:
The binary classification problem

Train data: \((\vec{x}_1, y_1), (\vec{x}_2, y_2), \dots, (\vec{x}_n, y_n)\) where \(\vec{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(y_i \in \{1, -1\}\).
Test data: \(\vec{x}_1, \vec{x}_2, \dots \in \mathbb{R}^d\).
Goal: predict a label \(1\) or \(-1\) for each \(\vec{x}_i\).



Linearly separable data
A binary problem is linearly separable if there exists an affine hyperplane \(\langle w, x\rangle - b\) that separates the data, i.e. \[
\exists\, w \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ b \in \mathbb{R}, \quad\text{s.t.}\quad
\operatorname{sign}\!\big(\langle w, x_i\rangle - b\big) = y_i,
\qquad \forall\, i = 1, 2, \dots, n .
\]
For a linearly separable problem there could be multiple choices of \(w\) and \(b\). A good choice for better generalization is to choose a plane that maximizes the margin.


Maximizing the margin
For linearly separable data, a separating plane \(\langle w, x\rangle - b = 0\) satisfies \[
\begin{cases}
\langle w, x_i\rangle - b \ge 0, & y_i = 1, \\
\langle w, x_i\rangle - b \le 0, & y_i = -1 .
\end{cases}
\] We may push the plane out on both sides until it touches the boundary of each class, giving the two supporting hyperplanes \[
\langle w, x\rangle - b = 1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\langle w, x\rangle - b = -1,
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
\begin{cases}
\langle w, x_i\rangle - b \ge 1, & y_i = 1, \\
\langle w, x_i\rangle - b \le -1, & y_i = -1 .
\end{cases}
\] The perpendicular distance between these two hyperplanes — the margin — is \[
\frac{2}{\|w\|_2} .
\]









Figure 13.1: Maximum-margin separating hyperplane. The solid line is the decision boundary \(\langle w,x\rangle - b = 0\); the two dashed lines are the supporting hyperplanes \(\langle w,x\rangle - b = \pm 1\); the circled points are the support vectors that lie on them. The margin (green) has width \(2/\|w\|_2\).





We wish to maximize this distance, so the classification objective is \[
\max_{w \in \mathbb{R}^d,\; b \in \mathbb{R}} \ \frac{2}{\|w\|_2}
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
\begin{cases}
w^{\mathsf T} x_i - b \ge 1, & \text{if } y_i = 1, \\
w^{\mathsf T} x_i - b \le -1, & \text{if } y_i = -1 .
\end{cases}
\]
Maximizing \(2/\|w\|_2\) is the same as minimizing \(\tfrac12\|w\|_2^2\), and the two constraints combine into the single condition \(y_i(\langle w, x_i\rangle - b)\ge 1\).

Definition 13.1 (Primal form of SVM) \[
\min_{w,\,b} \ \tfrac12 \|w\|_2^2
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
y_i\big(w^{\mathsf T} x_i - b\big) \ge 1,
\qquad \forall\, i = 1, \dots, n .
\]



Remark. 

The constraint condition is equivalent to the two-sided condition above.
This problem can be solved by constrained optimization methods.

title: 13  Classification
text:
13.2 Duality of Constrained Optimization
To introduce non-linearity into the SVM one uses the kernel trick. This requires the dual form of the SVM, so we first review the duality of a general constrained optimization problem.

The Lagrangian and the dual function
Consider the constrained optimization problem \[
\min_x \ f(x)
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
\begin{cases}
f_i(x) \le 0, & i = 1, \dots, m, \\
h_i(x) = 0, & i = 1, \dots, p .
\end{cases}
\] As in Lagrangian penalty methods, construct the Lagrangian \(L : D \times \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\), where \(D\) is the joint domain of the constraints: \[
L(x, \lambda, v) = f(x) + \sum_{i} \lambda_i f_i(x) + \sum_i v_i h_i(x) .
\]

Definition 13.2 (Lagrange dual function) The function \(g : \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \[
g(\lambda, v) := \min_{x \in D} L(x, \lambda, v)
\] is called the Lagrange dual function. When \(L\) is unbounded below, \(g \to -\infty\).



The primal value as a min–max

Remark. 

The optimal value \(p^\ast\) of the original problem is an upper bound of the dual function: \(g(\lambda, v) \le p^\ast\) for all \(\lambda \ge 0, v\).
The optimal value can be expressed as \[
p^\ast = \min_x \ \max_{\lambda \ge 0,\, v} \ L(x, \lambda, v).
\]


The second point is valid through the following argument. Observe that \[
\sup_{\lambda \ge 0,\, v} L(x, \lambda, v) =
\begin{cases}
f_0(x), & x \in D, \\
\infty, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\] Indeed, if \(x \notin D\) then there exists \(i\) with \(f_i(x) > 0\) or \(i\) with \(h_i(x) \ne 0\); either case lets us choose a proper \(\lambda_i\) or \(v_i\) so that \(L \to \infty\). Thus \[
\min_x \ \max_{\lambda,\, v} L = \min_{x \in D} f_0(x) = p^\ast .
\]


The min–max inequality

Theorem 13.1 (Min–max inequality) Let \(f : W \times Z \to \mathbb{R}\) with \(W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and \(Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m\). Then \[
\min_{w \in W} \ \max_{z \in Z} f(w, z) \ \ge\ \max_{z \in Z} \ \min_{w \in W} f(w, z) .
\]


Proof. Let \(w^0 \in W\). Then \[
\max_{z \in Z} f(w^0, z) \ge f(w^0, z), \qquad \forall\, z \in Z .
\] Next let \(z^0 \in Z\). Then \[
\min_{w \in W} f(w, z^0) \le f(w', z^0), \qquad \forall\, w' \in W .
\] Combining, \[
\min_{w \in W} f(w, z^0) \le f(w^0, z^0) \le \max_{z \in Z} f(w^0, z) .
\] Let \(h(z) = \min_{w \in W} f(w, z)\) and \(g(w) = \max_{z \in Z} f(w, z)\). Then \[
g(w) \ge h(z), \qquad \forall\, w \in W,\ z \in Z ,
\] so \(g(w) \ge \max_{z \in Z} h(z)\) for all \(w \in W\), and therefore \[
\min_{w \in W} g(w) \ge \max_{z \in Z} h(z)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\min_{w \in W} \max_{z \in Z} f(w, z) \ge \max_{z \in Z} \min_{w \in W} f(w, z) . \qquad\blacksquare
\]

Applying this inequality to the primal problem yields the Lagrange dual problem.


The Lagrange dual problem

Definition 13.3 (Dual problem) Let \(L\) be the Lagrangian of the primal problem. The corresponding dual problem is \[
\max_{\lambda \ge 0,\, v} \ g(\lambda, v) .
\]


Remark. From Theorem 13.1, the primal and dual are related by \[
p^\ast = \min_x \ \max_{\lambda \ge 0,\, v} L(x, \lambda, v)
\ \ge\
\max_{\lambda \ge 0,\, v} \ \min_x L(x, \lambda, v) = d^\ast ,
\] so the dual optimum \(d^\ast\) bounds the primal optimum \(p^\ast\) from below.


Weak duality and duality gap. When \(d^\ast < p^\ast\), we have weak duality, and \(p^\ast - d^\ast\) is called the duality gap.
Strong duality and Slater’s condition. When \(d^\ast = p^\ast\) holds, we have strong duality. A specific condition that must hold for strong duality is called a constraint qualification; one simple example is Slater’s condition.

Proposition 13.1 (Slater’s condition) For the primal problem \[
\min_x \ f_0(x)
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
\begin{cases}
f_i(x) \le 0, & i = 1, \dots, m, \\
A x = b,
\end{cases}
\] Slater’s condition holds if

\(f_0, f_1, \dots, f_m\) are convex, and
there exists \(x \in D\) such that \(f_i(x) < 0\) for \(i = 1, \dots, m\) and \(Ax = b\).

title: 13  Classification
text:
13.3 Kernel SVM: The Dual Form
Back to the SVM objective: it is not hard to see that the primal SVM satisfies Slater’s condition. Thus we can find the dual form of the SVM using the Lagrangian \[
L = \tfrac12 \|w\|_2^2 + \sum_i \lambda_i\Big(-\big(\langle w, x_i\rangle - b\big) y_i + 1\Big) .
\]
We first find \(\min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^d,\, b \in \mathbb{R}} L\) for the Lagrange dual function. Setting the derivatives to zero, \[
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w_i} = w_i - \displaystyle\sum_j \lambda_j x_j^{\,i} y_j = 0, \\[2mm]
\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial b} = \displaystyle\sum_i y_i \lambda_i = 0,
\end{cases}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\begin{cases}
w^\ast = \tfrac12 \displaystyle\sum_i y_i \lambda_i x_i, \\[2mm]
\displaystyle\sum_i y_i \lambda_i = 0 .
\end{cases}
\]

Substituting back, \[
\min_{w,\,b} L =
\begin{cases}
\tfrac12 \|w^\ast\|_2^2 + \displaystyle\sum_i \lambda_i\Big(-\big(\langle w^\ast, x_i\rangle - b\big) y_i + 1\Big), & \sum_i y_i \lambda_i = 0, \\
-\infty, & \sum_i y_i \lambda_i \ne 0 .
\end{cases}
\] (If \(\sum_i y_i \lambda_i \ne 0\), the term \(-b \sum_i \lambda_i y_i\) can be driven to \(\to -\infty\).) The two pieces evaluate to \[
\tfrac12 \|w^\ast\|_2^2 = \tfrac12 \langle w^\ast, w^\ast\rangle
= \tfrac18 \sum_{i,j} y_i y_j \lambda_i \lambda_j \langle x_i, x_j\rangle,
\] \[
\sum_i \lambda_i\Big(-\big(\langle w^\ast, x_i\rangle - b\big) y_i + 1\Big)
= -\sum_i \lambda_i \langle w^\ast, x_i\rangle y_i + \sum_i \lambda_i
= -\tfrac12 \sum_{i,j} \lambda_i \lambda_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j\rangle + \sum_i \lambda_i .
\] Therefore \[
\min_{w,\,b} L =
\begin{cases}
-\tfrac14 \displaystyle\sum_{i,j} \lambda_i \lambda_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j\rangle + \sum_i \lambda_i, & \sum_i y_i \lambda_i = 0, \\
-\infty, & \sum_i y_i \lambda_i \ne 0 .
\end{cases}
\]

Definition 13.4 (Dual form of SVM) \[
\max_{\lambda \ge 0} \ -\tfrac14 \sum_{i,j} \lambda_i \lambda_j y_i y_j \langle x_i, x_j\rangle + \sum_i \lambda_i
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
\sum_i y_i \lambda_i = 0 .
\]


Remark. In the dual form, \(x_i\) appears only as an inner product \(\langle x_i, x_j\rangle\), and can be replaced with a kernel function — this is the kernel trick.

title: 13  Classification
text:
13.4 Soft Margin for Non-separable Data
In many cases the data are not (strictly) linearly separable. The solution is to introduce a “soft” margin that allows misclassification. The constraints are modified to \[
y_i\big(\langle w, x_i\rangle - b\big) \ge 1 - \xi_i .
\]

Remark. 

Instead of the hard constraint that all data of a class lie on one side of the hyperplane, soft margins allow a set of hyperplanes that permit some violations.
We would hope the slack variables \(\xi_i\) are not too large.



Primal problem with soft margin
\[
\min_{w,\,b,\,\xi} \ \tfrac12 \|w\|_2^2 + C \sum_i \xi_i
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
y_i\big(\langle w, x_i\rangle - b\big) \ge 1 - \xi_i, \quad \xi_i \ge 0 .
\]

Here \(C\) (written \(\lambda\) in one place in the source) is the regularization parameter.



Dual problem with soft margin
Following a similar procedure to the hard-constraint problem, the dual form of the soft margin is \[
\max_{\lambda \ge 0} \ \sum_i \lambda_i - \tfrac14 \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_j y_i y_j \lambda_i \lambda_j \langle x_i, x_j\rangle
\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad
\sum_i \lambda_i y_i = 0 \ \ \&\ \ \lambda_i \le \frac{1}{2n\lambda} .
\]

title: 13  Classification
text:
13.5 Multi-class Classification
The multi-class classification problem can be reduced to the binary case using the “one-vs-all” scheme.
For a multi-class problem the data set is \((\vec{x}_1, y_1), \dots, (\vec{x}_n, y_n)\) as before, but now \(y_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, C-1\}\), for a total of \(C\) distinct classes.

One-vs-all scheme
The goal of a multi-class classifier is: given a data point, decide that it is in the \(i\)-th class and not in any other class. Therefore, for each class we can construct a binary classification problem — is the data point in this class or not? — which gives a decision boundary between points in this class and those not in it. Doing this for all classes yields a classification region based on these boundaries.
Example (3 classes). We build three binary classifiers, one for each of classes \(1, 2, 3\). For each binary classifier we create the one-vs-all label \[
\hat{y}_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if } y_i \text{ is in class } c, \\
-1, & \text{if not},
\end{cases}
\qquad c = 1, 2, 3 .
\] This creates \(3\) decision boundaries, one per class.

Each line separates the space into a region “\(\in C\)” and the other side “\(\notin C\)”. As before, if the weight for the classifier of class \(c\) is \(\vec{w}_c\), then \[
\begin{cases}
x_i^{\mathsf T} w_c - b > 0 \ \Rightarrow\ x_i \in C, \\
x_i^{\mathsf T} w_c - b < 0 \ \Rightarrow\ x_i \notin C .
\end{cases}
\] This separates the space into subdomains.


Decision regions
Combining the binary boundaries, a test point falls into one of three cases.
(1) Positive side of exactly one boundary. The straightforward case: the point is on the positive side of exactly one boundary and on the negative side of all others. Then the predicted class is the one on whose positive side it lies: \[
\hat{y}_i = \arg\max_c \big(x_i^{\mathsf T} w_c - b\big) .
\]
(2) Positive side of more than one boundary. The point could plausibly belong to two classes; we should choose the one that is more “plausible”. Note that for a binary classifier, a point further from the boundary is considered more confident, whereas a point closer to the boundary is more likely to be mistakenly labelled. Thus we use the distance to the decision boundary as a decision indicator: the class is the boundary that is furthest. The distance from \(x_i\) to the boundary for class \(c\) is \[
\frac{x_i^{\mathsf T} w_c - b_c}{\|w_c\|_2},
\] so \[
\hat{y}_i = \arg\max_{c = 0, \dots, C-1} \ \frac{x_i^{\mathsf T} w_c - b_c}{\|w_c\|_2} .
\]
(3) Negative side of all boundaries. We decide the class as the opposite of case (2): when a point is further from a boundary, it is more confident of not being in that class, so we assign the class whose boundary has the smallest distance. Since \(\dfrac{x_i^{\mathsf T} w_c - b_c}{\|w_c\|_2}\) is the signed distance, \[
\hat{y}_i
= \arg\min_c \ -\frac{x_i^{\mathsf T} w_c - b_c}{\|w_c\|_2}
= \arg\max_c \ \frac{x_i^{\mathsf T} w_c - b_c}{\|w_c\|_2} .
\]
All three cases therefore reduce to the same rule: predict the class with the largest signed distance.








Figure 13.2: Multi-class one-vs-all decision regions for \(3\) classes. Each pair of regions is separated by a linear boundary; a test point is assigned to the class with the largest normalized signed distance \(\dfrac{x^{\mathsf T} w_c - b_c}{\|w_c\|_2}\).







General procedure
The 3-class example extends to the general multi-class case, summarized as follows.






One-vs-all multi-class classification



Input: \(\{(\vec{x}_i, y_i)\}\) with \(y_i \in \{0, 1, \dots, C-1\}\).
For \(c = 0, \dots, C-1\):

Relabel each sample \(p\) by \[
\hat{y}_p =
\begin{cases}
+1, & \text{if } y_p = c, \\
-1, & \text{else}.
\end{cases}
\]
Solve the binary subproblem \(\{(\vec{x}_p, \hat{y}_p)\} \to (w_c, b_c)\).
Normalize the weights: \(\displaystyle w_c \leftarrow \frac{w_c}{\|w_c\|_2}, \quad b_c \leftarrow \frac{b_c}{\|w_c\|_2}\).

Predict the label by \(\hat{y} = \arg\max_c \ x^{\mathsf T} w_c\).




Remark. 

The normalization does not change the decision in case (1).
In practice one can use one-hot encoding, e.g. a class-\(1\) target \[
\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ \vdots \end{pmatrix}
\]

title: 14  Regression
text:
14.1 Linear (Ridge) Regression
Given a training set of predictor–response pairs, the goal of a regression problem is to learn a function \(f\) that predicts a (continuous) response from the predictors. This chapter develops linear and ridge regression, their solution via the normal equations, the extension to polynomial (linear-in-parameters) regression, and finally kernel regression together with the Woodbury identity that makes it computationally tractable.
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 14  Regression
text:
The general regression task

Let \(y_i \in \mathbb{R}\), \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\) be the response variables.
Let \(x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d\), \(i = 1, 2, \dots, N\) be the predictors.
The pairs \(\{(x_i, y_i)\}\) form the training set.

The regression task wishes to find a function \(f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) such that \(f(x_i) \approx y_i\), and that generalizes to the test set. This requires two ingredients:

a function form (parametric methods) — i.e. assume a family for \(f\);
a measure / metric for \(f(x_i) \approx y_i\) (the loss function).



Least squares (linear regression)
Take \(f\) to be linear: \[
y = w^{\mathsf T} x + b, \qquad w \in \mathbb{R}^d,\ b \in \mathbb{R},
\] or simply \(y = w^{\mathsf T} x\) if we absorb the bias by extending \[
x \ \longrightarrow\ \begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ \vdots \\ x_d \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} .
\] 
For the metric, use the least-square error \[
\min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^d} \ \sum_i \big(y_i - \langle w, x_i\rangle\big)^2
\qquad\longrightarrow\qquad \text{error between predicted and actual,}
\] or, in matrix form, \(\|Y - Xw\|_2^2\) if we denote \[
Y = \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ \vdots \\ y_N \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^N,
\qquad
X = \begin{pmatrix} x_1^{\mathsf T} \\ x_2^{\mathsf T} \\ \vdots \\ x_N^{\mathsf T} \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d} .
\] 


Ridge regression (regularization)
In some cases \(f\) could overfit (e.g. matching noise). This can be reduced by adding a regularization term to the loss function, as a penalty for too-large coefficients: \[
\min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^d} \ \|Y - Xw\|_2^2 + \lambda \|w\|_2^2, \qquad \lambda \ge 0 .
\]
From optimization theory, the resulting minimization problem is a strictly convex function (for \(\lambda > 0\)), so every local minimum is the global minimum.

Proposition 14.1 (Ridge regression solution (normal equations)) For \(\lambda > 0\), the ridge objective has the unique minimizer \[
w^\ast = \arg\min_w \ \|Xw - Y\|_2^2 + \lambda \|w\|_2^2
= \big(X^{\mathsf T} X + \lambda I\big)^{-1} X^{\mathsf T} y .
\]


Proof. (Sketch.) Set the gradient to zero, \(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w_i} = 0\), and check the Hessian \(\dfrac{\partial^2 L}{\partial w_i \partial w_j}\). This is straightforward since \(L\) is in quadratic form (and the \(\lambda I\) term makes \(X^{\mathsf T} X + \lambda I\) positive definite, hence invertible). \(\blacksquare\)


Remark. Choice of regularizer.

\(\lambda \|w\|_1 = \lambda \sum_i |w_i|\) — promotes a sparse weight vector.
\(\|w\|_\ast = \sum_i \sigma_i(w)\) (the nuclear norm) — promotes a low-rank matrix.



Remark. Multiple-label predictors. If \(y_i \in \mathbb{R}^p\) (multiple labels), we simply extend to a matrix of weights \(W \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times d}\): \[
y_i = W x_i,
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} y_1^i \\ \vdots \\ y_p^i \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
w_{11} & w_{12} & \cdots & w_{1d} \\
\vdots & & & \vdots \\
w_{p1} & w_{p2} & \cdots & w_{pd}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} x_1^i \\ \vdots \\ x_d^i \end{pmatrix} ,
\] and with \[
Y = \begin{pmatrix} y_1^{\mathsf T} \\ \vdots \\ y_N^{\mathsf T} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
X = \begin{pmatrix} x_1^{\mathsf T} \\ \vdots \\ x_N^{\mathsf T} \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
L = \|X W^{\mathsf T} - Y\|_F^2 + \lambda \|W\|_F^2 .
\]

title: 14  Regression
text:
14.2 Polynomial Regression
\(f\) need not be linear, as long as it is linear in its parameters.
Example (3rd-order polynomial fit). \[
y = w_3^{\mathsf T} x^3 + w_2^{\mathsf T} x^2 + w_1^{\mathsf T} x
= \big(\, w_3^{\mathsf T} \mid w_2^{\mathsf T} \mid w_1^{\mathsf T} \,\big)
\begin{pmatrix} x^3 \\ x^2 \\ x \end{pmatrix} ,
\] where \(x^k\) denotes the monomial (elementwise-power) feature expansion. This shares the same form as linear regression, so the same solution applies.

title: 14  Regression
text:
14.3 Kernel Regression
The kernel trick can be applied to the features \(x\). Suppose \(\phi : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^p\) is a feature map that transforms the original data to \[
\big(\phi(x_1), y_1\big), \big(\phi(x_2), y_2\big), \dots, \big(\phi(x_n), y_n\big)
\in \mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R} .
\] Then perform linear ridge regression in the transformed feature space: \[
\min_{w \in \mathbb{R}^p} \ \sum_i \big(w^{\mathsf T} \phi(x_i) - y_i\big)^2 + \lambda \|w\|_2^2 .
\] From Proposition 14.1, the optimal solution is \[
w^\ast = \big(\Phi^{\mathsf T}\Phi + \lambda I_p\big)^{-1} \Phi^{\mathsf T} y,
\qquad
\Phi = \begin{pmatrix} \phi(x_1)^{\mathsf T} \\ \phi(x_2)^{\mathsf T} \\ \vdots \\ \phi(x_N)^{\mathsf T} \end{pmatrix}
\in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p} .
\] Just as before, directly computing \(\phi\) and \(w^\ast\) is very costly when \(p\) is large. We want to apply the kernel trick, which relies on the following identity.

The Woodbury identity

Lemma 14.1 (Woodbury matrix identity) \[
\big(\Phi^{\mathsf T}\Phi + \lambda I_p\big)^{-1} \Phi^{\mathsf T}
= \Phi^{\mathsf T} \big(\Phi\Phi^{\mathsf T} + \lambda I_n\big)^{-1} .
\]



Proof. Take the SVD \(\Phi = U \Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\) (so \(\Phi^{\mathsf T} = V \Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T}\), \(\Phi^{\mathsf T}\Phi = V \Sigma^{\mathsf T}\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\), and \(\Phi\Phi^{\mathsf T} = U \Sigma \Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T}\)).

Left-hand side. Using \(U^{\mathsf T} U = I\) and \(I_p = V V^{\mathsf T}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{LHS}
&= \big((V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T})(U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}) + \lambda I_p\big)^{-1} V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T} \\
&= \big(V\Sigma^{\mathsf T}\Sigma V^{\mathsf T} + \lambda V V^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T} \\
&= \big(V(\Sigma^{\mathsf T}\Sigma + \lambda I_p) V^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T} \\
&= V(\Sigma^{\mathsf T}\Sigma + \lambda I_p)^{-1} V^{\mathsf T} V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T}
= V(\Sigma^{\mathsf T}\Sigma + \lambda I_p)^{-1}\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T} .
\end{aligned}
\]
Right-hand side. Using \(I_n = U U^{\mathsf T}\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{RHS}
&= V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T}\big((U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T})(V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T}) + \lambda I_n\big)^{-1} \\
&= V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T}\big(U\Sigma\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T} + \lambda U U^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} \\
&= V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T}\big(U(\Sigma\Sigma^{\mathsf T} + \lambda I_n) U^{\mathsf T}\big)^{-1} \\
&= V\Sigma^{\mathsf T} U^{\mathsf T} U(\Sigma\Sigma^{\mathsf T} + \lambda I_n)^{-1} U^{\mathsf T}
= V\Sigma^{\mathsf T}(\Sigma\Sigma^{\mathsf T} + \lambda I_n)^{-1} U^{\mathsf T} .
\end{aligned}
\]
A detailed calculation on \(\Sigma^{\mathsf T}(\Sigma\Sigma^{\mathsf T} + \lambda I_n)^{-1}\) and \((\Sigma^{\mathsf T}\Sigma + \lambda I_p)^{-1}\Sigma^{\mathsf T}\) shows that both equal the same \(p \times n\) “pseudo-diagonal” matrix with entries \(\dfrac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2 + \lambda}\). Thus \(\text{LHS} = \text{RHS}\). \(\blacksquare\)



Kernel ridge regression prediction

Theorem 14.1 (Kernel ridge regression predictor) Using Lemma 14.1, the prediction at a new point \(x\) is \[
y = w^{\ast\mathsf T}\phi(x)
= \phi(x)^{\mathsf T} \Phi^{\mathsf T}\big(\Phi\Phi^{\mathsf T} + \lambda I_n\big)^{-1} y
= k_x^{\mathsf T}\big(K + \lambda I_n\big)^{-1} y ,
\] where \(K_{ij} = \phi(x_i)^{\mathsf T}\phi(x_j) = K(x_i, x_j)\) is the kernel (Gram) matrix, and \(k_x = \Phi\phi(x)\) has entries \((k_x)_i = \phi(x_i)^{\mathsf T}\phi(x) = K(x_i, x)\).


Proof. Expanding the products directly, \[
\Phi\Phi^{\mathsf T}
= \begin{pmatrix} \phi(x_1)^{\mathsf T} \\ \vdots \\ \phi(x_n)^{\mathsf T} \end{pmatrix}
\big(\phi(x_1), \ \dots, \ \phi(x_n)\big)
= \begin{pmatrix}
\phi(x_1)^{\mathsf T}\phi(x_1) & \phi(x_1)^{\mathsf T}\phi(x_2) & \cdots \\
\vdots & \ddots & \\
\end{pmatrix}
= \big(K(x_i, x_j)\big) = K ,
\] and \[
\Phi\phi(x)
= \begin{pmatrix} \phi(x_1)^{\mathsf T} \\ \vdots \\ \phi(x_n)^{\mathsf T} \end{pmatrix} \phi(x)
= \begin{pmatrix} \phi(x_1)^{\mathsf T}\phi(x) \\ \vdots \\ \phi(x_n)^{\mathsf T}\phi(x) \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} K(x_1, x) \\ \vdots \\ K(x_n, x) \end{pmatrix} = k_x . \qquad\blacksquare
\]



Computational cost






Cost of kernel ridge regression



Using the kernel trick, the cost breaks down as:

Precompute \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) — cost \(O(n^2)\) kernel evaluations.
Precompute \((K + \lambda I_n)^{-1} y\) — cost \(O(n^3)\) flops and \(O(n)\) storage. 
Compute \(k_x\) — cost \(O(n)\) kernel evaluations.
Compute \(k_x^{\mathsf T}(K + \lambda I_n)^{-1} y\) — cost \(O(n)\) flops.

title: 15  Markov Chains
text:
15.1 Discrete-Time Markov Chains
A discrete-time Markov chain is a sequence of random variables in which each step depends only on the previous one (the Markov property), which greatly simplifies the calculation of long-time transition probabilities. This chapter covers the definition and transition matrix, \(n\)-step transition probabilities, communicating classes and irreducibility, stationary (invariant) distributions, periodicity, and the convergence theorems — the last of which underpin Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods.
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 15  Markov Chains
text:
Definition 15.1 (Discrete-time Markov chain) A sequence of random variables \((X_n)_{n \ge 0}\), where \(X_n : \Omega \to S \subseteq \mathbb{Z}\), is called a Markov chain with initial distribution \(\lambda\) if

\(X_0\) has distribution \(\lambda\);
it satisfies the Markov property \[
P\big(X_{n+1} = i_{n+1} \mid X_n = i_n, \dots, X_0 = i_0\big)
= P\big(X_{n+1} = i_{n+1} \mid X_n = i_n\big) .
\]



Remark. 

\(X_n\) denotes the state of the chain at time \(n\).
\(S\) is the state space — all possible outcomes of each state.
Writing \(P(X_{n+1} = i_{n+1} \mid X_n = i_n) = P_{i_n i_{n+1}}\), then for finite \(S\) the matrix \(P \in \mathbb{R}^{|S| \times |S|}\) is the transition matrix, and \(P_{i_n i_{n+1}}\) is the transition probability from state \(i_n\) to \(i_{n+1}\).
Being probabilities, the entries satisfy \[
P_{ij} \ge 0, \qquad \sum_{j \in S} P_{ij} = 1 .
\]
crumbs: Machine Learning and Data Science Basics

title: 15  Markov Chains
text:
15.2 \(n\)-Step Transition Probabilities
The Markov property and the total-probability formula let us compute the \(n\)-step transition probability from the single-step transition matrix. We wish to calculate the probability that the chain is at state \(j\) after \(n\) steps starting from \(i\), and, more generally, the probability of being at \(j\) after \(n\) steps from any initial state.

Theorem 15.1 (\(n\)-step transition probability) Let \((X_n)_{n \ge 0}\) be a Markov chain with initial distribution \(\lambda\) and transition matrix \(P\). Then for all \(n, m \ge 0\):

\(P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) = (P^n)_{ij}\);
\(P(X_n = j) = (\lambda P^n)_j\).



Proof. The calculation is straightforward using total probability and the Markov property. For (2), sum over all intermediate paths and apply the Markov property repeatedly: \[
\begin{aligned}
P(X_n = j)
&= \sum_{i_0 \in S} \cdots \sum_{i_{n-1} \in S}
P\big(X_n = j \mid X_{n-1} = i_{n-1}, \dots, X_0 = i_0\big)\, P\big(X_{n-1} = i_{n-1}, \dots, X_0 = i_0\big) \\
&= \sum_{i_0} \cdots \sum_{i_{n-1}}
P\big(X_n = j \mid X_{n-1} = i_{n-1}\big)\, P\big(X_{n-1} = i_{n-1} \mid X_{n-2} = i_{n-2}\big) \cdots P\big(X_1 = i_1 \mid X_0 = i_0\big)\, P(X_0 = i_0) \\
&= \sum_{i_0} \cdots \sum_{i_{n-1}} \lambda_{i_0}\, P_{i_0 i_1} P_{i_1 i_2} \cdots P_{i_{n-1} j}
= (\lambda P^n)_j .
\end{aligned}
\] For (1), condition on \(X_0 = i\) (so \(\lambda\) is replaced by a point mass at \(i\)): \[
P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i)
= \sum_{i_1 \in S} \cdots \sum_{i_{n-1} \in S} P_{i\, i_1} P_{i_1 i_2} \cdots P_{i_{n-1} j}
= (P^n)_{ij} . \qquad \blacksquare
\]


Remark. 

Using the matrix form assumes a finite state space; the summation identity, however, remains true when the state space is infinite.
Statement (1) extends to the Chapman–Kolmogorov form \[
P(X_{n+m} = j \mid X_n = i) = (P^m)_{ij} .
\]

title: 15  Markov Chains
text:
15.3 Communicating Classes and Irreducibility
We now examine the asymptotic behavior of the state distribution: as \(n \to \infty\), does the chain tend to an equilibrium? Different states can behave very differently. The following example illustrates this.








Figure 15.1: A 4-state chain. State \(1\) is transient: it has a self-loop (\(0.2\)) and leads to state \(4\) (\(0.5\)) and to state \(2\) (\(0.3\)). State \(4\) is absorbing (self-loop \(1\)), forming the closed class \(\{4\}\). States \(\{2,3\}\) form a second closed communicating class. Once the chain leaves \(1\) it is trapped in \(\{4\}\) or \(\{2,3\}\) and never returns to \(1\).






For the chain above, note that:

State \(1\) can access \(2, 3, 4\), while \(2, 3, 4\) cannot access \(1\).
Once the chain enters state \(2\), it only transitions within \(\{2, 3\}\); similarly \(4\) is absorbing.
When \(n\) is large enough, the state is “trapped” in \(\{4\}\) or \(\{2, 3\}\).

The following definitions formalize this observation.

Definition 15.2 (Leads to / accessible) We say state \(i\) leads to \(j\) (equivalently, \(j\) is accessible from \(i\)) if there exists a finite sequence \(i_1, i_2, \dots, i_{n-1}\) such that \[
P_{i\, i_1} > 0, \ P_{i_1 i_2} > 0, \ \dots, \ P_{i_{n-1} j} > 0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) > 0 \ \text{ for some } n \ge 0 .
\]


Definition 15.3 (Communicate) We say \(i\) and \(j\) communicate if \(i\) leads to \(j\) and \(j\) leads to \(i\).


Definition 15.4 (Communicating class and closed class)  

A set of states is a communicating class (or recurrent class) if every pair \(i, j\) in it communicate. (Equivalently, a strongly connected component when the chain is viewed as a graph.)
A communicating class \(C\) is closed if, for every \(i \in C\), whenever \(i\) leads to \(j\) then \(j \in C\).



Remark. 

Once the chain enters a closed class, it never leaves.
An absorbing state is simply a singleton \(\{i\}\) that is a closed class.
If a state \(i\) is not in any (closed) communicating class, then there is a state \(j\) accessible from \(i\) but with \(i\) not accessible from \(j\); for large \(n\) the \(i \to j\) transition occurs and the chain never returns. Hence we will focus on chains with a single communicating class, called irreducible.

title: 15  Markov Chains
text:
15.4 Stationary (Invariant) Distributions
For an irreducible chain, does the probability of being in each state stabilize in the long run? By “stable” we mean that the state distribution does not change after a transition — hence the following definition.

Definition 15.5 (Stationary / invariant distribution) Let \(\lambda\) denote the probability distribution of state \(X\), i.e. \(\lambda_i = P(X = i)\). We say \(\lambda\) is a stationary (or invariant) distribution if \[
\lambda = \lambda P, \qquad \sum_i \lambda_i = 1 .
\]


Remark. The definition means that a one-step transition of the current distribution, \[
\sum_j \lambda_j P_{ji} = \lambda_i ,
\] leaves it unchanged.

It can be shown that if the transition probability converges to a number independent of the initial state, then the limiting distribution is stationary/invariant (for finite state space).

Theorem 15.2 (A convergent limit is invariant) Let the state space \(S\) of a Markov chain \((X_n)_{n \ge 0}\) be finite, and suppose that for some \(i \in S\), \[
P(X_n = j \mid X_0 = i) = (P^n)_{ij} \to \pi_j \quad\text{as } n \to \infty, \ \ \forall j \in S .
\] Then \(\pi\) is an invariant distribution.


Proof. Using \((P^n)_{ij} = \sum_{k \in S} (P^{n-1})_{ik} P_{kj}\) and interchanging limit and (finite) sum, \[
\pi_j = \lim_{n \to \infty} (P^n)_{ij}
= \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{k \in S} (P^{n-1})_{ik} P_{kj}
= \sum_{k \in S} \Big(\lim_{n \to \infty} (P^{n-1})_{ik}\Big) P_{kj}
= \sum_{k \in S} \pi_k P_{kj} ,
\] so \(\pi = \pi P\). Also \[
\sum_{j \in S} \pi_j
= \sum_{j \in S} \lim_{n \to \infty} (P^n)_{ij}
= \lim_{n \to \infty} \sum_{j \in S} (P^n)_{ij} = 1 .
\] Thus \(\pi\) is a stationary distribution. \(\blacksquare\)


Remark. 

The interchange of limit and summation is permitted for a finite state space.
The theorem guarantees that a convergent distribution is invariant; the converse need not hold (invariance does not imply convergence — see below).
For the probability to converge we must restrict to a single communicating class; otherwise \(\lim_{n \to \infty}(P^n)_{ij}\) depends on the initial state, as different initial states may lead to different recurrent classes.



Periodicity
Even for a single communicating class, existence of an invariant distribution does not guarantee convergence.








Figure 15.2: A 2-state chain with \(P_{12} = P_{21} = 1\) (i.e. \(P = \left(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right)\)). The distribution \(\pi = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\) is invariant, yet the probabilities oscillate and never converge, since \(P^{2k} = I\) and \(P^{2k+1} = P\).






To exclude such cases we define the aperiodic property.

Definition 15.6 (Aperiodic) A state \(i\) is aperiodic if \((P^n)_{ii} > 0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). A Markov chain is aperiodic if every state \(i \in S\) is aperiodic.

title: 15  Markov Chains
text:
15.5 Convergence to Equilibrium

Theorem 15.3 (Irreducible + one aperiodic state \(\Rightarrow\) all states aperiodic) Suppose a Markov chain is irreducible and has an aperiodic state \(i\). Then for all states \(j, k \in S\), \((P^n)_{jk} > 0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\). In particular, all states are aperiodic.


Proof. Since the chain is irreducible, there exist \(r, s\) with \((P^r)_{ji} > 0\) and \((P^s)_{ik} > 0\). Then for sufficiently large \(n\), \[
\begin{aligned}
(P^{\,n + r + s})_{jk}
&= \sum_{i_1, \dots, i_n \in S} (P^r)_{j\, i_1}\, P_{i_1 i_2} P_{i_2 i_3} \cdots P_{i_{n-1} i_n}\, (P^s)_{i_n k} \\
&= \sum_{i_1, i_n \in S} (P^r)_{j\, i_1}\, (P^n)_{i_1 i_n}\, (P^s)_{i_n k} \\
&\ge (P^r)_{ji}\, (P^n)_{ii}\, (P^s)_{ik} > 0 ,
\end{aligned}
\] choosing \(i_1 = i_n = i\), since \((P^n)_{ii} > 0\) (\(i\) aperiodic) and the end factors are positive (irreducibility). \(\blacksquare\)

For an aperiodic chain, the existence of an invariant distribution guarantees convergence to it.

Theorem 15.4 (Convergence to the invariant distribution) Suppose \((X_n)_{n \ge 0}\) is an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with transition matrix \(P\) and initial distribution \(\lambda\). If \(P\) has an invariant distribution \(\pi\), then \[
P(X_n = j) \to \pi_j \quad\text{as } n \to \infty, \ \ \forall j \in S .
\] In particular, \((P^n)_{ij} \to \pi_j\) as \(n \to \infty\) for all \(i, j \in S\).


Theorem 15.5 (Finite irreducible aperiodic chains) Suppose \((X_n)_{n \ge 0}\) is an irreducible and aperiodic Markov chain with a finite state space. Then there exists a unique invariant distribution \(\pi\), and \(P(X_n = i) \to \pi_i\) for any initial distribution \(\lambda\).

title: 17  Martingales
text:
17.1 Discrete time martingle
fair game: Consider \(Y_1, Y_2 \cdots\) are independent “fair” gambling game, \(E(Y_i) = 0\).
\(S_n := Y_1 + Y_2 \cdots \cdots + Y_n\) as accumulated. total wining
\(Q\): what is the best guess of \(S_{n+k}\) given \(S_1, S_2 \cdots S_n\)?
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(S_{n+k} \mid S_1, S_2, \cdots S_n)
&= E(Y_1 + Y_2 \cdots + Y_{n+k} \mid S_1, S_2, \cdots S_n) \\
&= \underline{E(Y_1 + Y_2 + \cdots + Y_n \mid S_1, \cdots S_n)} + E(Y_{n+1} + \cdots Y_{n+k} \mid S_1, \cdots S_n) \\
&= Y_1 + Y_2 + \cdots + Y_n + E(Y_{n+1} + \cdots + Y_{n+k} \mid S_1, \cdots S_n) \\
&= Y_1 + Y_2 + \cdots + Y_n + E(Y_{n+1} + \cdots + Y_{n+k}) \\
&= S_n
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, for a fair game, the best estimate of future value \(S_{n+k}\) given the history up to \(n\), is just \(S_n\).
Def. consider probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\). \((X_m)_{m=0,1,\cdots}\) be a stochastic process, i.e. \(X_m\) is R.V. for each \(m \geq 0\), and integrable \((E(|X|) < \infty)\)
Then \((X_m)_{m=0,1,\cdots}\) is called a Martingle if \[
X_m = E(X_{m+1} \mid X_0, X_1, \cdots X_m), \quad \text{for } \forall m \geq 0
\]
a submartingle if \[
X_m \leq E(X_{m+1} \mid X_0, \cdots X_m), \quad \text{for } \forall m \geq 0
\]
a supmartingle if \[
X_m \geq E(X_{m+1} \mid X_0, \cdots X_m) \quad \text{for } \forall m \geq 0
\]
Remark: A martingle means that if we have the observation of the history of the process \(X_0, \cdots X_m\), then the observed. value of present is the expected value of future.

title: 17  Martingales
text:
17.2 Filtration
In many practical example, our observation may not be just \(X\), for example if we have a sequence \((X_m, Y_m)_{m=0,1,\cdots}\) where \(X_m, Y_m\) might be correlated, in this case, it is reasonable to define martingle as \[
X_m = E(X_{m+1} \mid (X_0, Y_0), \cdots (X_m, Y_m)) \quad \text{or} \quad = E(X_{m+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_m)
\] where each \((Y_m, X_m)\) is measurable w.r.t. to \(\mathcal{F}_m\), and of course \(X_m\)
we thus can redefine martingle under a more generalized language, we we. introduce the concept of filtration
Def: a set of sub-\(\sigma\)-field \(\{\mathcal{F}_n\}\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\) is called a filtration s.t. \(\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_2 \subseteq \cdots \mathcal{F}_n \subseteq \mathcal{F}\), \(\forall \mathcal{F}_n\) is \(\sigma\)-field
Remarks: A filtration represents any procedure of collecting more and more information as time goes on.
Def: let \((X_m)_m\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and \((\mathcal{F}_m)_m\) be a filtration. we called. \((X_m)_m\) is adapted to \((\mathcal{F}_m)\) if \(\sigma(X_n) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_n\)

title: 17  Martingales
text:
17.3 Martingle w.r.t. filtration.
consider \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), \((X_m)_{m=0,1,\cdots}\) and filtration \((\mathcal{F}_m)_{m=0,1,\cdots}\) then \((X_m)_m\) is called a martingle w.r.t. to filtration \((\mathcal{F}_m)_m\) if

\(\forall m \geq 0\), \(X_m\) is \(\mathcal{F}_m\) measurable. (adapted)
\(X_m = E(X_{m+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_m)\)

Remarks: This definition keep the essense of martingle that when the past information is known (conditional), the present value is the expected future value.
Lemma: let \((X_m)_m\) a martingle w.r.t. \((\mathcal{F}_m)_m\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) then \(X_m = E(X_n \mid \mathcal{F}_m)\), \(\forall n > m\).
proof: \[
X_m = E[X_{m+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_m] = E[E(X_{m+2} \mid \mathcal{F}_{m+1}) \mid \mathcal{F}_m]. \quad \text{Since } \mathcal{F}_m \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{m+1}
\] \[
= E[X_{m+2} \mid \mathcal{F}_m]
\] continous this process can show the lemma.

title: 17  Martingales
text:
17.4 Natural filtration
prop: suppose we have discrete time process \(X_0, X_1, \cdots X_m \cdots\), we can define \(\mathcal{F}_m^X := \sigma(X_0, X_1, \cdots X_m)\), \(m = 0, 1 \cdots\) natural filtration of \((X_m)_m\), \((\mathcal{F}_m^X)\) is the smallest filtration s.t. \((X_m)_m\) is adaptive.
Remark: \(\mathcal{F}_m^X\) is the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by previous history \((X_0, X_1, \cdots X_m)\), i.e. the smallest ‘information’ of the entire history.
proof: need to show that if \(X_m\) is \(\mathcal{F}_m\) measurable, then \(\mathcal{F}_m^X \subseteq \mathcal{F}_m\), \(\forall m\).
suppose we have \(\sigma(X_0) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_0\), \(\sigma(X_1) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_1\), \(\cdots \sigma(X_m) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_m\). and \(\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_2 \cdots \subseteq \mathcal{F}_m\).
then we know \(\sigma(X_0) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_m\), \(\sigma(X_1) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_1 \subseteq \mathcal{F}_m\), \(\cdots \sigma(X_m) \subseteq \mathcal{F}_m\).
i.e. \(X_0, \cdots X_m\) are all \(\mathcal{F}_m\) measurable.
thus \(\sigma(X_0 \cdots X_m) = \mathcal{F}_m^X \subseteq \mathcal{F}_m\).

title: 17  Martingales
text:
17.5 Martingle Transformation.
The martingle transformation of a discrete martingle can be viewed as a “discrete” form of later defined stochastic Integral
Consider a discrete model of stock price \((X_m)_{m=0,1,\cdots 2}\) adaptive to \((\mathcal{F}_m)_{m=0,1,\cdots}\). let \(U_m := \#\) of share from \(m-1\) to \(m\). This should be \((\mathcal{F}_{m-1})\) measurable, as we only know the information till \(m-1\) to make decision how much to hold till next day. Then my profit would be \[
U_1(X_1 - X_0) + U_2(X_2 - X_0) + \cdots + U_n(X_n - X_{n-1})
\]

The formal definition of martingale transformation is as follows
Def let \((X_m)_{m=0,\cdots}\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), adapted to \((\mathcal{F}_m)_m\), let \((U_m)_{m=1,2,\cdots}\) measurable respet to \(\mathcal{F}_{m-1}\)
let \[
Z_m = U_1(X_1 - X_0) + U_2(X_2 - X_1) + \cdots + U_m(X_m - X_{m-1})
\] \[
Z_0 = 0
\] \((Z_m)_{m=0,1,2,\cdots}\) is called the martingle transformation of \(X_m\).
As the name suggest, the martingle transformation transform a martingle to another martingle
Th: if \((X_m)_m\) is a martingle and \((Z_m)_m\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{m-1}\) measurable \(\forall m = \{0, 1, 2, \cdots\}\), then \((Z_m)_m\) is a martingle.

Proof: for a martingle \(M_m = E(M_{m+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_m) \iff E(M_{m+1} - M_m \mid \mathcal{F}_m) = 0\). \[
\begin{aligned}
E(Z_{m+1} - Z_m \mid \mathcal{F}_m)
&= E(U_{m+1}(X_{m+1} - X_m) \mid \mathcal{F}_m) \\
&= U_{m+1} E(X_{m+1} - X_m \mid \mathcal{F}_m) = 0. \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 18  Stopping Time
text:
18.1 Stopping time
One advantage of a martingle process is that it provide. properties in the stopping time of the sequence. First we need to know what is a stopping time and its definition
Consider the stock model example again. Suppose we buy one share, at \(t=0\) and. hold tile random time \(T\). Then \[
U_m \equiv \mathbf{1}_{\{m \leq T\}} = 1 - \mathbf{1}_{\{T \leq m-1\}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad Z_m = X_{\min(m,T)} - X_0
\]
obs: \[
U_m \text{ is } \mathcal{F}_{m-1} \text{ measurable} \iff \{T \leq m-1\} \text{ is } \mathcal{F}_{m-1} \text{ measurable}
\] \[
\iff \{T \leq m\} \text{ is } \mathcal{F}_m \text{ measurable}
\]
Def A R.V. \(T : \Omega \to \{0, 1, \cdots 2, \cdots \infty\}\) is called a stopping time. for filtration \(\{\mathcal{F}_m\}\) if \(\{\omega \mid T(\omega) \leq n\}\) is \(\mathcal{F}_n\) measurable for. each \(n \geq 0\).
Remark: Essentialy, a stopping time is to make a decision that a process stop at time \(n\) or not, based on the information only avaible so far (not future). The Def above is exactly this in the formal probability language (\(\{T \leq n\}\) is the to decide stop or not; \(\mathcal{F}_n\) measuribility make sure the information).

title: 18  Stopping Time

18.2 Stopped process
Def let \((X_m)_m\) be a stochastic process and \(T\) be a stopping time, Then a stopped process at \(T\) \(X_{\min(n,T)}\) or \(X_{n \wedge T}\) is \[
X_{\min(n,T)(\omega)}(\omega) = \begin{cases} X_n(\omega), & n \leq T(\omega) \\ X_{T(\omega)}(\omega), & n > T(\omega) \end{cases} \qquad \omega \in \Omega.
\]
prob: let \(T, S\) be stopping time. on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) with filtration \((\mathcal{F}_n)_{n=0,\cdots}\), then \(T \wedge S = \min(T, S)\) and \(T \vee S = \max(T, S)\) are also stopping time

title: 18  Stopping Time

18.3 Stopped martingle
For a martingle process, a nice result is that a stopped. martingle (or sub, sup) is still a martingle (sub, sub)

Th let \((X_n, \mathcal{F}_n)\) be a martingle (sub, sup) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), and \(T\) is a stopping time for \((\mathcal{F}_n)_n\), then \((X_{n \wedge T}, \mathcal{F}_n)\) is also a martingle (Sub, sup).

title: 18  Stopping Time
text:
18.4 Doob’s optional stopping
The martingle property allow ones to find the expectation of stoped value. Conviniently using the following th-
Th (Doob’s optional stopping) let \((X_n, \mathcal{F}_n)\) be a submartingle and \(T < \infty\) a.s. is a stopping time (will stop) s.t. \((X_{n \wedge T})_n\) is uniformly integrable. then \[
E(X_T) \geq E(X_0).
\] In perticular for a martingle \(E(X_T) = E(X_0)\)
The Doob’s optional sampling th is useful for finding the “probability to ruin” in random walk problem.
Ex: Consider a simple symmetric random walk \((\xi_n)_n\) on an interval \((-a, b)\), starting at \(0\). \(T_{ab}\) be the stopping time hit \(-a\) or \(b\). \(S_n = \sum_k \xi_k\) is a martingle, thus \[
E(S_{T_{ab}}) = E(S_0) = 0 = -a \, P(T_{ab} = -a) + b \, P(T_{ab} = b) = 0
\] \[
P(T_{ab} = -a) + P(T_{ab} = b) = 1 \implies P(S_{T_{ab}} = -a) = \frac{b}{b+a}
\]
the probability of hits \(-a\) before hit \(b\).


Remark: should make sure the Th condition is statisfied. If in above example the walk is bound \((-\infty, b)\), then \((S_{n \wedge T_{ab}})\) is not integrable and. \(E(S_{T_b}) \neq E(S_0)\)

title: 19  Brownian Motion
text:
19.3 Brownian Motion (definition)
Def \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), \((B_t)_{t \geq 0}\) is a stochastic process, i.e. for \(\forall t \geq 0\), \(B_t\) is a. R.V.
\((B_t)_{t \geq 0}\) is called BM if \(B_0 = 0\) and \(\forall\, 0 = t_0 < t_1, \cdots < t_i\) \[
B_{t_1} - B_{t_0}, \ B_{t_2} - B_{t_1}, \ \cdots B_{t_i} - B_{t_{i-1}} \quad \text{all independent}, \quad \forall s < t, \ B_t - B_s \overset{(d)}{=} N(0, t-s)
\]
Def2 (using filtration), \((B_t)_{t \geq 0}\) is called BM w.r.t. \((\mathcal{F}_t)\) if

\(B_t\) is continous path, \(B_0 = 0\)
\(\forall t\), \(B_t\) is measurable w.r.t. \(\mathcal{F}_t\) \(\rightsquigarrow \mathcal{F}_t^B \subseteq \mathcal{F}_t\)
\(B_t - B_s \perp \mathcal{F}_s\) and \(B_t - B_s \overset{(d)}{=} N(0, t-s)\)

from the definition we can show that the \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_t, B_s) = E(B_t B_s) = s \wedge t\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Cov}(B_t, B_s) &= E(B_t B_s) - E(B_t)E(B_s) = E(B_t B_s) \\
&= E(B_s(B_t - B_s) + B_s^2) \qquad \text{if } t \geq s \geq 0 \\
&= E(B_s(B_t - B_s)) + E(B_s^2) = s = s \wedge t.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the BM can also be defined from Gaussian process.

title: 19  Brownian Motion
text:
19.4 Gaussian process
Def Gaussian process
\((X_t)_{t \geq 0}\) SP on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) is called a Gaussian process if \((X_{t_1}, X_{t_2}, \cdots X_{t_d})\) form a multi dimensional Gaussian, \(\forall t_1 \leq t_2 \leq \cdots \leq t_d\).
Then the BM motion is a Gaussian process with \(B_0 = 0\), \(E[B_t] = 0\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_s, B_t) = s \wedge t\) \(\ \forall s, t\).
Def \((X_1, \cdots X_n) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is a multi-dimensional Gaussian with mean \(\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d\), and cov matrix \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}\), symmetric, semi def if \[
P(x_1, \cdots x_n) = P(\vec{x}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^d \det(\Sigma)}} \, e^{-\frac12 \langle \Sigma^{-1}(\vec{x} - m), (\vec{x} - m)\rangle}
\] or can write further \[
E[e^{i \langle \vec{a}, x\rangle}] = e^{\, i \langle \vec{a}, \mu\rangle - \frac12 \langle \Sigma \vec{a}, \vec{a}\rangle}.
\]

title: 19  Brownian Motion
text:
19.5 Properties
(1) \((B_t)_{t \geq 0}\) is a martingle w.r.t. to \(\mathcal{F}_t\), \[
E(B_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = E(B_s + B_t - B_s \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = B_s + E(B_t - B_s \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = B_s + E(B_t - B_s) = B_s
\]
(2) \(B_t^2 - t\) is a martingle w.r.t. \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \geq 0}\) \[
\begin{aligned}
E(B_t^2 - t \mid \mathcal{F}_s) &= E\big((B_s + (B_t - B_s))^2 - t \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big) \\
&= E\big(B_s^2 + 2B_s(B_t - B_s) + (B_t - B_s)^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big) - t \\
&= B_s^2 + 2B_s E(B_t - B_s \mid \mathcal{F}_s) + E\big((B_t - B_s)^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big) - t \\
&= B_s^2 - s
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 19  Brownian Motion
text:
19.6 Quadratic variation of BM
we denote the QV of BM \((B_t)_t\) as on a partition \(0 = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 \cdots < t_n = T\) as \[
[B, B]_{t_n} := (B_{t_1} - B_{t_0})^2 + (B_{t_2} - B_{t_1})^2 + \cdots + (B_{t_n} - B_{t_{n-1}})^2
\]
obs: denote \[
\langle B, B\rangle_{t_n} := E[(B_{t_1} - B_{t_0})^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_0}] + E[(B_{t_2} - B_{t_1})^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_1}] + \cdots + E[(B_{t_n} - B_{t_{n-1}})^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_n}]
\]


Since \(B_{t_n} - B_{t_{n-1}} \sim N(0, t_n - t_{n-1})\) and are independent from previous \[
\langle B, B\rangle_{t_n} = (t_1 - t_0) + (t_2 - t_1) + \cdots + (t_n - t_{n-1}) = t_n - t_0 = t_n.
\]
One important property for the QV of BM is that \([B, B]_{t_n} \to t_n\) when the partition is tend to infinitesmal small.
Th: let \(\|\sigma\| := \max_{i=1 \cdots n} |t_i - t_{i-1}|\), then we have. \[
\lim_{\|\sigma\| \to 0} [B, B]_{t_n} = \langle B, B\rangle_{t_n} = t_n. \qquad \text{or more precisely.}
\] \[
P\big(\{\omega \mid [B, B]_{t_n}(\omega) = t_n\}\big) = 1.
\]
proof: we first consider \[
E\big([B,B]_{t_n} - t_n\big) = E\Big(\textstyle\sum_i (B_i - B_{i-1})^2 - \sum_i (t_i - t_{i-1})\Big) = \sum_i E\big((B_i - B_{i-1})^2 - (t_i - t_{i-1})\big) = 0.
\]
next consider the variation \[
\begin{aligned}
E\big(([B,B]_{t_n} - t_n)^2\big) &= E\Big(\big[\textstyle\sum_i ((B_i - B_{i-1})^2 - (t_i - t_{i-1}))\big]^2\Big) \\
&= E\Big[\textstyle\sum_i ((B_i - B_{i-1})^2 - (t_i - t_{i-1}))^2 + 2\sum_{i \neq j} ((B_i - B_{i-1})^2 - (t_i - t_{i-1}))((B_j - B_{j-1})^2 - (t_j - t_{j-1}))\Big] \\
&= \textstyle\sum_i E\big[((B_i - B_{i-1})^2 - (t_i - t_{i-1}))^2\big] + 2\sum_{i \neq j} E\big[((B_i - B_{i-1})^2 - (t_i - t_{i-1}))((B_j - B_{j-1})^2 - (t_j - t_{j-1}))\big]
\end{aligned}
\]
from independent intervals, we have. \(B_i - B_{i-1} \perp B_j - B_{j-1}\), \(i \neq j\) \[
\Rightarrow E\big[((B_i - B_{i-1})^2 - (t_i - t_{i-1}))((B_j - B_{j-1})^2 - (t_j - t_{j-1}))\big] = E[\cdots]\,E[\cdots] = 0.
\]
denote \(B_i - B_{i-1} = N_i\), \(\operatorname{Var}(N_i) = t_i - t_{i-1}\) \[
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow E[\ ] &= \textstyle\sum_i E\big((N_i^2 - \operatorname{Var}(N_i))^2\big) = \sum_i E\big((N_i^2 - E(N_i^2))^2\big) \\
&= \textstyle\sum_i E\big(N_i^4 - 2N_i^2 E(N_i^2) + E^2(N_i^2)\big) \\
&= \textstyle\sum_i 3(t_i - t_{i-1})^2 - 2(t_i - t_{i-1})^2 + (t_i - t_{i-1})^2 \\
&= 2\textstyle\sum_i (t_i - t_{i-1})^2 \leq 2\|\sigma\| \sum_i |t_i - t_{i-1}| \leq 2|\sigma| \, t_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
thus \(\lim_{\sigma \to 0} E\big[([B, B] - \langle B, B\rangle)^2\big] = 0\)
Remark: It is Convinient to memorize the \([B, B]_t = t\) in “differential” form as \[
(dB)^2 = dt
\] The simply means BM cumulate QV at rate one per unit time.

title: 20  Stochastic Integral
text:
20.1 Step process
suppose we have a stock price \((X_t)_t\) and a trading strategy \((a_t)_t\), which essentially a Random variable that tells me how much share to hold. The How do I Calculate my total profit from \(0, to\ T\)
one simple model turn descret time into interval \(t_0 < t_1 < t_2 \cdots < t_n\), and we hold \(\xi_i\) # of share between \([t_{i-1}, t_i]\), decide at \(t_{i-1}\) (no future information) \(\Rightarrow \xi_i\) is \(\mathcal{F}_{t_{i-1}}\) measurable. and BM \((B_t)_t\) as price movement
Then the profit is \(I_t = \xi_1(B_{t_1} - B_{t_0}) + \cdots + \xi_n(B_t - B_{t_{n-1}})\)
when \(\sigma t = t_i - t_{i-1}\) is very small, this looks like an integral in regular calculous sense. However due to the QV of BM, the exact stochastic Calculous is more Complicated the intuitive argument above. but the general idea is similar.
we start with define the stochastic integral (Ito integral specificaly) for Simple step function \[
0 = t_0 < t_1 < t_2 \cdots < t_n = T. \quad \text{a partition}
\]
Def step process \(G_t\): \[
(G_t)_{t \in [0,T]} := \sum_{k=1}^{n} \xi_{k-1} \mathbf{1}_{\{t_{k-1} < t \leq t_k\}}, \qquad \xi_{k-1} \text{ is } \mathcal{F}(t_{k-1}) \text{ measurable.}
\] \[
\mathbf{1}_{\{t_{k-1} < t \leq t_k\}} = \begin{cases} 1 & t_{k-1} < t < t_k \\ 0 & \text{other} \end{cases}
\]

title: 20  Stochastic Integral
text:
20.2 Itô’s stochastic integral (on step processes)
Def Itô’s stochastic integral (on step processes) \[
I_t^n = \int_0^t G_u^n \, dB_u = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} \xi_i(B_{t_{i+1}} - B_{t_i}) + \xi_k(B_t - B_{t_k}), \quad t \in [t_k, t_{k+1}], \quad (B_t)_{t \geq 0} \text{ is BM} \iff dI_t^n = G_t^n \, dB_t
\]
Remark: An intuitive under standy of this definition is to think \(t_0, t_1 \cdots t_n\) as the trading days, \(B(t_i)\) be the price at these days and \(\xi_i\) as number of shares acquired at date \(t_i\), hold tile time \(t_{i+1}\). Then the total gain of asset (which would stans for ‘integral’) would be \(\sum(\text{share} \times \text{price})\) all trades.

title: 20  Stochastic Integral
text:
20.3 Properties of the Itô integral
Th \(I_t^n\) is a continous martingle with \(I_0^n = 0\)
proof: (1) let \(0 \leq s < t\), to show \(I_s^n = E(I_t^n \mid \mathcal{F}_s)\), we need to show \(E(I_t^n - I_s^n \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = 0\). suppose \(s \in [t_l, t_{l+1}]\), \(t \in [t_k, t_{k+1}]\), \(l \leq k\)
then \[
\begin{aligned}
I_t^n - I_s^n &= \xi_k(B_t - B_{t_k}) + \xi_{k-1}(B_{t_k} - B_{t_{k-1}}) \cdots + \xi_l(B_{t_{l+1}} - B_{t_l}) - \xi_l(B_s - B_{t_l}) \\
&= \xi_k(B_t - B_{t_k}) + \cdots + \xi_l(B_{t_{l+1}} - B_s)
\end{aligned}
\] \[
E\big(\xi_k(B_t - B_{t_k}) \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big) = E\big(E(\xi_k(B_t - B_{t_k}) \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_k}) \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big) = E\big(\xi_k E(B_t - B_{t_k} \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_k}) \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big) = 0
\] \[
E\big(\xi_l(B_{t_{l+1}} - B_s) \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big) = \xi_l E(B_{t_{l+1}} - B_s \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = 0.
\] \(\to I_t^n\) is continous martingle.
Th Ito isometry \[
E(I_t^{n2}) = E\Big[\int_0^t G_u^{n2} \, du\Big]
\]
proof: Ito isomety \(E(I^2) = E\big((\sum_i \xi_i \Delta B_i)^2\big)\) \[
= E\Big(\sum_i \xi_i^2 \Delta B_i^2 + 2\sum_{i \neq j} \xi_i \Delta B_i \, \xi_j \Delta B_j\Big)
\] when \(i \neq j\), assume \(i < j\), \(\Delta B_j\) is independent of \(\Delta B_i, \xi_i, \xi_j\) thus \(E(\xi_i \xi_j \Delta B_i \Delta B_j) = 0\) \[
\begin{aligned}
E(I^2) &= E\Big(\sum_i \xi_i^2 \Delta B_i^2\Big) = \sum_i E(\xi_i^2 \Delta B_i^2) \\
&= \sum_i E(\xi_i^2) E(\Delta B_i^2) \\
&= E\big(\xi_i^2 (t_{i+1} - t_i)\big) = E\Big(\int_0^t G_s^{n2} \, ds\Big)
\end{aligned}
\]
Th The QV of \(I_t^n\) \[
[I_t^n, I_t^n] = \int_0^t G_u^{n2} \, du, \quad \text{and.} \qquad \langle I_t^n, I_t^n\rangle = \int_0^t G_u^{n2} \, du
\]
proof: Calculate the QV on each piece wise interval. \[
\begin{aligned}
[I_{t_i}^n, I_{t_i}^n] &= \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_{j=1}^{m} (I_{h_j} - I_{h_{j-1}})^2, \quad \text{where } t_{i-1} = h_0 < h_1 \cdots < h_m = t_i. \\
&= \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_{j=1}^{m} \xi_{t_{i-1}}(B_{h_j} - B_{h_{j-1}})^2 = \xi_{t_{i-1}} \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_{j=1}^{m} (B_{h_j} - B_{h_{j-1}})^2 \\
&= \xi_{t_{i-1}}(t_i - t_{i-1})
\end{aligned}
\] notice that the QV on \(0, t\) is then sum of all this \[
\text{thus} \quad [I_t^n, I_t^n] = \sum_j \xi_{t_{j-1}}(t_j - t_{j-1}) = \int_0^t G_u^{n} \, du.
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle I_{t_i}^n, I_{t_i}^n\rangle &= \sum_{c=1}^{k} E\big[\xi_{i-1}^2(B_{t_i} - B_{t_{i-1}})^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{i-1}}\big] = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \xi_{i-1}^2 E\big[(B_{t_i} - B_{t_{i-1}})^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{i-1}}\big] \\
&= \sum_{i=1}^{k} \xi_{i-1}^2 (t_i - t_{i-1})^2 = \int_0^t G_t^2 \, dt.
\end{aligned}
\]

Remark: We can denote the integral form \(I_t^n = \int_0^t G_u^n \, dB_u\) in “differential form” \(dI_t^n = G_t^n \, dt\) and the QV \[
(dI_t^n)^2 = (G_t^n \, dB_u)^2 = G_t^{n2}(dB_u)^2 = G_t^{n2} \, dt.
\] or. \(I_t^n\) accumulate \(G_t^{n2}\) QV per unit time.
Th Martingle Property \[
I_t^{n} - \int_0^t G_u^{n2} \, du \quad \text{is a martingle.}
\]

Remark: the QV is computed path-by-path. chosing different \(a_t\) would leads to different integral. QV can be regarded. as a measure of risk, and it depends on the size of position \((a_t)\) we take.

20.4 From simple step process to General process
use \((G_t^n)_{t \in [0,T]}\), a step process to approximate any \(G\) to defines \(\int_0^T G_t \, dB_t\)
let \(T\) be fixed, \[
L^2(0,T) = \Big\{(G_t)_{0 \leq t \leq T}, \ G_t \text{ measurable w.r.t. } (\mathcal{F}_t), 0 \leq t \leq T, \text{ and } E\Big[\int_0^T |G_t|^2 dt\Big] < \infty\Big\}
\] \[
\exists (G^n)_t \in L^2(0,T), \text{ bounded step process (sequence of) s.t. } E\Big[\int_0^T |G_u - G_u^n|^2 du\Big] \to 0.
\]
Def let \(G_t \in L^2(0,T)\) and \((G^n)_t\) as bound sequence of step process above then \(L_t = \lim_{n \to \infty} \int_0^t G_u^n \, dB_u\) exist and defined as \(\int_0^t G_u \, du\).
Properties:

\(L_t\) is continous martingle, \(L_0 = 0\)
\(E(L_t^2) = E\big(\int_0^t G_u^2 \, du\big)\) — Ito isomety
\(\langle L_t, L_t\rangle = \int_0^t G_u^2 \, du = [L_t, L_t] := \lim_{\sigma \to 0} \sum_{k=0} (L_{t_k} - L_{t_{k-1}})^2\) — QV
\((L_t)^2 - \int_0^t G_u^2 \, du\) is a martingle
\(E(L_t) = 0\).

Justification on the QV. \[
E\Big[\big(\textstyle\sum_k (L_{t_k} - L_{t_{k-1}})^2 - \langle L, L\rangle_t\big)^2\Big] = E\Big[\big(\textstyle\sum_k \underbrace{((L_{t_k} - L_{t_{k-1}})^2 - (\langle L,L\rangle_{t_k} - \langle L,L\rangle_{t_{k-1}}))}_{A_k}\big)^2\Big]
\] observation \(E[(L_t - L_s)^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_s] = E[L_t^2 - L_s^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_s]\), let \(s = t_{k-1}\), \(t = t_k\) \[
E\big[(L_{t_k} - L_{t_{k-1}})^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{k-1}}\big] = E\big[L_{t_k}^2 - L_{t_{k-1}}^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{k-1}}\big] = E\big[\langle L,L\rangle_{t_k} - \langle L,L\rangle_{t_{k-1}} \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{k-1}}\big]
\] as \(E[(L_{t_k} - L_{t_{k-1}})^2 \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{k-1}}] = \langle L,L\rangle_{t_k} - \langle L,L\rangle_{t_{k-1}} = E[\langle L,L\rangle_{t_k} - \langle L,L\rangle_{t_{k-1}} \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{k-1}}]\) \[
\Rightarrow E(A_k \mid \mathcal{F}_{t_{k-1}}) = 0
\] \[
E\big((\textstyle\sum_k A_k)^2\big) = E\big(\textstyle\sum_k A_k^2\big) + 2E\big(\textstyle\sum_{i \leq k} A_i A_k\big) \quad \text{since } E(A_i A_k \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}) = A_i E(A_k \mid \mathcal{F}_{k-1}) = 0 \text{ and } E(A_k^2) \text{ close to } 0.
\]
Remark: again we denote \(dL_t = G_t \, dB_t\) and \((dL_t)^2 = G_t^2 \, dt\).
