20.5 Itô processes and Itô’s chain rule
we then extend the integral process defined above to more generalise Ito processes.
Def - Itô processess let \((B_t)_{t \geq 0}\) a BM on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) with filtration \(\mathcal{F}_t\) and some \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \geq 0}\), \((a_t)_{t \geq 0}\) sp adapted to \(\mathcal{F}_t\) and \(F_t \in L^1(0,T)\), \(G_t \in L^2(0,T)\) and \[
X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t F_u \, du + \int_0^t G_u \, dB_u
\] is called the Ito process, which often denote in differential form \[
dX_t = F_t \, dt + G_t \, dB_t.
\]
Remark: 1. the differential form is a notation for the integral expression, \(dX_t, dt, dB_t\) has no stand alone meaning

Almost all sp, exlept the one with jumps (Levy-processes) are Ito process.
Tthe \(F_t \, dt\) are refered as drift term (over all motion. due to external field) and Brownian term is called diffusive term.

Lemma: \([X, X]_t = \int_0^t G_u^2 \, dt\). \(\to\) QV come from BM, drift has no QV.
The natural Question next is to ask if there is a “chain” rule. in stochastic Integral that tell us \(d(U(X_t))\) is. The such rule in stochastic Calculous is called Ito’s chain rule. Similar to regular chain rule with extra term as result of none zero QV of BM.
Th - Itô’s Chain Rule. Suppose \(dX_t = F_t \, dt + G_t \, dB_t\) is an Ito processes defined above, let \(U: \mathbb{R} \times [0,T] \to \mathbb{R}\) and \(U(x,t)\) is continous and \(\frac{\partial U}{\partial t}, \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial x^2}\) exists and continous, then \(Y_t = U(X_t, t)\) has diff eventtutw \[
\begin{aligned}
dY_t &= U_t \, dt + U_x \, dX_t + \tfrac12 U_{xx}(dX_t)^2 \\
&= U_t \, dt + U_x(F_t \, dt + G_t \, dB_t) + \tfrac12 U_{xx} G_t^2 \, dt.
\end{aligned}
\]
Similar question can be asked, if there is a product rules in stochastic sense, and the answer is Yes, with also additional term due to QV of BM
Example: \(d(B_u^2) = 2 B_u \, dB_u + dt.\) \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^t d(B_u^2) &= \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i (B_{t_i}^2 - B_{t_{i-1}}^2) = \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0}\Big(\textstyle\sum_i (B_{t_i} - B_{t_{i-1}})^2 + 2B_{t_{i-1}}\sum_i (B_{t_i} - B_{t_{i-1}})\Big) \\
&= \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i (B_{t_i} - B_{t_{i-1}})^2 + 2\lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i (B_{t_i} - B_{t_{i-1}}) B_{t_{i-1}} \\
&= [B, B]_t + 2\int_0^t B_u \, dB_u = \int_0^t dt + \int_0^t 2 B_u \, dB_u
\end{aligned}
\] \[
\iff dB_u^2 = 2 B_u \, dB_u + dt
\]
Example: \(d(t B_t)\) \[
\int_0^t d(u B_u) = \lim \sum_i (t_i B_{t_i} - t_{i-1} B_{t_{i-1}}) = \lim \sum_i t_i(B_{t_i} - B_{t_{i-1}}) + \lim \sum_i (t_i - t_{i-1}) B_{t_{i-1}} = \int_0^t u \, dB_u + \int_0^t B_u \, du
\] \[
\iff d(t B_t) = t \, dB_t + B_t \, dt
\]

Th - Itô’s product rule. let \(dX_t^1 = F_t^1 \, dt + G_t^1 \, dB_t\) be two Ito process on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\), \(dX_t^2 = F_t^2 \, dt + G_t^2 \, dB_t\) \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{then} \quad d(X_1 X_2) &= X_2 \, dX_1 + X_1 \, dX_2 + dX_1 \, dX_2 \\
&= X_2 \, dX_1 + X_1 \, dX_2 + G_t^1 G_t^2 \, dt.
\end{aligned}
\]
lemma: \(dX_1 \, dX_2 = G_t^1 G_t^2 \, dt\)
proof let \(G_t^1, G_t^2, F_t^1, F_t^2\) has its Converging step sequence \(G^{1n}, G^{2n}, F^{1n}, F^{2n}\) and let \(X_n^1, X_n^2\) defined as. \[
X_n^1 = \sum_i F_{t_{i-1}}^1(t_i - t_{i-1}) + \sum_i G_{t_{i-1}}^1(B_i - B_{i-1})
\] \[
X_n^2 = \sum_i F_{t_{i-1}}^2(t_i - t_{i-1}) + \sum_i G_{t_{i-1}}^2(B_i - B_{i-1})
\] \[
\text{then} \quad \sum_i (X_{t_i}^1 - X_{t_{i-1}}^1)(X_{t_i}^2 - X_{t_{i-1}}^2) = \sum_i \big(F_{t_{i-1}}^1(t_i - t_{i-1}) + G_{t_{i-1}}^1(B_i - B_{i-1})\big)\big(F_{t_{i-1}}^2(t_i - t_{i-1}) + G_{t_{i-1}}^2(B_i - B_{i-1})\big)
\]
taking \(|\sigma| \to 0\), the two drift-drift and drift-diffusion sums vanish (in \(L^2\) sense): \[
\lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i F^1 F^2 (\Delta_i t)^2 = 0, \qquad \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i F^1 G^2 \, \Delta_i B \, \Delta_i t = 0
\] \[
\lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i (X_i^1 - X_{i-1}^1)(X_i^2 - X_{i-1}^2) = \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i G^1 G^2 \, \Delta_i B^2 = \int_0^t G_u^1 G_u^2 \, du
\]

proof: \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^t d(X^1 X^2) &= \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i (X_{t_i}^1 X_{t_i}^2 - X_{t_{i-1}}^1 X_{t_{i-1}}^2) \\
&= \lim_{|\sigma| \to 0} \sum_i \big[X_{t_{i-1}}^1(X_{t_i}^2 - X_{t_{i-1}}^2) + X_{t_{i-1}}^2(X_{t_i}^1 - X_{t_{i-1}}^1) + (X_{t_i}^1 - X_{t_{i-1}}^1)(X_{t_i}^2 - X_{t_{i-1}}^2)\big] \\
&= \int_0^t X_u^1 \, dX_u^2 + \int_0^t X_u^2 \, dX_u^1 + \int_0^t G_u^1 G_u^2 \, du
\end{aligned}
\]
Def \(dX_t = F_t \, dt + G_t \, dB_t\), and \((a_t)_t\) be a adapted process \[
\int_0^t a_u \, dX_u := \int_0^t a_u F_u \, du + \int_0^t a_u G_u \, dB_u.
\] or. \(a_t \, dX_t = a_t F_t \, dt + a_t G_t \, dB_t.\)
proof - Itô’s Chain Rule. using Itô’s product, an proof chainrule
① using product rule can show for \(U(x) = x^m\), we ①,\(\cdots\) \[
dX_t^m = m X^{m-1} \, dX_t + \tfrac12 m(m-1) X^{m-2} G_t^2 \, dt.
\] (using induction), which satisfy the chain rule. The linearity of integration give that all polynomial satisfied.
② then we show for \(f(x), g(t)\) that are both polynomial, \[
\begin{aligned}
d(U(X_t)) = d[f(x) g] &= f(x) \, dg + g(t) \, df(x) \\
&= f(x) g' \, dt + g(t)\big(f'(x) \, dx + \tfrac12 f''(x) G_t^2 \, dt\big) \\
&= \frac{\partial U}{\partial t} \, dt + \frac{\partial U}{\partial x}(x) \, dx + \tfrac12 \frac{\partial^2 U}{\partial x^2} G_t^2 \, dt.
\end{aligned}
\] due to linearity, \(U(x,t) = \sum_i f_i(x) g_i(t)\) also Satisfies Ito formula. That is, all polynomial function \(U\) of \(x, t\) satis fy.
③ For then \(U\) in Ito’s chain rule statement, \(\exists (U^n)_{n=0,1,\cdots}\), ’a sequence of polynomial function s.t. \(U^n \to U, U_t^n \to U_t, U_x^n \to U_x, U_{xx}^n \to U_{xx}\) uniformly on compact subset of \(\mathbb{R} \times [0,T]\). \[
\text{sun} \quad \int_0^t dU^n = \int_0^t U_t^n \, du + \int_0^t U_x^n \, dX + \tfrac12 \int_0^t U_{xx}^n G_u^2 \, du \quad \text{a.s.}
\] passing the limit yet chain rule in general.
Summary: The way remember this is to reconize that \(dB_t \, dB_t = dt.\) instead of \(0\), as in regular calculus \(\ dB_t \approx \sqrt{dt}\)

then for product \[
\begin{aligned}
d X_1 X_2 &= X_1 \, dX_2 + X_2 \, dX_1 + dX_1 \, dX_2 \\
&= X_1 \, dX_2 + X_2 \, dX_1 + (F^1 dt + G^1 dB)(F^2 dt + G^2 dB) \\
&= \cdots + G^1 G^2 \, dt
\end{aligned}
\] the result we higher order term, ignored as usual.
Itô’s chain rule then can be view as lowest order Tyler expansion. \[
f(X_t) = f(0,0) + \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \, dX_t + \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \, dt + \tfrac12 \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2}(dX_t)^2.
\] as \((dX_t)^2 = G_t^2 \, dt\), and should be keep.

20.6 General Itô’s chain rule
Itô’s chain rule can be similarly extend to multip variable.
let \(dX_t^i = F_t^i \, dt + G_t^i \, dB_t\) on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) with \(F^i \in L^1(0,T)\), \(G^i \in L^2(0,T)\) adapted, \(i = 1, \cdots n\), and \(u: \mathbb{R}^n \times [0,T] \to \mathbb{R}\) is continous, with continous \(u_t, u_{x_i}, u_{x_i x_j}\) \(\forall t_i\), then \[
d u(x^1, x^2, \cdots, t) = u_t \, dt + \sum_i \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i} \, dX_t^i + \tfrac12 \sum_{ij} \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} G_t^i G_t^j \, dt
\]

title: 20  Stochastic Integral
text:
20.7 Examples
1. Geometric Brownian Motion. \[
dX_t = G_t \, dB_t + (\alpha_t - \tfrac12 \sigma^2) \, dt, \qquad B_t \text{ is BM w.r.t. } \mathcal{F}_t \text{ filtration and } G_t, \alpha_t \text{ be adapted process.}
\]
and consider an asset price given by \[
S_t = S_0 \exp(X_t)
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
\text{then} \quad dS_t &= d(S_0 \exp(X_t)) = S_0\big(\exp(X_t) \, dX_t + \tfrac12 \exp(X_t) \, dX_t \, dX_t\big) \\
\text{and} \quad dX_t \, dX_t &= G_t^2 (dB_t)^2 = G_t^2 \, dt. \\
\Rightarrow \quad dS_t &= S_0 \exp(X_t)\big(G_t \, dW_t + (\alpha_t - \tfrac12 \sigma^2) \, dt\big) + \tfrac12 S_0 \exp(X_t) G_t^2 \, dt \\
&= \alpha_t S_t \, dt + G_t S_t \, dB_t.
\end{aligned}
\]
the asset price would have instantaneous mean rate of return. \(\alpha_t\) and volatility \(G(t)\).

This example includes all possible asset price model that is always positive, has no jumps and driven by a single BM.

Def - characteristic function \(\hat{\mu}(z)\) of probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is \[
\hat{\mu}(z) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i\langle z, x\rangle} \, \mu(dx)
\]
Prop: the characteristic function of the distribution \(P_X\) of a R.V. \(X\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is \[
\hat{P}_X(z) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i\langle z, x\rangle} \, P_X(dx) = E[e^{i\langle z, X\rangle}]
\]
Properties of \(\hat{\mu}(z)\)

If \(\mu = \mu_1 \otimes \mu_2\), then \(\hat{\mu}(z) = \hat{\mu}_1(z)\hat{\mu}_2(z)\). If \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are independent R.V. on \(\mathbb{R}^d\), then \(\hat{P}_{X_1 + X_2}(z) = \hat{P}_{X_1}(z)\hat{P}_{X_2}(z)\)

\]

21.3 Compound Poisson process
Compound Poisson R.V. \(\to\) each arrival associated with R.V.
let \(N \overset{(d)}{=} \operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)\), and \(Y_1, \cdots Y_n\) be iid. with dist \(f(dx)\) \[
X := \sum_{n=0}^{N} Y_n \quad \text{is called compound poisson R.V.}
\]
chara fun of \(X\) \[
\begin{aligned}
E[e^{i\langle z, X\rangle}] &= E\big[e^{i\langle z, \sum_n Y_n\rangle}\big] = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} e^{-\lambda} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!} E\big[e^{i\langle z, \sum_k Y_k\rangle}\big] \\
&= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} e^{-\lambda} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!} \big(\underbrace{E[e^{i\langle z, Y\rangle}]}_{\hat{G}(z)}\big)^k = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} e^{-\lambda} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!} \hat{G}(z)^k = \exp\big(-\lambda + \lambda \hat{G}(z)\big) \\
&= \exp\Big(\lambda\big(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d} e^{i\langle z, x\rangle} f(dx) - 1\big)\Big) = \exp\Big(\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}(e^{i\langle z, x\rangle} - 1) \lambda f(dx)\Big).
\end{aligned}
\]

title: 22  Risk-Neutral Pricing
text:
22.1 Change of measure
we wish to change how we measure probability from \(P\) to \(\hat{P}\) using Random Variable \(Z\).
Th let \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) be a prob space and \(Z\) be a a.s. non-negative. random variable with \(E(Z) = 1\). for \(A \in \mathcal{F}\), define \[
\hat{P}(A) = \int_A Z(\omega) \, dP(\omega)
\] then \(\hat{P}\) is a probability measure
Coll let \(\hat{P}\) be the prob measure defined, and \(X\) be a nonnegative random variable, then \[
\hat{E}(X) = \int_\Omega X(\omega) \, d\hat{P}(\omega) = \int_\Omega X(\omega) Z(\omega) \, dP(\omega) = E(ZX).
\] if \(Z\) is a.s. stricly positive, then \[
E(X) = \hat{E}\Big(\frac{X}{Z}\Big) \qquad \text{for all nonnegative R.V. } X.
\]
Next, defines the meaning of equivalent between \(P\) and \(\hat{P}\)
Def. let \(P\) & \(\hat{P}\) be two prob-meas on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F})\), \(P\) & \(\hat{P}\) are said equivalent if they agree which set in \(\mathcal{F}\) have probability zero.
Remark:
In finance, the model has a sample space, where all possible future scenario lies. The probability measure for the event can be estimated through empirical data in real world, or in the price of derivatives securities. a risk-neutral measure \(\hat{P}\). The risk netural measure helps to solve the equation. though \(\hat{P}\) assign different prob to price paths, the equivalent property make sure that a hedging strategy works a.s. in \(\hat{P}\) will also work in \(P\)
Notice that from the fact \[
\int_\Omega X(\omega) \, d\hat{P}(\omega) = \int_\Omega X(\omega) Z(\omega) \, dP(\omega) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \int_\Omega Y(\omega) \, dP(\omega) = \int_\Omega \frac{Y(\omega)}{Z(\omega)} \, d\hat{P}(\omega)
\] we can “regard” \(Z(\omega) = \dfrac{d\hat{P}(\omega)}{dP(\omega)}\) as in regular calculous, as a somehow “ratio of probability”. \(Z(\omega)\) is refered as Radon-Nikodym derivative.

\(P\) & \(\hat{P}\) defined in Th are equivalent

title: 22  Risk-Neutral Pricing
text:
22.2 Risk-Neutral Measure
Next, we perform similar change of measure. for the process. on \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and filtration \(\mathcal{F}_t\), defined on \(0 \leq t \leq T\). let \(Z\) be the a.s. positive R.V. with \(E(Z) = 1\) and \(\hat{P}\) defined above. Then can define Radon-Nikodym derivative process as follow \[
Z_t := E(Z \mid \mathcal{F}_t)
\]
Coll \(Z_t\) is a martingle
proof: let \(t > s \in [0,T]\), and \[
E(Z_t \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = E\big((E(Z \mid \mathcal{F}_t)) \mid \mathcal{F}_s\big) = E(Z \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = Z_s.
\]
lemma: let \(t \in [0,T]\) and \(Y\) is \(\mathcal{F}_t\) measurable, then \(\hat{E} Y = E(Y Z_t)\)
proof: \(\hat{E} Y = E(YZ) = E[E(YZ \mid \mathcal{F}_t)] = E(Y E(Z \mid \mathcal{F}_t)) = E(Y Z_t)\)
lemma: let \(s, t\) satisfy \(0 \leq s \leq t \leq T\) and \(Y\) be a \(\mathcal{F}_t\) measurable R.V. then \[
\hat{E}(Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = \frac{1}{Z(s)} E(Y Z(t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s)
\]
proof: \(\frac{1}{Z(s)} E(Y Z(t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s)\) is \(\mathcal{F}_s\) measurable, to show that it equal to conditional expectation, we need. \[
\int_A \hat{E}(Y \mid \mathcal{F}_s) \, d\hat{P} = \int_A \frac{1}{Z(s)} E(Y Z(t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s) \, d\hat{P} = \int_A Y \, d\hat{P} \qquad \forall A \in \mathcal{F}_s
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
\int_A \frac{1}{Z(s)} E(Y Z(t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s) \, d\hat{P} &= \hat{E}\Big(\mathbf{1}_A \frac{1}{Z(s)} E(Y Z(t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s)\Big) \\
&= E\big(\mathbf{1}_A E(Y Z(t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s)\big) = E\big(E(\mathbf{1}_A Y Z(t) \mid \mathcal{F}_s)\big) \\
&= E(\mathbf{1}_A Y Z(t)) = \hat{E}(\mathbf{1}_A Y) = \int_A Y \, d\hat{P}. \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]

22.3 Change of measure for 1D Brownian motion
Th (change of measure for 1D BM) Let \((W_t)_{0 \leq t \leq T}\) be a BM on a probability space \((\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)\) and \((\mathcal{F}_t)_{0 \leq t \leq T}\) be its filtration, and \((\Theta_t)_{0 \leq t \leq T}\) be another adapted process to this filtration, then define \[
Z_t = \exp\Big(-\int_0^t \Theta_u \, dW_u - \tfrac12 \int_0^t \Theta_u^2 \, du\Big)
\] \[
\widetilde{W}_t = W_t + \int_0^t \Theta_u \, du
\] assuming \[
E\Big(\int_0^T \Theta_u^2 Z_u^2 \, du\Big) < \infty
\] Then, we have \(E(Z_T) = 1\) and \(\widetilde{W}_t\) is BM under \(\hat{P}\) defined above.

22.4 Stock under risk-neutral measure
consider a stock price \(S_t\) described by \[
dS_t = \alpha_t S_t \, dt + G_t S_t \, dW_t, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq T
\] or in the integration form \[
S_t = S_0 \exp\Big(\int_0^t G_u \, dW_u + \int_0^t (\alpha_u - \tfrac12 G_u^2) \, du\Big)
\] now consider an interest rate process \(R(t)\) and defines the discount process as \(D_t = e^{-\int_0^t R_u \, du}\). \(\implies dP_t = -P_t R_t \, dt\)

Discounted stock price. \[
D_t S_t = S_0 \exp\Big(\int_0^t G_u \, dW_u + \int_0^t (\alpha_u - \tfrac12 G_u^2 - R_u) \, du\Big)
\] \[
\begin{aligned}
d(P_t S_t) &= S_t \, dP_t + P_t \, dS_t + dS_t \, dP_t = -S_t P_t R_t \, dt + P_t(\alpha_t S_t \, dt + G_t S_t \, dW_t) \\
&= P_t S_t(\alpha_t - R_t) \, dt + G_t S_t D_t \, dW_t = G_t S_t P_t(\Theta_t \, dt + dW_t)
\end{aligned}
\] where \(\Theta_t = \dfrac{\alpha_t - R_t}{G_t}\) is the market price of risk.
Remark: for discounted stock price. the mean rate of return of the stock reduce while the volatility remains the same.
now we consider the discounted price in the prob measure \(\hat{P}\) defined in theorem with \(\Theta_t\) used the market price of risk. then \[
d(D_t S_t) = G_t D_t S_t \, d\widetilde{W}_t \iff D_t S_t = S_0 + \int_0^t G_u P_u S_u \, d\widetilde{W}_u.
\] and thus the discounted Stock price is martingle under this measure. The new probability measure is called Risk-Neutral measure.
Stock price under risk-neutral measure. \[
dW_t = -\Theta_t \, dt + d\widetilde{W}_t \implies dS_t = R_t S_t \, dt + G_t S_t \, d\widetilde{W}_t.
